The following suggestion, which is perfectly trii.e, will be ; real with interest :—An army chaplain, being asked for a ' Suitable text for a tombstone to the men of a regiment who died in Egypt during the late war, suggested, "Egypt was glad at their departing, to they were afraid of them." To float in with the tide is, undoubtedly, very pleasant ; but He who hath infinite wiedoue has decreed that the re. ward shall ever be commensurate with the effort. Where- fere, be who battles successfully against adverse ways, though he lie for a time exhausted upon the sands, experi-1 ences a sense of satisfaction to which the simple pleasure of , the former is as a tiny brook to the broad ocean. A ROTHSCHILD STORY.—The fellowing is told of one of the Retbschilde—be of Frankfort :—Oarne the Baron von. G. into the office of the great banker. "Take a chair, sir," said he, not even raising his head from his writing. "Sir !" said G.; " why, sir? I am, like yourself, a baron of the Empire, and I think should be addre3sed as each." "A I thousand perdons !" replied Rothschild; "a baron of the; Emelre ? Teen take two chairs until I can attend to you." 1 How Meeeneett fUItiNGOISUED A BORE —Macaulay used to tell the following story of an incident which hap- pened to him during his residence in India. He arrived late one night, desperately tired, at the bungalow of the chap. lain of an out-of-the-way station, and, having supped' ESA desirous of getting to bed as soon as possible. But his host, haying got hold of a "lion," was determined to make the most of him. He at once mounted his favourite hobby, and 1 stopping his Inpatient guest, who in vain tried to escape, I said, in a tone of great solemeity, "Mr. Macaulay, I posi- tively cannot let you retire until you state your opinion as to the number of the Beast in the Revelation." To confess ignoranTe would have ruined his reputation for omniscience, and perhaps have exposed him to the risk of a lengthy ex• position. "I was driven into a corner," Macaulay would say, in telling the story, and answered on the spot, "I have no doubt as to what was foreshadowed by the mystical num. bet (686) —the British House of Commons; the members elected, 658; the threg clerks at the table, the sergeant-at. arms and the deputy-sergeant, the librarian, and the two doorkeepers making the exact number, 666 -" and rushed to my couch, leaving my host dazed and bewildered as mach at the promptitude and volubility of my reply, as at the startling novelty of the theory it contained.—London Society.

BESTV;G PAPA.—A man of considerable property and a great lover of field sports, living in the county of West. math, had a daughter who found the country very dull, and asked her father to take a house and live in Dublin. Tnis he declined to do. and went on with his field sports as usual. He was beloved by his neighbours, but one fine morning he received a threatening letter. He thought no more of it, but in a few days he received another, and soon afterwards another, and at last one came bearing a drawing of a coffin. The gentleman then became alarmed, and sent for the stipendiary magistrate. The magistrate inspected the letters and put himself in communication with Dublin Castle. A number of detectives were sent down, and domi- cilia-y visits were made at the houses of all the poor people in tee neighbourhood. Nothing, however, could be dis- covered, but still the threatening letters poured in, until at last the gentleman became alarmed and moved to Dublin. His dau4hter—a very beautiful girl—was shortly after- wards married to the man of her choice. When the wed- ding breakfast was over, and the young peoplo were about to leave, the daughter threw her arms round her fatherie neck, and said, "Go back to the country, father; no one will touch a hair of your head ; everybody loves you. I am the person who wrote the threatening letters and de- lineated your coffin. I wanted to come to town, finding the country 83 dull, and, as you would not come, I thought I would adopt the Riband scheme, and it succeeded."

Mn. RrSICIN TO YOUNG LADIES.—D) you want to be better dressed than your schoolfellows? Some of them are probably poor, and cannot afford to dress like you; or, on the other hand, you. may— be poor yourself, and may be moat- &d at their being dressed better than you. Put an end to all thata'at Once by resolving to go down into the deep depths your. girl o heart, where you will find inlaid by Christ's own hand a better thiag than vanity —pity. And be sure Of this, thlt although in a truly Christian land every young girl w.eild be dressed beautifully anel delightfully, in this ent re'y heathen and Baal-wors6ipping land of ours not one girl in ten has either decent or healthy clothing; and that you have no business now to wear anything fine yourself, but are bound to use your full strength and resources to dress as many of your neighbours as you can. What of fine dress your people insist upon your wearing take, and wear proudly and prettily for their sakes; but, so far as in YOU lies, be sure that every day you are labouring to clothe some poorer ere stares And if you cannot Olathe, at least help with your hands. You can make your own bed, wash your own place, brighten your own furniture—if nothing else. "Bat that'd servants' work ?" Of course It is. What business have you to hope to be better than a servant of servants? "God made you a lady ? " Yes; Ho has put you, that is to say, in a position in which you may learn to speak your own language beautifully; to be accurately acquainted with the elements of other languages; to behave with grace, tact, and sympathy to all around you; to know the history of your country, the commands of its religion, and the duties of its race. If you obey His will in learning these things, you will obtain the power of becoming a true " lady ;" and you will become one if, while you learn these things, you set yourself, with all the strength of your youth and women- hood, to serve His servants, until the day come when He to say " Well, done, good and faitttfal servant; t, ter tl.ou into the joy of thy 1.,,n1"

"Dear me !" exclaimed the old lady, "what wonderful improvements they do make. Now, in my younger dart, they just made a hole; at each end and sucked." He came home its the wee sma' hours, and his loving spouse confronted him with wrath in her eye and a telegram In her hand, saying," Here's news has been waiting for you since sapper time." He blinked, looked wise, sued, bracing up against the hat rack, felt through his pockets, murmur- ing, "I ghleft my glasses down town." "Yes," she replied, with scathing irony, "but you brought their contents with you !" And the bedroom door was slammed. Nothing is ever lost by being pleasant and agreeable. Yen aek for two pounds of steak—no more, no lees. Gee butcher growls that he can't cut off just two pounds, and you leave him, thoroughly vexed. At the next stall the man of meat:hears your request with unruffled visage, cuts off a pound and a half, slaps it into the scale and out again In double-quick time, rolls it up neatly, and says, with a sweet smile,'" Just two pounds, ma'am." He is- the man who succeeds. A rather aeedy.looking customer enters a well-known Turkish bath establishment, where the emplov el view him with alarm and apprehension, make him wait an uncon- scionably long time, and serve him with a damp towel. He takes all their spurns uncomplainingly, and when he de. parts he gives the attendant half.a-crown. Stupefaction and regret of the employes, who, when next the seedy cus- tomer appears, neglect all the other bathers to anticipate his every want. On going out he graciously tips them two coppers. Renewed surprise and stupefaction of the atten- dants. " Gentlemen," said the seedy customer blandly, "the two coppers are for your services yesterday. The hell crown I gave you then was for what you have done to-day."

"Lam going to send my boy to have his picture takes," said a druggist to a photographer. "Think you can get along without me ?" "Well, I should say so," was the cenfideat rejoinder. "I'm not so sure of that. You'll find h'm 4 teug,h customer to manage: however," he added re- flectiy, -Iy, "I can put the directions on the bottle," and he bale ,:he puzzled photographer good day. In due time the drug ; iet'e son, a mischievous youngster, visited the photo- graph gallery, and the artist found him indeed hard to man- age. He exhausted all the known devices for keeping the boy quiet, and invented a host of new ones, but in vain ; finally, he remembered the apothecary's odd remark about the directions, and upon inspection of the boy he discovered pasted upon the back of his neck the legend—" To be well shaken before taken." Acting at once and vigorously upon the suggestion, he succeeded in intimidating the boy and obtainiag a picture. REPARTEE AND BATHOS IN THE SETPREMN COURT.—The Sanreme Court is a bad place for a pretentious display of legal learning, or a flourish of oratory. The most success- ful advocates who practise at its bar are those whose style is most c mdensed and lucid, and who never travel away from the essential matter in controversy. They no doubt remember the anecdote of Chief Jastice Marshall--an anecdote, by the way, which has been tacked on to many emineet judges, bat which Marshall's biographers claim as belonging to him. A pompons and tedious advocate was reheariing well known and undisputed rules of law, when the Chief Justice interrupted him, and Faid, " Mr. think this is unnecessary. There are some things which a eerirt, constituted as this is, may be presumed* to know." Not always, even in recent times, however, have the lawyers confined their speeches to the clarified common sense and direct logic which judges like to hear. Now and then the court is forced to listen to flights of rhetoric which bring half etmaeed and half-impatient looks to the faces of the Pas- tices. Here, for example, is a specimen of florid eloquence with which, not many years ago, a lawyer opened his brief in am important writ of error case. The brief is still shown as a curiosity in the office of the clerk of the court:— " May it please the court: When the bonnie blue flag' went down before the star-spangled banner,' and that glorious emblem of the Union, the Constitution, andlthe Enforcement of the Laws' again waved in triumph From Maine's dark pines and crags of snow To where magnolian breezes blow, It was fondly hoped that civil strife and contention were at an end, and that peace, quiet, and repose had returned to bless tbe land. But there were Hopes which but allured to fly; they were, indeed, but Joys that vanished whilst we sipped. For scarcely had the roar of artillery ceased and the smoke of battle cleared off, and scarcely had the ink become dry on the parchmenta of pardon which fell from the executive hand, Thick as autumnal leaves that strew the brooks In Vallambrosa, before some _ _

Of the last few, who, vainly brave, and who would, theoretically merely, Die for the cause they could not save, rushed into the courts, renewed the contest in another form, and we are here to-day on a writ of error to the Supreme Court of Louisiana to reverse a victory obtained in this new mode of hostility and attack upon the power and authority at the United States, and the rights of one which are firmly based upon the same."—E. V. Smalley, in the Century. Excactsz.—What would you think of a man who—hie family physician having ordered him a dozen quinine and iron pills, the box being 'labelled "One twice a day " should swallow the whole lot on Monday morning to save time, and keep him whole and strong for the six days to come? But as regards exercise, thousands of people are constantly making the same foolish and ridiculous mistake. —"I have a day off on Tuesday," says one; " go in for a regular constitutional." And accordingly on the Tuesday he starts, and walks until he is ready to drop; then perhaps takes a stimulant and goes on again. He feels rather tired and sleepy, not to say stupifi, on Wednesday morning; but he sincerely believes, for all that, that his long walk has done him good.—" Well, now," says another, "Saturday is a half-holiday. I shall mount my 'cycle, and do my little sixty; for the weather has been so queer of late that I haven't been astride far a month." The very fact of his not having been astride for a month should warn him not to take violent exercise so recklessly, for from disuse the muscles get flabby and the tendons slack. The tendons, I may remark parenthetic thy, may be likened to the great leather belts that stretch from one broad wheel to another in the machinery of a mill and transmit the power. What would you think of an engine-driver who would attempt to do a big day's work with slackened belts ?—" My liver wants stirring up a bit," says gentleman number three ; "I have not been on horseback for weeks, bat I'll do a glorious ride 'erns country to-morrow, and come home as fresh as a lark." He does not come home as fresh as a lark though, nor any- thing like it, albeit he has "stirred his liver up." Why, it is perfectly ridiculous the way some people talk about their livers, especially city men—l speak advisedly. That poor ill-used organ is used anyhow all the week, and shaken up for all the world as if it were a bundle of hay on Saturday or Sunday. It would be amusing to think of were it not so sad. It trate me in mind of a remark that an Irish woman, Biddy O'Flagherty,made to me the other day.—" You don't make your bed often enough, Biddy," I said.—" Troth, indade, sort," she replied, "I don't make it moren onct a month, but I gives a rale shakin' up then, sorr."—Cassell's Magazine.

GAMBETi'A AS A JOURNALlST.—Gambetta's chief fault was an irrepressible restlessness, which be carried into every- thing. He could prepare a large, fine plan of political ac- tion, and wait natie.ntly for its accomplishment as wnole ; but, meanwhile, he would meddle and muddle with the de- tails. Instances of this can be furnished from his doings as conductor of the Republique Francais. He wrote often for that paper and sometimes sent in to the printer articles re- markable for their statesman-like views, but, in the very same issue to which he had contributed some leader that was intended to conciliate a particular politician or faction, he would suddenly shoot in a paragraph tending to quite a contrary effect. M. Challemel-Laconr and M. Isambert, who were successively editors of the journal, had a dread of him when he strolled into the editorial room with a bundle of the winning's papers under his arm, and proceeded to read, as he called it. He would do this on idle days, when the Chambers were not sitting, and when he could treat himself to the relaxation of performing as much work as would have fatigued a sub-editor. His reading would be Interrupted by violent snorts, and, catching up a sheet of paper, he would scrawl off twenty lines which seemed to splutter fire like crackers. No topic was beneath his notice, and no enemy was too small for his shot. By his para- graphs he frequently did mischief which it took his cold, cautious fellow-workers days to repair. Gambetta was not a good writer. The best of his articles read like written I speeches, and were turgid; many of them, too, were of in- ordinate length. He used to come In powerfully excited after a great debate and saw, "I shall want about half-a- column to-night," and, sitting down, be would begin to cover page after page with his close, cramped handwriting. For so impetuous a man he wrote a curiously stiff hand, and, though his fingers moved fast, their motion was feverish and spasmodical. It could never be said of him that he "dashed off" any of his effuelone •, he rather jerked them off, swaying the upper part of his body ponderously to and fro as he wrote, and now and then collecting his thoughts by passing his large left hand rapidly through his hair. Black coffee would be brought him, and he would go on writing; then he would call for a bottle of Burgundy and gulp down two or three glasses, munching sweet biscuits afterwards, or else sticks of chocolate in lieu of dinner. The editor, who had been makingeallowances for half a column, would see Gambette's article overflow one column after another, washing away all other articles and notes, till it , spread like an inundation over the entire front page of the ' I paper. Then with a hearty " Ouf," the French exclama- \ then of relief, he would throw down his pen and say, " Tnere, I think those few lines will state our case plainly: what! do they really run to five columns? Saerebteu! it seemed to me as if I had only been writing ten minutes !" and upon this he would break into a laugh that resounded teeovoune ent hri ol Irne ,ew workohfo l oh Gsaatd.mbbetlettnt a p,visuol ! all over the office, and partly dispelled the gloom of his wul ilnrdigt iwnn gur yt. fdaouc ees forwata tssbeteehieeditor ettioor laugh at the exaggerated developments of his articles once they had appeared in print; but when they were going to Press he showed a nervous impatience of correction, and a sort of puerile vanity in repeating that "every hyphen and comma" had its importance.—Mentories of Leon Gambetta, in the Cornhtll Magazine for February. It is said that all of the eighty or more Verm3nt dairy- men who have tried the ensilage system, some for three years, are well pleased it with without exception. Plank I rAther than stone silos are the rule.

Tne farm of Esbie, Dumfriesshire, on the property of the Rev. Mr. Gardner, has been let on a fifteen years' lease to Mr. M'Noe Barbush, at an annual rent of £290. Six years ago it was tenanted at 450 a year. • A. S. Downing, who was one of the best horticulturists America has ever known, said, "If I were to preach a sermon on horticulture, I should say, ' Stir the Soil.' Frequent and deep stirring will enaide one to grow fine vegetables on com- paratively poor and slightly manured soil, while without it one fails to gain the proper advantage, even from the richest and finest soil."

CABBAGE Wonars.—Secretary Shaffer, of the lowa Agri- cultural Society, says the cabbage worms have destroyed whole fields and acres of cabbages, and the remedies of lime, ashes, brine, salt, and lye have been failures. Birds do not take them, and hens and chickens tied among the plants, which were previously covered with meal, never touched a worm, or drove away the swarms of butterflies, which were so numerous as to appear like a snowstorm. But the use of pyretham was attended with entire success. A pound of lee leaves of this plant, mixed with 150 gallons of water. killed every young worm with which it came in contact, while it is harmless to man.

Place the neck of the bottle within the lips on the left side of the face, between the teeth and cheek, and poor small quantities into the mouth, not giving any more until the preceding has been swallowed. Some dogs are rather obstinate in taking medicine and will hold it some time before swallowing, when if more be put in it will let part ran out. With a little patience and by keeping the head elevated, he will soon swallow, and this patience mast be freely exercised. Another way of giving liquid medicines is by means of capsules, and this we prefer to any other plan, and as simple to manage as is a pill or bolus. As these capsules are now obtainable filled with almost every kind of medicine necessary to the dog keeper, it will be seen that they are very valuahle indeed. The most nauseous medicines can be administered without the dog tasting them—a very decided advantage—and there is no doubt of it getting the dose. PIGEONS.—THE BARB.—The Barb is a variety of pigeons which ianot very striking at first, but improves consider- ably on further acquaintance. Some varieties attract the attention at once, either by some peculiarity of shape. grace- fulness of carriage, or beauty of plumage, but none of these can he claimed for the Barb; in fact, it is somewhat lumpy and clumsy-looking at first, but on a close inspection shows points which make it most attractive to any lover of feathered pets. It is not, however, very commonly kept. Although at first only a toy pigeon, the modern develop- ment of its properties has made it so difficult to breed a first- class show specimen, that it is now looked ripen as one of the "high-class" varieties. It has been said that there are fewer good Barbs than good Carriers, bat we are somewhat disposed to doubt this assertion. The chief points of the Barb are the head properties, for the bird is a wattled one. A good notion of the ideal may be got from an old-fashioned reel of cotton, a little unwound. The eye wattles represent the two projecting ends or rims of the reel, the middle part of which roughly represents the skull of the bird. Of course it is to be desired that these wattles should be as smooth and round as possible, free from spouts or square projections. They should be thick and bright red. Then the head itself should be round and equal in width behind and before, thus preserving the idea of the cotton reel. The beak is desired as thick and as short as possible, especially the lower mandible, and having a downward inclination, but not as:much as is sometimes seen—the result of pressure when [the bird is young. The colour should always be white, but this is difficult to get, and dark or .smoky beaks are very common. Above is the beak-wattle, which should be of a moderate—size, just filling up the indention that would otherwise be found between the beak and skull, and thus making the conformation of the head, including the beak, perfectly symmetrical. If this wattle is large then the appearance of the bird is very greatly spoiled. The neck of tqe Barb should be short, and the legs the same, the latter giving to the bird in walking a waddling gait, not by any means graceful. And, as to size, the question can scarcely be decided by any measurement,bat it is decidedly a small bird; this, however, is of small consequence so long as the head of the bird appears large in proportion to the body. It must be the most prominent part of the whole. The colours shown are red, yellow, black, dun, and white, the last of which is the rarest. All the colours should have white or" pearl" eyes, excepting whites, the eyes of which are nearly always black. Tan Aatfmaium.—One of the pleasantest household re- creations is in the keeping of a small aquarium, which, in one form or another, is within the reach of almost everyone, and if cheapness is to be considered, a few shil logs judi- ciously spent will be sufficient to fit up a case and stock it, or if something more elaborate is wanted, there need scarcely be any limit to the cost. And the pleasures of watching this little world in miniature, and of caring for the fish therein, will not only be a pleasure, but at the same time suggest much as to the wonderful things to be found in the realm of nature. And in addition a neat and well kept aquarium is an attractive furnishing to any room, filling in a vacant space, or ornamenting the window. In order, therefore, to assist our readers in forming and managing one of these, we prOpose to give directions for the same in our notes. It is not sufficient to do as has been too often done in the past, namely, procure a glass bowl, place in it a few fish, and when they die, which they will in a short time from want of natural food, give the thing up in despair. To support animal life, certain natural operations mast be car- ried on, and on the proper provision for these, succese will depend. If a gold fish he placed in a globe of water, it will at first glide comfortably round, about half way between the surface and the bottom, but after a few hours it will be- come languid, get nearer to the surface, and ultimately raise its mouth out of the water, as if gasping for breeth— a sure sign that the water does not furnish it with what is required for its comfort. No animal can exist without air, and fish need a supply of oxygen, which is the gaseous ele- ment in air that supports life, as much as anything living on land. Animals give off by respiratian a poisonous gas, called carbonic acid, which must by some means be disposed of, or it impregnates the surrounding air or water and causes death. Thus, in a plain bowl of water, the fish die because the water has become exhausted of its oxygen, and, therefore, in order to make an aquarium self-supporting, it is necessary to supply air or oxygen, and absorb the car- bonic acid gas. Following nature's own instrnction book, we find that this is done by vegetable growth, and hence the necessity of having vegetation in the bowl, and as far as possible of the same kind as would be found were the fish In their natural state. How this can be done we shall en- deavour to show in succeeding notes. BREEDING OF FOREIGN BIRDS.—The great difficulty experienced in getting fresh importations of these birds lies in the fact that our summer is their winter, and this not only occasions a spring moult, but is apt to throw them into an entire moult just when they ought to be pairing. This cannot be helped, but with a little careful study of their habits even the current of nature may be turned off its channel. By the time they have been in the country two or three seasons the moulting season falls later and later every year, so that in time the birds will accustom themselves to the customs here found. Young birds, hatched in this country, moult and breed naturally at the proper season, and, therefore, when obtain- able these are to be preferred to newly imported ones. If the stump of a small decayed tree can be obtained that will make the beat nesting place when hollowed out, with an aperture in the side by which the birds can get in and out. But if that cannot be obtained, the outer bruit of the cocoa nut will do equally as well, if a hole be bored in the upper ' part of it, as closely as possible to resemble nature. The birds will require plenty of sand, mixed with a little lime, and it does not matter whether this be from the sand hill or sea shore. Nest materials will be needed and the usual egg mixture, and then it may be hoped that in due time parental instincts will be developed, the nests built, the eggs laid, and finally, let us hope, the youngsters hatched.

A meeting of the Nairnshire Society for the Destruction of Rooks and Pigeons was held at Nairn on Friday, Mr. Anderson, of Lochdhu, presiding. The secretary reported that the total number of crows killed last year was 5,000, and pigeons 1,000. After paying a penny per bird the society had a balance of £2O in hand. Mr. Jose, secretary of the Farming Society, said he must admit that there were more crows about Cawdor this year than he had ever seen before. Several other farmers expressed the opinion that the number killed had made no appreciable diminution in the number of crows. It was agreed to carry on the opera. tions of the society for another year, each farmer to assess himself at the rate of 23. 61 per plough.

A Meavnamus POTATO has been introduced into France by M. Ohrond, a naval surgeon, who discovered it in a sandy island at the month of the Rio de la Plata. According to Le Fermier it will give two crops every year in a fairly wtrm climate, which practically would amount to a perma- nent crop. M. Blanchard has experimented with it at Brest, and has found it capable of amelioration, the result of care- ul attention being a potato about the size of a hen's egg ; and M..Langier, of the Museum of Natural History at Paris, having analysed the Ohrond potato, has found it entirely to consist of starch, very compact, and therefore of great weight relatively to its size. It is found also to be healthy and able to withstand a little frost, and mature very quickly, as it can be taken up about two months after planting. In a report by Peofessof Brewer to the American Associa- tion for the Advancement of science, ills pointed out that from a number of observations it seems to be a rule that black, brown, and particularly bay horses have very com- monly one or more white feet—that is, a white belt of hair, forming a ring just around the hoof, which may or may not share in the white colour. More hsrses have white feet on the left side than on the right. The right fors foot is the one least Glen marked, while the left hind foot is most fre• quently marked. The order of frequency for the four feet is left hind, right hind, left fore, and right fore feet. Some combinations of foot-markings are very rare. A bay horse with a white right fore foot only, or with both fore feet white, is so uncommon as to be of great value in legal iden- tidcation. The majority of horses spotted on the body have more white on the left than on the right side, and when the horse is mach spotted the largest area of white is on the left side of the animal.

A FASHIONABLII DAIRYMAID'S DISASTER.—Among the brilliant coterie of beauties that surrounded the Prince of Wales at Brighton in the early part of the present century was Lady Haggerstone, whose charms had at first sight at- tracted the admiration of the amorous Fierizel. But not content with the general admiration which his Royal High- ness was disposed to grant to all pretty women, her ladyship was ambitious to completely captivate the heart of the Heir- Apparent. Accordingly a fête champare was announced to come ,stY at her pretty little villa near the Spa, and her ladyship was determined to charm the Prince by assuming a rustic dress that would have satisfied the taste of a Watteau. At her residence she had a miniature farmyard, and three pretty little Alderneys. When the Prince with his friends and attendants arrived, the fair hostess came forward from a side wicket, dressed as a milkmaid, for the purpose of making a syllabub for the Prince. She had a silver pail in one hand and an ornamental stool in the other. Thus equipped she tripped along, with ribbons flying from her dainty little milking-hat, that hung on one side of her graceful head, and the smallest little apron tied below her laced stomacher, till she came opposite his Royal Highness, to whom she dropped a carefully studied, bewitching rustic curtsy. Then passing lightly over the beautifully-plaited straw, her tucked•up gown showing her neat ankle as well as her coloured stockings, she placed her stool and pail con- veniently for use. Leaning against the flank of one of the CIOSSeBt-looking of the Alderneve, she was about to begin her pretty task; bat, not relishing this new and strange companion, the animal at once commenced kicking out, up- setting stool, pail, and milkmaid, and then trotting coolly away. Lady Haggerstone rose, covered with confusion, and beat a hasty retreat into her little dairy, whence she did not emerge again that day.—London Society.

SECURITY FOR TENEdiTS' CAPITAL.—A QUEER QUE6TION BY Mx. Warrees.—At a meeLing of the Newbury Chamber of Agriculture, Mr. John Walter, M.P., is reported to have spoken thus:—" They heard much talk now about what se- curity the tenant was to have for the investment of his capi- tal. That was the phrase now; it was in every mouth; they read it in the Mark Lane Express. Now, he would travel 500 miles if anyone would tell him how the capital he had invested in his land was to be secure. He wanted to know what royal road there was for the security of capital in any business whatever. If a farmer said "I want to lay out £3OO in chalking my land, and I want security for that," that was all very well; but that was not what the werde in general nse implied. When a tenant invested his capital he did it subject to all the risks which any other man incurred in laying out his capital. Suppose he himself laid out a large sum of money in raising 200 or 309 acres of wheat. What Act of Parliament would secure him against the loss of it? No ; these losses were inseparable from all the con- ditions of trade, and farmers had no more right to expect 1 that they would be exempt from the risks incidental to 1 every business whatever." It is only fair to Mr. Walter to , regard this as a rhetorical trick, as no-One would insult him by supposing that he is so lacking in intelligence as not to know whet is meant by security for tenants' capital. The phrase has invariably been used to imply security against confiscation for capital invested by tenants in the improve- ment of their holdings, so that no one has been deceived by a brevity used to avoid awkward repetitions. Mr. Walter might as readily object, when he hears a:Doan talkiog about insuring his life, that he would travel five hundred miles if anyone would tell him how he could insure himself against death. No one in the world, as far as I know, has ever been I so absurd as to ask that a tenant should be secured against the ordinary risks of business.—Mark Lane Express. CHEESE MAKING.—A writer, who must be accepted as well Informed, tells us of a danger threatening cheese. Under the ensilage system, he says, the land which sustains the 15,000,000 mulch cowa now in the country will sustain 50,000,000, but producers of batter and cheese need not be troubled, for the room for export is almost boundless. Within the past five years the extension of what is known as the creamery system has improved the average quality of butter 25 to 50 per cent., the home consumption has in- creased in proportion as the masses get good butter, and people who were before accustomed to good butter eat more of it, in consequence of getting a better article. The factory system in cheese making first appeared in 1857, in Herkimer County. In this State, which is the chief seat of the cheese Industry, now 150 cheese factories are running, and over 3,000 are also running in the United States. The chief drawback has been poor quality, that is skimmed-milk cheese. This has been sold at from one.fourth to three-fourths the price of fullemilk cheese, according to the extent of the skimming, but it has disgusted those who eat it, and has created an indiscriminating prejudice against cheese. The skimmed article is asserted to be unfit for food, and although 50,000,000 to 60,000,000 lbs. of it are made annually in the United States, and although the product of fine butter has been increased, this has been at the expense of the cheese I interest, injuring home consumption and export demand both. In order to attain cheap production of butter, the I skimmed milk must be put to use, and under proper condi- tions it can be made into a fine cheese, whereby 25,000,000 I dohs. to 35,000,000 dole. may be saved to the farmers of this county annually, even on the present number of cows, and the public supplied with an excellent article. This desirable , stroke of economy is to be effected "by the substitution of 1 pure sweet animal or vegetable oil for the cream taken from the milk," and used to make butter. A simple machine is ; used, consisting of a fixed vertically-placed cylinder, within which another snugly-fitting cylinder is revolved at a high speed. Two vats, containing respectively sweet skimmed milk and pare sweet vegetable or animal oil, each heated to 130 degrees, discharge their contents into the cylinder, at ; the uniform rate of two parts milk to one part oil; ,the two I are discharged into a receptacle below as a "pure, rich, per- feet cream." Each globule of milk is coated with oil within ' the cylinder—we should naturally state it thus, but the I writer whom we are quoting says that each globule of oil is coated with milk. This artificial product, in the propor- tion of nibs. to the 1001bs., is introduced into milk which I has been skimmed 24 and 36 hours, and the process of cheese I making is then the same as the regular one. The artificial ' cream "sours the same as natural cream,and can be churned into butter likewise producing a fine quality." So broad an assertion may seem questionable, and 'if the natural cream first removed for butter making can be thus replaced by a , substitnte equally good, the question at once arises whether the artificial cream, so long as it is the cheaper, cannot be substituted for the natural in butter making as well. This practical age, it may be supposed, will finally put down qualmish scruples, and will not care, if the actual fine butter is only got, whether it is got from cream or from old India- rubbers.—New York Times.

CANARY LOSING FEATHERS. - Ta.king advantage of your offer of information respecting canaries. kc I should be mush obliged if you would tell me of any remedy for the falling off of the feathers when the bird is not in moult. My bird (a hen) has lost nearly all its feathers from the shoulders to the crown, and as it is a great pet I should like it eured.-11. 11, Warring- ton. _ _ .

This may arise from two causes. In the first place, it may result from keeping the bird in too warm a place, which thus brings on a false moult; or it may be produced by too stimu- lating food, in which case the remedy is not far to .3eak. If the latter, give only canary seed and plenty of green food, and if the former put in a cool—not cold—room; or, on the o her hand, it may be caused by the presence of insects or parasites in the feathers, which causes the bird to pluck its feathers. If you suspect thia latter as the cause,get some concentrated solu- tion of quassia, of which put two or three table spoonsful in the bath water, and see that the bird gets a good soaking with it; then put the cage in a moderately warm place and cover it over with a white cloth The insects will come on to the cloth. and if left in this way over night can be killed next morning, Any raw places should be rubbed with a little raseliee or gly- cerine to allay the irritation —Amt.

After the officials of a town had vainly endeavoured to disperse a mob, a minister mounted a box and made the simple announcement, "A collection will now be made." The result can be easily guessed. A jockey lord met his old college tutor at a great horse fair. " Ah, doctor," exclaimed the jockey," what brings you here among these high-bred cattle? Do you think you can distinguish a horse from an ass?" "My lord," replied the tutor, "I soon perceived you among those horses." Johnny came home from school the other day very Much excited. "What do you think, pa, Joe Steward, one of the big boys, had an argument with the teacher about a question in grammar." "What position did Joe take?" " His last position was across a chair, with his face down." A gentleman, observing a servant-girl who was left- handed placing the knives and forks on the dinner-table in the same awkward position, remarked to her that she was laying them left-handed. "Oh, indeed," said she, "so I 'have! Be pleased, sir, to help me to turn the table round !" This is authentic: The chaplain of a station in the Pon- jaub was asked recently what action he intended to assume towards a detachment of the Salvation Army about to take up its quarters in a neighbouring city. His reply was characteristic. " Oh, to to show I b?ar them no professional I intend to ',save a turd at thA mess."

Gowran Castle, Kilkenny, was an ancient seat of the Butlers, which was besieged in the Irish Wars of the Com- monwealth, and, with the surrounding lands, was granted to Ireton, then Lord Deputy. It did not revert to Ormonde at the Restoration, but was granted, with other forfeited estates of the regicides, to James, Duke of York, from whose trustees it was purchased by a certain Charles Agar. The Agars are said to have been a Huguenot family, who escaped from France in timo of persecution, and settled in York- shire. How Charles Agar was able to buy this extensive estate I know not, but it must be remembered that Irish lands were very cheap in those days. Not very long after another Yorkshire adventurer, a certain Sir William Ellis, went over to Ireland, and became secretary to Tyrconnel. Sir William had a brother, Welbore Ellis by name who also went over to Ireland, and, being in Holy Orders,-obtained the Bishopric of Meath. The Bishop ultimately became the heir of his brother, the Secretary, and the grandson of Charles Agar married the only daughter of the Bishop. The eldest son of this marriage, after having held lucrative offices in Ireland, was created Viscount Clifden in 1781. The second son was a Commissioner of Custlms ; the third was created Earl of Norrnanton, of whom I shall have ntore to say hereafter.

The Bishop of Meath had a son, also named Welbore Ellis. The father, being only a poor Bishop, had his son educated free of expense, first of all as a King's scholar at West- minster, and afterwards at Christ Church, Oxford. Wel- bore soon entered Parliament, and for many years held highly-paid offices, as a Lord of the Admiralty, Vice- Treasurer of Ireland, Secretary at War, Treasurer of the Navy, and Colonial Secretary. The only distinguished services which I can discover that he rendered to his country were that he strenuously opposed any concessions to the American colonists, and that he moved the committal of Lord Mayor Crosby to the Tower for daring to maintain the freedom of the Press against a tyrannical House of Commons. He was the " Grildrig" of Junius, who describes him as a little mannikin and the most contemptible creature in the world, who, whether he made or suppressed a motion, was equally sure of disgrace. Even Lord Stanhope ,speaks of him as "a man who was ridiculed for his diminutive stature, not in him redeemed by any loftiness of mind." Nevertheless he appears during the many years in*hich he held office to have amassed a large fortune. Having gone over to Pitt in 1793, he was rewarded the following year with an English peerage, under the title of Baron Mendip. As he left no issue, his title and fortune passed to his great-nephew, the second Viscount Clifden.

This nobleman, by the way, was one of those Irish borwgh-mongers who rqceived bribes at the passing of the Act of Union in the shape of compensation for the loss of their patronage. Almost ever since the Agars obtained possession of Gowran they had possessed two seats for the borough of-that name in the Irish Parliament. One of them usually occupied one of the seats, and, judging by the number of offices they obtained, it must have been quite a mine of wealth to them. When the Act of Union passed Viscount Clifden received £15,000 for the extinction of his pocket borough. With this comfortable sum in ham', coupled with his placeman great-uncle's fortune, it need not surprise us that soon after he appears as a considorable pur- chaser of. land in England. About 1830, Viscount Clifden purchased the manor and estate of Lenborough, in Bucking- hamshire, and the still larger estate of Holdenby, in Nor- thamptonshire, came into his hands in the same manner. Floldenby, the ancient seat of the Hattons, was purchased by James 1., who gave it to his son Charles, with whose later history its name will always be associated. It was confiscated and sold during the Commonwealth, but at the Restoration Charles 11. resumed possession of it. He appears to have granted it to • his brother James, Duke of York, who in turn gave it to a French officer, whom he created Earl; of Feversham. Feversham's representative sold it to the Duke of Marlborough, in whose family it remained till the third Duke sold it to Viscount Clifden, who had married his eldest daughter. This nobleman held the office of Clerk of the Privy Council in Ireland, a sinecure with £1,450 a year. At this period the Agar- Ellises were steady and consistent Whigs, being staunch advocates of Catholic Emancipation and Paeliamentary Reform. The eldest son of the second Viscount Clifden was created a peer of the United Kingdom, With the title of Baron Dover, in the lifetime of his father, whom be pre- deceased. His grandson, the present holder of the title, is a minor.

I have previously mentioned that a younger brother of the first Viscount Clifden was created Earl of Normanton. Many of my readers have unconsciously trodden upon his tombstone on entering the door at the north transept of Westminster Abbey, and in the fourth bay of the north aisle of that Abbey they may see his monument. It is a sommhat curious production. There is a representation in bas-relief of the new Protestant Cathedral at Cashel, which his lordship was instrumental in building. There is a figure, too, of the Earl, in full canonicals, handing to another clergyman an open book, on which are the words, "Be not weary in well-doing"—a maxirn'which he certainly did not lose sight of, especially when; we remember the Apostolic dictum that " He that desires the office of a bishop desireth a good thing." The sculptor has also introduced two or three forlorn Irish beggars to indicate the prelate's kindly disposition. But the most remarkable feature of the monument is a little cherub putting a mitre upon his lordship's head. As the Yankee editor said, when he received a poem describing how the angels laid a new- born baby on the young mother's lap, "That may be very good poetry; but it's not the road such things usually come in this world." Leaving the realms of imagination, and coming down to plain facts, Charles Agar, having taken Holy Orders, was so fortunate as to be appointed Chaplain to the Lord Lieutenant; and soon after the first piece of preferment fell to him, in the shape of the Deamery of Kilmore. When about thirty years of age, he was elevated to the Bishopric of Cloyne ; and, about ten years after, to the Archbishopric of Cashel. In 1801 he was translated to the Archbishopric of Dublin, and he lived on till 1809. He had an eye to temporal well as spiritual dignities, for he was successively created a Baron, a Viscount, and an Earl. I cannot discover that either he, or his son, or his grandson, married rich heiresses; so I must couclude that the greater part of the landed possessions of the Earl of Normanton were derived from the savings of the Arch- bishop and his heir. As the first Lord Norrnanton was a Prelate of the Irish Church for nearly forty years, he had ample opportunities of saving a considerable sum; and I believe his son achieved yet greater things by studious frugality. However that may be, the present Earl of Normanton, whose grandfather was only the younger son of an Irish commoner, now owns no less than 37,336 acres of land n half-a-dozen English andlrish counties, with a rent-roll of £41,011.

ST. JOHN'S CHURCH CHOIR CONCERT AT THE VIADUCT INSTI- TUTE.—A concert was given by the members of the choir of St. John's Church, Earlestown, in the Viaduct Institute, on Monday evening, in aid of what is known as the choir fund. The concert was a decided success so far as the number of those present was concerned, the attendance being a very large and appreciative one. Most of the selections were given with much taste and expression, and the audience manifested their appreciation by hearty and tapturous ap- plause. The glees by the choir under the - leader- ship of Mr. Durman were excellently rendered. The concert opened with the glee "May day" (Muller), following which was the song "Under the old flag" (Godfrey Marks), by Mr. Wright. It was enthusiastically encored, after which Mrs. Dewse pretty fairly acquitted herself in the song " Tara's Hall " (Moore.) The glee, "The anvil" (Adolphe Adams), by the male voices was greeted with much applause, and the beating-in-time of an anvil in an ante-room added much to the interest excited by it. Miss E. Lewis sang "Guardian angels" (G. Adel- mann), and Messrs. Lewis, Durman, and Wills gave the trio "She will, she won't," which was most excellently rendered, and created the utmost enthusiasm, an encore being demanded, but it was not responded to. Mr. Durman then sang "The little hero" (Stephen Adams) with much expression, after which the Misses Lewis very nicely gave the duet " Hope and Springtime" (Franz Abt.) Mr. W. Wills sang Benedict's song " The forging of the anchor," and the choir having given the glee "The Forester" (Elizabeth Stirling), the first part of the programme was brought to a close. The second part was resumed with the glee " Here in cool grot and mossy cell " ( Lord Mornington), which was beautifully rendered. It was followed by the song "The brave old tar" (J. Pridham), by Mr. J. Squire, who received a de- served encore, and responded with "The bo's'n's mate." Miss M. E. Jackson sang Behrend's "Firelight fancies." She possesses a sweet voice, though rather weak, and the song was excellently given. "Children of the sun " (James Battye), sung as a glee by the choir, was followed by Mr. J. White singing the well-known song " Death of Nelson " (Braham). This piece was about the most successful of the evening, and Mr. White received a well-earned recall. He thereupon gave "The anchor's weighed' in excellent style. Mr. George Wright's song "Jack's reward" (Barn) which followed, was also rapturously encored, and he responded with "Rocked in the cradle of the deep." The catch, "Celia's charms" (Webb), by Messrs. Lewis, Wills, Dar- man, and Millard, caused much amusement, and the song, 1 "Laugh while You may " (Grazia), by Miss M. L. Lewis, was des,,rvediv encored, and the last verse was repeated. The choir thn gave the glee "Lullaby " (Hatton) and the concert couc:uded with the singing of the National.Anthein.

div.head: •THE STATE OF IRELAND.
div.p: •THE STATE OF IRELAND.

THE CONSPIRACY ro MURDER OFFICIALS. ASTOUNDING REVELATIONS. Evidence of the highest importance was given on Saturday in the Fenian conspiracy case, which came on before two magistrates at Kilmainhatn gaol. The particular charge gone into was nothing less grave than that of the murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. T. H. Burke, in Phcenix Park, on the 6th May last, and the prisoners placed in the dock were James Carey, Peter Carey, Joseph Brady, Timothy Kelly, Lawrence Hanlon, Edward O'Brien, Edward M'Caffrey, and Peter Doyle. James Carey is a Dublin city councillor. The first witness called was John Fitmimems, described es a very intelligent old man, whose personal appearance bespoke a position of respectability. He had occupied a room as tenant to James Carey, and he deposed to having seen that prisoner visit a loft above it in which shortly after the murder witness found under a heap of rubbish a rifle and two knives. Later, he said, when lames Carey had been arrested under the Coercion Act, his wife and son, together with Peter Carey and a stranger, came to Se place, and all but Mrs. Carey went up into the loft, and then they went away. The knives, which were now produced, were surgical instru- ments, corresponding with the description of the knives used in the assassination of Lord Frederick and Mr. Burke, and one of them bore marks of blood. After Fitzsimons had handed the weapons to the police, Mrs. James Carey, Peter Carey,.ani the wife of the latter visited his premises. The question whether they asked him if the police bad been there was objected to by the counsel for the defence, and it was not pressed. Fitzsimons was followed in the witness box by a chairmaker named Hands, an Englishman, who deposed to seeing four men lying on the grass, faces downwards, near the Phoenix column on the evening of the murder. He only saw the face of one man, and he identified the prisoner Edward O'Brien as the man. The four men were a short distance from the pathway, and on the other side of the walk there lay four other men, in exactly the same posture. A few yards further on he saw a horse and car, and standing beside it was the prisoner Joseph Brady. The wife of Hands, who was with him at the time, also identified Edward O'Brien as the onlk man whose face was visible, and she too identified Joseph Brady as the cardriver, who was further identified by George Godden, an assistant at the deerkeepers' lodge as the driver of a car having five men on it which he saw rapidly driven through the park on the evening of the 6th of May, and who recognised in the prisoner Edward M'Caffrey one of the four men whom he saw standing by a clump of trees close by where the car was. The inquiry was resumed on Monday. At the outset Joseph Brady, Timothy Kelly, and Myles Kavanagh were placed in the dock charged with the attempt on the life of Mr. Field, in Frederick-street, Dublin, on the night of the 27th November, and evidence was given by h servant girl to show that Myles Kavanagh was the driver of the car em- ployed on that eccasion. There was then placed in thu dock besides these three Prisoners James Carey, Peter Carey, Jas. Mullett, Joseph Mullett, and Patrick Whelan, and the eight men—four of them being men who were not so charged on Saturday were charged with the murder of Lord Frederick Cavendish and Mr. Burke. A Mr. Devlin deposed to haying in March, 1877, let to James Carey a large room in Peter-street, Dublin, •which he said he wanted for a reading-room or a lecture-room. Another witness gave evidence of this room having been used as a meeting place by about 50 or 60 men, and stated that a man stood at the door, and if witnesshappened to pass through the yard in that direction this man tapped at the door or kicked with his heel. James Carey was there almost every Sunday, and witness had heard the persons visiting the room say they were waiting for him. Witness used to see Joseph Brady there'. A Mr. Winter gave evidence that five years ago he let a hall in Prussia-street to one Patrick Whelan (whom he could not recognise as any of the pri- soners) and a man named Cullen. He re- ceived back possession a year and ten months since. Police - Inspector Marshall described the finding, in December, 1881, of a quantity of arms, ammuni- tion, dynamite, Sze., including a dozen hand grenades, in • premises in Brabazen-street and Cross Keven-strest. At the latter place, Whelan's address, there was found a book which contained some entries relating to dealings in arms and to the affairs of the Fenian organisation. This seizure, according to the statement of the counsel for the prosecu- tion, was made on information by a man named Riley, who in February last was mysteriously murdered in Skipper's Alley. Evi'lence of the arrest of Joseph Mullett and the _discovery of certain arms and documents at his home had been opened, when, on the application of the Crown counsel, the prisoners, along with the 13 other men in custody, were remanded till next Saturday. THE PIKENIX PARK MURDERS.

The Crown authorities on Wednesday morning accepted the evidence of one of the three prisoners charged with the assassination of Detective Cox, in Abbey-street, Dublin. 'This man, it is believed, is Devine, and the counsel engaged to defend him has received notice that he will not be wanted. The evidence of this last informer will be of a very startling character, and will still further open out ths murder con- spiracy. It is believed that be will identify some of the prisoners now in custody as the principals in various assas- sinations, and will corroborate the important testimony of the independent witness at last Saturday's investigation.

div.head: MURDER OF A DUBLIN CONSTABLE
div.p: THE MURDER OF A DUBLIN CONSTABLE

The man Dowling, one of the armed party with whom a number of Dublin police officers came into collision on a night in November, with the result that one of the constables, named Cox, was shot dead, was put on his trial in Dublin, on Thursday, before Mr. Justice Harrison. The prisoner was not charged with the capital offence, there being, it is said, considerable doubt on the question whether tht fatal shot came from the prisoner's party or from that of the con- stables, the men being engaged at close quarters. He was charged with shooting at Cox with iritent to murder, and on this indictment be was found guilty. The extreme sentence was passed—penal servitude for life.
ARREST- OF MESSRS DAVITT,- HEALY, AND
QUINN.

On Thursday morning, at 10 o'clock, Messrs. Davitt, Healy, and Quinn were arrested under the warrants issued by the Queen's Bench. A detective called at the Imperial Hotel, Dublin, for Mr. Davitt, who drove with the officer to Kilmainham Gaol. The warrants in the cases of Messrs. Healy and Quinn were executed similarly at their resi- dences. After partaking of breakfast each gentleman was conveyed in a cab to Kilmainham prison, escorted by a detective. There was no demonstration in either case.
It appears from statistics just issued that during last year there was an increase in the sayings deposited in joint- stock banks'in Ireland of more than two millions and a half sterling.
The Duchess of Marlborough has decided to devote the balance of £3,000 from the relief fund started by her Grace in 1871 to the purpose of assisting the poor people to emigrate. _ _

A—fund has been opened in County Wicklow for present- ing Mr. Parnell with a testimonial. At a meeting of the Avoca branch of the National League it was decided that it should be a handsome one, and: :nore than adequate to clear off the inherited mortgage on his estate. In the Dublin Bankruptcy Court, on Tuesday, the tenant right in a farm of about 20 acres in the county Down, the rent of which is abont Ll an acre, sold for £l,lOO, or about £52 an acre. The landlord's interest in an estate in county Roscommon was put up for sale in the Landed Estates Court, but there were no bidders. Two officers of a convict prison, with a man in custody, went to London on Tuesday, and took their charge to the Treasury Offices, where he was examined by the solicitors of that department for over an hour, when he was conveyed back under the same surveillance to the convict prison. It is stated that most important evidence with reference to the alleged secret societies in Ireland has been offered to and accepted by the Treasury. A return of all agrarian crimes in Ireland reported during January appears in Tuesday night's Dublin. Gazette. The total number is 90, of which 58 are cases of threatening letters or notices, and nine cases of other intimidation. There has been one murder in county Leitrim, one con- spiracy to murder in North Tipperary, four incendiary fires, five cases of taking and holding forcible possession, three cases of killing or maiming cattle, and one attack on a horse.

DEATH OF COLONEL TAYLOR M.P.—Colonel Taylor, senior member for county Dublin, at his residence, Bal- ., brlggan, Dublin, on Saturday afternoon in his 71st year. The deceased gentleman had held office under the Conserva- tive Administration as a Lord of the Treasury and Chan- cellor of the Duchy of Lancaster. He had represented county Dublin since 1841. In consequence of the sad event the annual banquet of the Dublin ponstitutional Club, fixed for Tuesday, was abandoned. Mr. Davitt was on Wednesday waited upon by a represen- tative of the Press Association. To give bail to be of good behaviour to Irish landlordism was, he said, an impossible thing. He looked forward with certainty to the overthrow of land monopoly, and he expected in a few years after the enfranchisement of the industrial classes to see the land re- cognised as national property. No other settlement of the land question would meet the exigencies of the impending social upheavals.

NARROW ESCAPE FROM DROWNING IN THE CANAL.— On Sunday afternoon last, a lad named Arthur Howarth, nine years of age, residing in Earle-street, narrowly escaped being drowned. It appears that about four o'clock a number of lads were playing on the canal bank near the viaduct, when Howarth fell into the water, and but for a man named Smith, who jumped into the canal and rescued him, would probably have been drowned. PRESENTATION TO A RETIRED MANAGER AT NEWTON.— A very pleasant meeting took place at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, on Friday evening last, when a presentation was made to Mr. Wm. Aitken, sem, manager of the machine printing department at the woks of Messrs. Geo. McCor- quodale and Co., who is retiring after 35 years' services. Mr. Aitken has endeared himself to antis fellow workmen. Together they subscribed a handsome sum of money, and to show their respect for him they presented him with a pair of gold spectacles, enclosed in a handsome silver case, along with a purse of gold. The case bore the following inscription :—" Presented to William Aitken as a mark of esteem by the employes of McCarnuodale and Co.. on his retirement after 35 years faithful service. Newton-le-Wil- lows, 15th December, 1882." Mr. P. Grace presided over the proceedings, and the presentation was made on behalf the men by Mr. Shaw, one of the oldest employes in that department of the works. The gift was acknowledged in appropriate terms. There were also present at the gather- ing represenfatilis from each of the other departments in connection wit. WOOKQ. The evening was afterwards spent in a very enjoyable manner.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 10, 1883.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 10, 1883.
MISCELLANEOUS.

Mr. Gladstone was on Tuesday a sbectator At the cele- bration of the carnival of Nice, returning to Cannes in the evening. The prosecution at Leeds Assizes of a surgeon named 1 Noake and a woman named Hudson on a charge of murder ended on Tuesday in a verdict of acquittal. The Dublin magistrates on Tuesday committed for trial a young gentleman named Butler, who, under pretence of visiting a lady who is a distant relative of his, went into the drawing-room, and, it is alleged, carried away rings and jewellery valued at £lOO. At a meeting of the Swinford Board of Guardians, on Tuesday, it was announced that the Duchess of Marlborough - had decided to devote the balance of £3,000 from the re- lief fend started by her Grace in 1871 to the purpose of assisting poor people to emigrate. A SINGULAR SHROVE TUESDAY CUSTOM.—A singular CRS- torn was observed at Nuneaton oti Tuesday, namely, that of playing football in the public streets of the town. Most of the tradesmen put up their shutters at noon, and the game was continued until nightfall. The town has been canvassed for subscriptions to defray the cost of repairing any windows that may be broken during the continuance of the play. Tem NEW PRIMATE—The arrangements for the cere- mony in connection with the enthronisation of the new Primate at Canterbury Cathedral are nearly complete. The Archbishop will arrive the day previous, and is expected to remain the guest of the Dean of Canterbury several days. In addition to the reopening of Thanington Church, when his Grace will deliver a sermon, it is proposed to hold a levee. Several bishops have signified their intention of being present at the enthronisation, admission to witness which, both as regards clergy and laity, will be by ticket. The clergy of the diocese will wear their surplices and hoods. ALLEGED NEGLECT OF SIGNALS OF DISTRESS. An inquiry was held at Springvale, near Rvde on Tuesday, on the bodies of Charles Warne, captain of the Snowdrop, the maee Richards, and three seamen, who were washed ashore at Sea-view since Friday night last, when the Snowdrop is supposed to have driven ashore. It appeared that a police- constable had seen from high ground inland rockets and lights, but the coastguard observed no signals. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidentally drowned," and requested the coroner to call the attention of the chief-officer of the Coastguard to the fact that signals of distress were not noticed by his men. MR. GLADSTONE'S MIDLOTHIAN SPEECHES. MORE TORY MISREPRESENTATIONS.—" A Middlesex Elector" writes to the Daily News :—" On Wednesday night; at a meeting of the Conservative electors ' at the Drill Hall, Crouch-end, I heard Mr. Littler, Q.C., repeat the statement that Mr. Gladstone, being ashamed of his Midlothian speeches, had suppressed the corrected reports, adding that he had himself applied at every bookseller's shop in London to obtain a copy, but had failed to do so. This morning I went into the first bookseller's I saw in Fleet-street, and at once bought a copy. Inquiring at the next bookseller's, in the same street, I found the speeches on sale there also." A CARGO OF DYNAMITE.—On Saturday two Hull smacks to-wed into that port the German brigantine Cato, of Blau- kense, disabled in the late storm- The vessel was moored in the Albert Dock. The Custom authorities were after- wards informed that the Cato had fifty tons of dynamite on board. Means were at once adopted to isolate her as much as possible whilst the authorities in London were commu- nicated with, and early on Tuesday morning she was towed into the Humber and anchored eight miles below Hull. When abandoned the master of the Cato said the vessel was loaded with stone, and from subsequent contradictions the theory is set up that the cargo was intended for Ire- land. LORD DERBY AND CYPRUS.—A. correspondent writes:— "A gooa deal ,of interest is felt as to what will be Lord Derby's management of Cyprus. It is there that the new Colonial Minister touches most nearly the circumstances of his past career. It is well known that Lord Derby does not like the possession which those circumstances have placed in his hands. It remains to be seen in the course of the summer what will be the attitude of the British Government to the Khedive when he is 'set on his legs.' The opinion prevails that the Government will not advise the immediate reconstruction of the fortresses of Alexandria, and that they will not place a force in Cyprus to watch over the peace of Egypt. The tribute of 00,000 a year which we pay to the Sultan for Cyprus stands much in the position of that of Egypt. But Lord Derby, it is thought, is so averse to any useless addition to the dominion of the Crown that he will not desire to reduce the deficit in the balance sheet by com- pounding with the Sultan. BREACH OF PROMISE CASE—KITCHEN COURTSHIPS.— In Dublin, on Friday, a lady's maid, named Torney, sued a gardener, named Cants, employed by Lady Gratton; for £250 damages for breach of promise to marry. Defendant broke off the match, alleging that the plaintiff was "courting the butler." Plaintiff indignantly denied that she proposed to the defendant, and added that she would not propose marriage to any man. She admitted writing; a letter to the defendant in reference to his charge of flirt- ing, in which she said she knew it was the wretched cook, who was madly in love with the butler herself, who had set the report aflcat. She declined to say whether she pre- tended to be flirting with the butler just to annoy the cook. The only plea for the defence was that no promise was made, but on being called into the witness box defendant admitted that he promised to marry the plaintiff. The Judge there- upon said it was only a question of damages, and the jury found a verdict for the plaintiff, with £25 damages. SERIOUS ACCIDENT ON BOARD A BRITISH IRONCLAD.—An accident occurred on Tuesday morning on board Her Majesty's ship Agincourt, which was lying in Plymouth Coaled. Signal was made from Devonport to the ships of the Channel Squadron to proceed to sea. Whilst the Agincourt was making preparations the foregallant mast broke off sheet at the cap. Three men who were on it were thrown offrand one alighted on an iron stanchion on the forecastle, the stanchion passed through his body and killing him. Another fell across the fprecastle bridge and was killed, whilst the third caught in the rigging and escaped with a shaking. One of the three men is named Gimlet, and lived at Devonport, and the second was an Irishman. Where the mast snapped off the wood was found tube completely rotten. The squadron is detained awaiting Admiralty instructions. At the inquest held in the afternoon Senior Lieutenant Gardiner, who witnessed the accident, stated that the mast was supplied from Devonport Dockyard a few days ago. He saw no defect in it now, although an expert might give a different opinion. No expert was called. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death." DOUBLE MURDER BY A GANG OF POACHERS.—NINE

Frederick Ripley, a labourer, was, on Monday, at Taun- ton, found guilty of deliberately murdering a paramour named Rowsell, and was duly sentenced to be hanged. At the Liverpool Assizes, on Tuesday, Hugh Calderbank, spinner, of Sharpies, near Bolton, who a few days ago Strangled his wife, was acquitted on the ground of insanity. Mr. Rothery, Wrecks Commissioner, on Monday sus- Winded for three months the certificate of the master of the emigrant ship Wild Deer, which was wrecked on the county Down coast a few weeks ago. A surprising change has taken place in the condition of Mr. Gladstone since he arrived at Cannes. His countrymen generally will be glad to learn that he "sleeps well, has a good appetite, and is enjoying himself immensely." A meeting of the Cabinet was held on Tuesday under the presidency of Earl Granville. The Earl of Derby took his seat for the first time in a Liberal Cabinet. Sir Charles Dilke and Earl Spencer were also present. At Forfar, on Monday, Hugh Townley, only 18 years of age, pleaded guilty to having two wives alive, and to lfaving committed perjury with a view to marrying a third. He was Sentenced to nine months' hard labour. It is now within two months of the end of the financial year, and the revenue receipts to 3rd February are only £660,000 more than up to the corresponding date last year The prospect of a surplus does not improve. In a letter to the Kincardineehire Farmers' Association, Mr. Gladstone says Her Majesty's Government are anxious to approach the question of land law reform prudently and at thee earliest period permitted by the state of public business. The Gorton shooting case came on at the Liverpool Assizes on Tuesday. The accused, Martin Henry O'Malley, was found guilty of shooting at the woman Arden and her brother, with intent to murder, and was sentenced to penal servitude for 20 years. On Monday George William Foote, the editor, William James Ramsay, the publisher, and Henry Arthur Kemp, the printer of the Freethinker, were committed for. trial on a charge of publishing a blasphemous libel in the Christmas number of that journal. The Daily News understands that if the Queen's Speech contains any reference to South Africa the Coeservative leaders intend in the debate on the Address to criticise very fully the policy of the Government in relation both to Zulu- land and to the Transvaal. The Address, in answer to the-Speech from the Throne on the meeting of Parliament will be moved by the Earl of Durham, and seconded by Lord Reay, in the House of Lords; and it will be moved by Chas.T. Dyke Acland, 111. P , and seconded by Mr. Thomas R. Buchanan, M.P., in the House of Commons. Mr. John Rowland Jones, a Birkenhead eurveyor and estate agent, was killed recently owing to the overturning of a tramcar, and at the Chester Assizes on Monday his repre- sentatives recovered from the Birkenhead Tramway Com- pany damages to the amount of £2,875. The accident was said to be due to the inefficiency of the brakes of the car. Mr. Justice Williams drew attention at the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday, to an irregularity which has marked the conduct of assize business for the last 30 years. He said it was one of his duties tie "deliver the goal," and in future the Governor must make out a list of his prisoners, and make arrangements for the production in Court of every untried prisoner then in custody. On Saturday Mr. H. Broadhurst, M.P., replying to the toast of "Trades Congress," given at the annual dinner of a London branch of the Amalgamated Union of Operative Bakers, said his belief was that it would be a fatal mistake for workmen to permit Parliament to give any vote that Would in the most remote sense have a tendency to upset our immunity from labour on one day in the seven. AN IscounrotheE WIFE BEATER.—At Buckingham, on Tuesday, a labourer named Benjamin Cox was sentenced to four tmenths' imprisonment for a murderous asault upon his Wife. A separation crder was also granted to the wife, and a weekly allowance of 3s on the termination of the sentence. Seven previous convictions were recorded against Cox, and on the last occasion he received three mouths' im- prisonment. He has been married three times. The Roman Catholic Archbishop of the Diocese of St. Andrews and Edinburgh has issued a pastoral letter on the Subject of secret societies. "It is hereby declared," he says, "that all who are enrolled, or shall enroll themselves in any Of these societies, whatever name they give themselves, fall under the censure of the Church, and, without any abso- lute reeunciation of the membership, are debarred from the use of the sacraments in life, and even at the hour of death." A STEAMER ON FIRE OFF GRAVESEND.—At 10 p.m. on Monday night the British India steamer Ethiopia was ob- served from the Custom House at Gravesend to be on fire. On vieiting the vessel the fire was found to be in the neigh- bourhood of the engine room. Two tugs were engaged play- ing on the ship, and by 5-30 on Tuesday morning the fire Was put out. The damage is said to be censiderable. The Ethiopia arrived at Gravesend on Monday evening from Eurrachee. BANKRUPTCY OF A LANCASHIRE Ex-M.P.--At London Bankruptcy Court, on Saturday, Mr. Registrar Brougham aPpointed a receiver in the failure of Mr. Montague Joseph Fielden, described as of The Cedars, Sunbury Bridge, Ham- mersmith, and the Reform Club, a lieutenant-colonel, whose debts are £25,000. The assets, amount unknown, consist of interests in patents and collieries and shares in -public ecnnPanies. His honour restrained creditors to the amount of over £22,000. The debtor was formerly M.P. for Black- burn. COMMITTAL OF A COLLIERY ENGINEER FOR MIN- SLAUGHTER.—On Tuesday evening, an adjourned irquiry was held at Wednesbury respecting the death of three miners who were killed at Willingsworth Colliery through the breaking of a rope. The evidence showed that, although Benjamin Banks, colliery engineer, knew the rope was de- fective, he allowed it to be tred for drawing men up the pit. Upon three men ascending the shaft the rope broke, and they fell and were killed. A verdict of manslaughter against Banks was returned.

A,,IKTRAORDINARY COLLIERY COMPLIC XTION.—A. curious wmculty has arisen in Neath Valley. Some scores of men 7orking in Gnoll Colliery suspended work because of al- leged percolation of water from old workings and apprehen- SlOllB of inundation, the workings having been flooded 80 Years since, and skeletons recently discovered in the pit. The Management summoned six of the men for ceasing work without justifiable cause, and the bench have fined them 103 4aCh. The men, however, at a mass meeting on Tuesday, again resolved not to resume work unless the manager or- dered boring, to obviate a possible flooding disaster. They !leelded to communicate with the Home Secretary. Work "at a complete standstill, and the matter has created great excitement in the district. THE NEW M.P. Hugo Richard Charteris, Lord Oche., nt Amisfield, Haddingtonshire, who has been elected in the Conservative interest to the seat vacated by his father, Francis Lord Etch°, on his accession to the Eerldom of Wemyss, was born in August, 1857, his mother being Lady Anne Frederica Anson, second daughter of Thomas William, first Earl of Lichfield. Lord Etch() was educated at Harrow and at Balliol College, Oxford, where he took a second class in modern history. He accompanied Mr. Bourke as assistant private secretary on his financial mission to Constantinople. Lord Elcho, who now enters Parliament for the first time, is the 73rd new member returned to St. Stephen's since the last general election. His return on the present occasion makes no difference in the balance of parties in the House. On Thursday mor fling, a decently dressed female called on Mrs. Fore:,ter, wife of the Vicar of St. John's, Wolver- hampton, and stating she and her family were in neces- sitous circumstances induced Mrs. Forester to purchase a piece of cloth off Ler for 255. A NOVEL CARGO.—The Hilda, just arrived from Mont- serrat, W. 1., has for almost her entire cargo lime juice. She brings no less than 464 pipes or nearly 50,000 gallons, the largest shipment on recerd. It is consigned to the sole con- signees of the Montserrat Company, Evans, Sons, axd Co., Liverpool. The temperance movement has caused a very largely increased demand for the Montserrat lime fruit juice and cordials. SUNDAY DRUNKENNESS IN ENGLAND AND WALES —By a Parliarnenta-:y return issued on Wednesday, it appears that between Michaelmas, 1881 and 1882, the number of persons arrested for drunkenness on Sunday, in England and Wales, was 15,921. Of thpse 15,612 were arrested in England, and and 3Q9 in Wales. Of the English arrests. 10,677 persons residel in the districts in which they were apprehended, and 4,935 were strangers. Of the Welsh persons arrested, 224 were residents, and 85 strangers. The steamer Kenmure Castle has foundered at sea. The vessel was bound from London to Shanghai, and passed down Channel on January 29. All the passengeis, with seven of the crew and the second officer, have been landed at Boulonge. The steamer Silksworth was wrecked at Sun- derland on Wednesday. The collier Clara has been wrecked at Carrickfergus, and five of the crew drowned. There was another gale On the east coast on Tuesday night, and several disasters to shipping, with some loss of life are reported. The Beaumaris schooner Savant nes wrecked at Crail, and the captain and one of the crew were drowned. The Board of Trade returns for the last month, issued onl Wednesday, sh)w that the total declared value of British and Irish exports for the month was £20,608,659, against £19,820,683 in January, 1882, and £17,318,911 in January, 1 1881. The total value of the imports for the month was £35,736,846, against £32,019,467 in the same month in 1882, and £26,742,962 in 1881. The bullion and specie account shows that the total value of gold and silver im- ported in January was £1,413,846, against £791,818 in January, 1882, and £990,343 in 1881. The total value of the gold and silver exported last month was £1,206,443, against £3,129,125 for the same month in 1882, and £2,051,528 in 1881. BRUTAL OUTRAGE BY BURGLARS : A POLICEMAN SERIOUSLY INJURED.—At an early hour on Thursday morn- ing a man was observed by Police-sergeant Lord trying to force an entrance into the shop of Mr. Simson Wood, Man- chester-road, Droylesden, near Manchester. The man, ob- serving the officer, made off, but was pursued by Lord, who overtook and arrested him, whereupon a second man CAMS round an adjacent corner and advanced to the burglar's assistance. A desperate struggle ensued, which ended in the sergeant, who is an elderly man, being thrown to the ground. He was then kicked about the lower parts of the body in a most brutal manner and left in a condition of un- consciousness. He was found in that state two hours later by another constable, lying on the footpath. He was at once removed and medical assistance called in, but he re- mains in a precarious state. He has been in the district for many years. Die neighbourhood has been scoured, but as yet no trace of the two men has been found.
