MEN IN CUSTODY.—A double murder was committed on

Saturday evening on the farm of Auchinleck, about two mike from Port Glasgow, the victims being Robert Fyfe, gamekeeper, and David M'Coughtrie, assistant-gamekeeper to Mr. Richard Richardson, of Ralston. Early in the evening a gang of poachers were observed on a hill behind Port Glasgow, several of whom had guns in their posses- sion. A number of shots were heard fired, but it was not until nine o'clock at night it was discoveied that there had been foul play. The body of Fyfe was found in a field close to a private road leading to the farm. He was lying on his face, and had a large-barrelled pistol firmly grasped in his right hand, with which he appeared to have been trying to defend himself. M'Coughtrie's body was discovered in a pool of blood. lie had been shot through the forehead. Nine well-known poachers are in custody, several of whom have ly:,en identified as those seen on the hill on the night of the murder. Fyfe, who was about forty-five years of age, leaves a widow and young family; IM`Coughtrie was about eighteen years of age. THE FARMERS' ALLIANCE.—The annual meeting of the Farmers' Alliance was held on Tuesday, in London, Mr. Jares Howard, president, in the chair. There was a large attendance, including Sir George Balfour, Bart., M.P., and Mr. S. Rowlandson. The report, which was adopted, stated that the Landlord and Tenant Bill, draftcd by the Alliance, was prevented from being read a second itime owing to factious opposition, but its influence upoepublic opinion was shown by the striking advance in the views which now so largely prevail on the subject of tenant-right. The com- mittee congratulated the members upon the steady progress towards the realisation of the association, and urged the organisation. A resolution was adopted thanking the -Government for the announcement made as to the intention of the Government to deal with the question of compensa- tion for agricultural tenants in the coming session, trusting that the proposed Bill would both ensure full security for repayment to the outgoing tenant of such unexhausted im- provements as have added to the letting value of the holding, and provide that the rent of sitting tenant shall not be raised on his own improvements, and expressing the .hope that the Bill will be passed this year. The annual dinner was held in the evening, Mr. G. Howard, M.P. presiling.

THE EESCFE OF ENGLISH 44 AHARs."—On Tuesday, Mr. Justice Chitty committed to Holloway Prison, for contempt of the order of the court, William Pritchard Jones, the father of William Jones, a lad who at one time formed one of the Beni Zoug-Zong Troupe of Arabs. The boy was rescued from a deplorable condition of servitude at Constan- tinople, where the troupe were acting, by Mr. Littler, Q.C., and placed in Dr. Barnardo's Home for Boys, baying pre- viously been made a ward of court. The father was ordered not to see or communicate with the lad until further orders, but within the hat two months he had made violent attempts to get poso.u.sion of his son. He was served with notice of motion for Tuesday, but did not appear, and his lordship committed him to prison for contempt. Later in the day the father appeared in court, and denied making any violent attempt to take his son away from Dr. Barnardo's Home. He met the boy, shook hands with him, and kiesed him. He now promised not to communicate with or kiss the boy again should he meet hirn.—His Lordship did not believe that a man who had sold his children into slavery would suddenly become so affectionate towards a lad of fifteen. Shaking hands and kissing would not have been such a breach of the court's order that hislordship would have sent him to prison. But he did not believe that was all the prisoner had done. His lordship, however, had no desire to be vindictive, and therefore counsel might apply for prisoner's release on Fri- day.—An order for instant committal was drawn up. Dr. Cooper, of Springfield, repeated the evidence pre- viously given to the magistrates, and said he had made a post-mortem examination of the body of the deceased on Friday afternoon. He was aceompanied by Dr. McLennan and his assistant. He examined the body externally, and found a dark appearance produced by the skin dronghing off the lower part of the spine. There was also a slight loss of skin over the curvature of one of the ribs. He considered that was caused by bed sores, through the deceased having lain for a very long time in one position. He opened the chest and the abdomen, and found the lungs, heart, liver, stomach, and bladder, and all the internal organs perfectly sound. He removed the scalp.* Over the bone on the left side he found an ulceration, which extended from the inner portion of the covering of the skull right through the entire scalp. It corresponded with the bruise on the temple. On the right side there was a discolouration inside corresponding to where the external bruise was in front of the ear. On opening the head he found a great quantity of lymph diffused over the surface of the brain. A great quantity of serum came from the brain when removed. The brain was highly inflamed. The cause of death was inflammation of the brain and membranes. He attributed these symptoms to violence of some sort. A blow from a stick would very likely cause the wound be saw on the left temple and the consequent inflammation. The deceased had also paralysis of the right arm, which might have been the result of violence. They could find no cause sufficient to account for it.—By Superintendent Barker: The wound on the left temple was a recent one.—The Foreman: The body was very much discoloured below the right shoulder.—Dr. Cooper: That is through lying a long time on her back. I dont think anything found on the back of the deceaaed arose from violence.—The prisoner had no questions to ask this witness. Inspector Barnett deposed to apprehending the prisoner at half-past three on Sunday afternoon. the 7th January. He told the prisoner that he had come to see what he had done at , his wife, and he said "I don't know." He (witness) cautioned the prisoner, and charged him with unlawfully wounding his wife, Margaret Percy, with intent to do he grievous bodily harm, by striking her about the head and other parts of the body with a walking stick, or some other weapon. He replied, "I never did that. I came into the house last night. She commenced calling me, and threw a chair at me, and whether I hit her or pushed her, and she fell over a chair or not, I cannot say, as I had rather too many glasses of drink. She has a very bad temper, and many a one would have killed her years ago.' Whilst in the house he (witness) found the walking stick produced in the front room near the clock. There was a similar one besides it, but the one produced seemed to have been more recently used. On the way to the station prisoner said," That's the stick I had with me." That (Saturday) morning he for- mally charged the prisoner that he did feloniously, wilfully, and with malice aforethought, kill and murder his wife, by striking her on the head. He replied, "That stick never hit her Mince it was a sfick."--The prisoner did not question the Inspector. Ihe Coroner said he was quite sure it was not necessary to address the jury at any length upon this painful case. They had given great attention to the case, which, unhap- pily, was too clear to admit of any doubt at all. Their first duty was to consider the cause of death, and with regard to that there was no reason to doubt the eVidence of Dr. Cooper. Death resulted from violence. The next :question was—How was that violence received ? Was it received accidentally? The wounds might have been caused by a fall, but there remained the spontaneous admission of the prisoners that he had the stick with him when the row took place, and having regard to that had they any reasonable doubt that the stick was the one which caused the injuries from whi'dli Mrs. Percy had died. If they thought so theta they must hold the prisoner respons- ible hi some degree at all events. He reviewed the evidence, and remarked that if the jury thought the violence was in- dicted by the prisoner, then the further question came, whether under the circumstances they would have to re- turn a verdict of wilful murder or manslaughter. The Coroner advised the jury on the matter, and said he could see nothing at all to justify them in returning a less ver- dict than wilful murder. It was a very painful case indeed, and rendered more so by the fact that the prisoner's own son was obliged to give evidence about the matter. In answer to the Coroner, the prisoner said he did not wish to make any statement at present. The jury then retired, and after the lapse of half an hour , returned into Court. , The Foreman said: We find that the prisoner is guilty of wilful murder. The Coroner: Is that the verdict of you all? The Foreman: That is the verdict of all, and the jury desire me to express that they think that the evidence of the prisoner's son has been very unsatisfactory all through this inquiry. ' The Coroner: I quite concur in the remark—most un- satisfactory to my mind. (To prisoner) Percy, the jury have returned a verdict of wilful murder, and I have,-there- fore, to commit you to the next assizes at Liverpool on that charge.

William Percy, a young fellow, said he was the son of William Percy, who was in custody. He resided with his father at Gorsey farm for about eight months "this last time." He had been frequently "on and off." He was at home on the 6th January. His father and mother were also there. He (witness) did not see any- thing, but he heard a few words passed. His mother spoke to his father about being away so long, and the latter told the former to mind her own business. He did not see his father strike his mother. He (witness) went out into the stable, where he remained about a quarter-of-an-hour. There was no one in the house besides his father and mother, after he and Roach went out. He (witness) re- turned home between seven and eight o'clock the following morning. He went into the stable and gave the horse some corn. He saw Margaret Roach standing in the yard; she ' came out of the shippon, he thought. His father was in the parlour at the time, but did not say
The prisoner was brought before Mr. Brock some time on Saturday evening, and remanded until Thursday.

The body of Mrs. Percy was interred in Farnworth Parish Churchyard on Monday afternoon, but it failed to call forth any of that morbid curiosity usually so prevalent on such occasions. The persons who followed the single mourning coach which conveyed the relatives of the deceased to the grave were few in number; owing, perhaps, to the distance of the spot from the town. Mrs. Whalley, the daughter, and the two sons of the deceased, were the chief mourners. The Rev. J. Holden read the burial service.

'1 RAD NOTES. The coalowners of tho counties of Fife and Clackmadnan have given their miners notice of a reduction of wages to the extent of eight per cent. A strike on a large sc:tle is threatened.

A threatened strike of colliers in North Wales to enforce the system of restricting the :output appears to have been abandoned. The majority of the men at most of the col- lieries resumed work on luesday morning. The executive of the Yorkshire Miners' Association has issued a notice to the members that all lodges of colliers in the West Riding shall seek an interview with the c,-)al- owners respecting a restriction of the output, and shall sub- mit reports to the adjourned conference at Barnsley. The strike of factory workers in Forfar terminated on Tuesday, when the last of the operatives resumed work. The rate of wages remains the same; and, not only so, but the operatives have forfeited two days' wages which they had earned before striking, and have, besides, lost a week's work.

BILLS OF SALE AND FAILUEES.—In the week ending Feb. 3, 1883,.there were 248 bills of sale in England and Wales. a decrease of 791 over those of the corresponding period last year; and the failures gazetted numbered 249, an in- crease of 41. The totals for portion of year to February 3, 1883, are—bills of sale registered for England and Wales, 1,212, a decrease of 3,685 ; the failures gazetted number 1,078, an increase of 34.—Stubb's Mercantile Gazette. WAGES DISPUTE AT SHEFFIELD.—The expectation of an amicable settlement of the wages dlspute in the Sheffield file trade has been disappointed. A meeting of the members of the File Cutters' Society was held on Monday, when the deputation appointed to wait upon the employers presented their report. The meeting, which was very largely attended, unanimously resolved that the demand for 10 per cent, re- duction was not warranted by the state of trade, and should be resisted. The forgers and grinders have passed similar resolutions.

- THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADB.—If anything a slightly better tone has been noticeable in the coal trade of this dis- trict during the past week. Since the commencement of the past month there has been a tendency in some cases to ease down in the price of the better qualities of round coal, and to move away quantities low figures are taken. It is, however, only in odd cases that there has been any actuary announced reduction of Hit rates, and the average prices at the:pit month may be given at about 10s. for best coals, 7s. ' 6d. to Se. for seconds, 63. to 7s. for common house fire coals, ss. 61 to 6s. for steam and forge caals, 4s. 6d. to ss. for burgy, and 3s. 6d. to 4s. per ton for good slack. The many complaints of a scarcity of orders for shipments still indi- cate a want of general activity in this branch of trade, hut many of the Lancashire collieries are doing fairly well with shipping orders, and the tendency seems to be towards im- provement. For good qualities of Lancashire shipping coal delivered at the high level, Liverpool, or the Garston docks 8.1. per ton is being obtained, but ordinary qualities are offered at 3d. to 6d. per ton under this figure.

Harriet Beasley, widow, 22, Cross-street, Widnes, who had nursed the deceased, having given evidence as to her death, Dr. Cooper gave evidence which will be found reported in the proceedings at the inquest. Mr. Swift: I believe, doctor, the first time you gave evidence you mentioned something about the deceased falling from the sofa ?—I might have said I was infornied that she had slipped off the sofa. Ido not remember that I got any information from anyone. Dr. McLennan said he assisted Dr. Cooper to make a post-mortem examination of the deceased on Friday, the 2nd instant, and his relation of that inquiry was in subst:nice a confirmation of the former gentleman's state- ment. Death was attributed to inflammation of the membranes of the +brain, probably arising from the external injuries on the left temple and the front of the right ear. Inspector Barnett deposed to apprehending the prisoner. Mr. Swift addressed ,the Bench, remarking that the only question which His Worship had to consider was whether he would commit -the prisoner on the charge of wilful murder or manslaughter, and he submitted with some confidence that this was clearly only a case of man- slaughter, assuming that the evidence for the prosecution was entirely correct. There were two points in the case which seemed to him to point to that view. One was that the whole of the son's evidence went to show that the prisoner was in a temper when he entered the house, that he was vexed apparently at his son, whom he threa- tened. He then went into tho parlour and did strike a blow at his wife, which might have caused her death, but neither of the witnesses stated that .the prisoner used any threat or violent language to his wife. They would not speak to threats of any sort, and there was nothing to show that the prisoner had any climinal intentions to- wards his wife. When the prisoner got Margaret Roach and his son outside, he evidently intended that they should remain out, for, as the former alleged, he placed 'a crowbar against the door. The deceased and the prisoner were apparently struggling together a quarter-of-an-hour, and this might be explained by the fact that the deceased was wishful to let Roach and her son in the house while the prisoner was wishful to keep them out. And at that time the prisoner had the gun in his hands, and if he had had any intentions towards his wife, could not he have mere easily used that than a crowbar four feet long? Looking at the evidence put before his worship it was perfectly clear that there was never more than one blow struck at the deceased, and when the doctors came to make the post mortem ex- amination there was only the mark of one blow—that seen by Roach and the son. It-did seem to him that this nT nothing more than a case of manslaughter, and just as it was his Worship's duty to commit the prisoner to the Assizes, so it was his duty, it seemed to him, to commit him, not on the serious charge of murder, but the less grave charge of manslaughter; and he (Mr. Swift) asked hun to do so.

IRONWORICERS' WAGES.—Alderman Avery, president of the South Staffordshire Mill and Forge Wages Board, pub- lished his award on Wednesday evening, directing that on and after April 2 wages shall be regulated by a sliding scale, that puidlers' wages shall be 9d. per ton in excess of is. for each pound sterling in selling price, that the sliding scale shall continue in operation for six months certain, and afterwards be determined by notice from either side ot one month, and that notwithstanding the award puddlers' wages shall not be less than 7s. 3d. per ton. TEE LANCASMRE IRON TRADE.—The iron trade of this district appears to be drifting towards a condition of general depression. On Tuesday the market was exceedingly fiat. with no parcels of any weight offering. For local brands of pig iron there are offers to a moderate extent. In district brands a few sales of Lincolnshire foundry qualities continue to be made, but otherwise there is very little doing. For delivery equal to Manchester quoted prices remain about as under :—Lancashire pi r iron, 46s Oct to 475; Lincolnshire, 46s to 48a; and Derbyshire, 488 6d to 50s, less 2. The finished iron trade is Exceedingly dull, and although makers still hold to about £6 7s 6d to £6 10 as their quoted rates for bars delivered into the Manchester .district, £6 51 is becoming a general figure at which orders could now be . placed._

WARRINGTON (14) —These clubs met for the first time this season, and had a pleasant and well-contested game. the result ending in a win for the visitors by one goal, two tries, four minor points to four Minor points. The home team, with a strong wind in their favour, set the ball in motion, but Helsby with a long kick quickly returned ,to the centre again, when the first VT immage was formed ; the game continued here until half time was called. On the resumption of hostilities the visitors began to assail the home team's quarters with vigour. Helsby kicked down field; Spencer, Potts, and Murray following up quickly rushed the leather over the line. Potts fallingbn the ball secured the try for the visitors. Vulcan dropped cut, and J. Williams follow- ing well up scored a try for the home team. 'Gilbert and Hough played well for the visitors in addition to those already named, and Poaches and Gooch for Vulcan. No side was called, 'he game ending is favour of the visit ws. Score—Wanderers, 1 try 5 minors, to 1 try 2 minors. LATCHFORD 3% MOSS RIDE (A TEAM). The above mate% was played on Saturday. on the ground of the latter. The Latchford captain won the toss, and decided to play agains t the wind. Mcss Sid kicked off, hut the ball was quickly returned by J. Baxter, and strong attempts were made to get in by Wrigley and Leigh, which were, however, frustrated. Ulti- mately Knowles obtained a try, which was not improved upon. During the second half of the game, the lime team playing with the wind, bad much the best of the game, and compelled their opponents to save. Buxton was prominent with a good run from mid-field, and on being collared close to the goal line he pissed to enother man, who succeeded in getting a try, which was not improved upon. Midgley, Knowles, and Lang- shaw played a cap4.tal game for Moss Side, as did Leigh, Green, and Buxton'(Wrigley M.F.O ) for Latchford. The game ended in a draw, both clubs scorings try each.

Stone, and Dr. Handvside.— k The Secretary (Mr. Dickson) read his annual report, which showed the club to be iu a very flourishing condition, there being on the books 316 ordinary members and 29 honorary members. The receipts for the past year, including a balance of £3O 15s 6d, were XlBB 17s 11d, and the egspendi- ture £163 16s id, o• leavin a balance to be carried forward of £5 is 10d. The report was adopted as read on the motion of Mr. Houghton, seconded by Mr. Shinn. Mr. Dickson regretted that, as tie now resided out of town, he could not devote as much time as he would wish to the business of the club, and he consequently felt compelled to decline to offer himself for re-election as secretary.—It was therefore pro- posed, seconded, and carried, that Mr. Isaac Bateman be , appointed secretary for the ensuing year.--The following were elected to servo on the Committee of Management : Messrs. B RADLAUGH. This 'At 4nd reported that the House tait.4l Ought, to prevent Mr. BRAD- th,'eeqllg ;through the form of o Le' t .ath but in order that he 3.°lia4„ 4d ms statutory rights determined doubt by a Court of Justice, recom-

mended that "should he again seek to make and subscribe the affirmation he be not pre- vented from so doing." Mr. BRADLAUGH accordingly affirmed at his peril, took his seat and voted, but he was proceeded against in the High Court for having done so without first subscribing the oath, and the decision of the judges being against him, his seat became vacant. But Mr. BRADLAUGH has been twice elected for Northampton since then—three times in all. His second election took place on the 9th April, 1881, and having been illegally prevented from sitting, he was ex- pelled from Parliament on the zznd February, 1382, because he insisted on complying with the law and taking the oath and his seat. Mr. BRADLAUGH'S third election was on the 2nd March, 1882, and on the 6th of the same month, without giving the hon. member thel opportunity of being heard, the House resolved that he should not be allowed to take the oath which the law requires him to take. The various scenes which have been enacted at intervals during the controversy j are altogether too painful to recapitulate; suffice it to say they have not added to the dignity of the House, and they are a standing discredit to the majority who provoked them. Mr. BRADLAUGH is now, therefore, in this position: He has been on three separate occasions elected for Northampton, his elec- tion is not impeached, and it is unimpeach- able. He is prepared to take the oath which the law says he must take before obtaining his seat, but the House declines to allow him; on the other hand the law holds he is not a person who can affirm. Moreover, a com- mittee of the House of Commons has said, "If the House of Commons prevent a duly- elected member from taking the oath or affirming. there is no power of reviewing or reversing that decision, however erroneous it may be in point of law." There does not , appear to be two opinions that the House has acted illegally, and its effect has been to , partially disfranchise the constituency which Mr. BRADLAUGH represents. The electors of Northampton have petitioned to be heard at the bar of the House in support of their claim to due representation by the voice and ' vote of two members, but no notice whatever has been taken of their petition. It will thus be seen that this is no longer a question affecting Mr. BRADLAUGH SO much as one affecting Northampton. The battle of Northampton to-day may be the battle of any other constituency to-morrow, and we should like to know whether the constituencies are prepared to submit to this? It may be, and is, a pity that this battle should be fought over a gentleman of Mr. BRADLAUGH'S un- popular religious tenets, but even this must not prevent us doing our utmost to win. It appears to us that it is the duty of every Liberal member to vote for Mr. BRADLAUGH'S admission to all the privileges of membership of the House whenever he presents himself, and on the other hand it is equally the duty of every Liberal constituency at any rate, whose memberdoes not so support Mr. BRADLAUGH, to take the first opportunity that offers of , sending him about his business. In crises such as these there is no place for weak-kneed Liberals, who, to gratify personal pique, would not mind surrendering the liberties for which their forefathers had many a tough fight.

THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 10, 1883.

WE have been perusing the return of deaths issued by authority of the registrar-general for the quarter ended December, 1882, and present our readers with a few extracts bearing upon the mortality of our immediate locality, which, we opine, will furnish food for reflection for our local governing bodies. It has often been urged that our highly concentrated chemicalised atmosphere secures us immunity from the severer forms of disease, but the return from which we quote chews that mortality in Runcorn and Widnes has been not only exceptionally high, but greatly in excess of the surrounding registration district. The population Of the Runcorn registration sub-district is 19,202, the number of deaths for the quarter just ended was 149, being 71 mole than the average of the three corresponding quarters previous. Of these 149 deaths 52 were of the zymotic or fever class ; 45 of which occurred in the Runcorn urban sanitary dis- trict, including 27 from measles, 6 from scarlet fever, and 4 from diphtheria. The total deaths from measles were 34, the other 7 occurring in the township of Weston. The Farnworth sub-registration district has a population of 27,679, the total deaths being 149, 27 more than the average of the three corresponding quarters previous. Of these 149 deaths 23 resulted from zymotic diseases, 22 of which occurred in Widnes urban sanitary district. Runcorn is stated as having the largest number of deaths from zymotic causes than any other Cheshire registration district. We do not cite the above information by way of drawing unfavour- able attention to either Widnes or Runcorn, but if these deaths are at all due to either insanitary conditions or want of pre- cautionary measures, we trust our references may lead our local authorities to institute, adopt, or enforce such regula- tions as may successfully cope with these diseases, and in great measure prevent their recurrence.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AIITHORITY.—The meeting of this Authority was held on Tuesday, at Dutton Work- house, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. The nuisance inspector (Mr. James Farrington) presented his re- port, which contained nothing of public interest. WIDNES LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.—The annual meeting will be held on Tuesday evening next, in Simm's Cross Board schools. • Mr. E. K. Muspratt will preside, and addresses will be delivered by Mr. E. R. Russell and Mr. C. Bosomworth. of Liverpool. RUNCORN AND THE SHIP CANAL.—We understand that a public meeting is being organised for the purpose of adopting a petition from the ratepayers praying that the standing orders of the House of Commons may be suspended with regard to the Ship Canal Bill. - - -

THE ENGLISH LAND SYSTEM. - Mr. Oliver Leak read a paper on the above subject before the msmbers of Runcorn Brunswick Mutual Improvement Class on Wednesday even- ing. He dealt with the subject in an able and comprehensive manner, and a vote of thanks was accorded him at the close.

Vesiorrisras.—A severe strain in put upon the Post Office in dealing with valentines which are trent in such large numbers. The Post Office does all in its power to en- sure the due despatch and delivery of correspondence at the valentine season; and it is hoped that the public will assist the department by posting their letters, ttc., early on Tues- day the 13th February Boy INJURED AT WIDNES.—John Doyle, ten years of age whose parents reside in Walmsley-street, was injured on the St. .Helens Railway, on Monday. The boy was passing the level crossing at Bradley footroad, when, in attempting to evade a passenger train, he came in contact with a goods train passing on the other line, and was knocked down. His hand was took off in a horrible manner. He is at the Accident Hospital, and, under the care of Dr. Cooper, is doing well. A DANGEROUS NEIGHBOURHOOD IN RUNCORN. On Monday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Edward Jones was summoned for keeping an unregistered lodging-house, in King-street.—Mr. C. Dutton, lodging-house inspector, proved the case, and Superintendent Williamson stated that the defendant lived in a very low neighbourhood, which was a source of much trouble to the police. It was not safe for any person, man or woman, to go down the street alone, as they would be sure to be maltreated in a shocking manner. —Defendant was fined £2, and costs Os 6d.

A BRUTAL DAUGHTER AT RUNCORN. - Before Mr. William Bankes and Mr. A. Thomas at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Hannah Brassendale, a woman about 30 years of age, was charged with assaulting her mother, Elizabeth Furnival.—Mrs. Furnival, who is an old woman with grey hair, said her daughter frequently got drunk, and when in that condition she was very violent, and sometimes illused her very much. About ten o'clock in the morning on the day in question the prisoner burst open the door of her house, and entering, seized the witness and acted in a very violent. manner. Her arms were yet black in the places where the prisoner had struck her.—The prisoner was also charged with being drunk and disorderly in Heath- mad, on the 4th February.—P.C. Thompson proved the case.—Mr. Bankes said the prisoner was no doubt a drunken, violent character, and had abused her mother in a shameful manner. She would be fined £1 and costs 10s. 6d., or, in default, 14 days' hard labour, for the assault; and for beinz drunk she would be mulcted in the further pena:ty cif 5!. and costs, with the alternative of seven days,

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 10, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 10, 1888.

THE BEGGING NUISANCE.—At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, Wm. Brown was committed to gaol for 14 days' hard labour for begging in Lowlands-road on the previous day. IVIDSES PARISH CHURCH ENTERTAINMENTS.—AI3Other Of the series of fortnightly entertainments was given on Tues- day evening, when an attractive and varied provramme was gone through. The Rev. W. H. Duggan presided. RUNCORN RATEPAYERS' ASSOCIATION.—The first quarterly meeting of the members of of this association was held in Bethesda schoolroom on Tuesday evening. Toe preeident, Mr. Coleman, occupied the chair. Mr. C. Cooke, the secre- tary, presented his report; and a general coaference took place on matters connected with local government. * FOOT AND Mount DISEASE.—This contagion con- tinues to spread in Lancashire. Extensions of the disease are reported from Padiham, Rochdale, and Blackburn in East Lancashire; Scarisbrick, Lathom' Rainhill, and Toxteth- park in West and South-West Lancashire; Bolton and Ashton-under-Lyne in South Lancashire; and Fleetwood, Elston, and Fulwood in North Lancashire. STAMPED ENVELOPES.—A Post Office announcement states that a cheaper class of stamped envelopes, called " Commercial Envelopes," are now sold to the public at the following prices :—One envelope, lid; two, 2±d; three, four, 41c1; five, 51d; ten, 10d; 20, is 9d; and 240, 21s. The exisiting B and D sizes will cease to be issued by the Controller of Stamps, Inland Revenue, when the present stocks are exhausted. PREVALENCE OF PERJURY IN LANCASHIRE.—At Liver- pool Assizes on Thursday, Mr. Justice Watkin. Williams, in sentencing John Pemberton, labourer, of Le,igh, to six months' imprisonment for perjury, said this offence was very prevalent in Lancashire, and the arm of the law was con- stantly in danger of being paralysed in maintaining the peace of the county. It was therefore necessary to read a lesson to people in the prisoner's class of life, to make them understand that the offence could not be committed without serious punishment following. MR. COHEN'S LECTURES AT THE VUBLIC HALL, RUN CORN.—lncreasing numbers have crowded, night after night to the Public Hall, to listen to Herr Cohen, the phrenologist, who has this week delivered a course of his highly-popular and valuable lectures. The subjects chosen have included such topics as the following:—" Formation of Charac- ter ' • " " Shams and Realities ; " " Tempers ; " " Noses; " and to-night the subject will be "Love, Courtship, and Marriage." Herr Cohen has decided to stay in Runcorn one week longer, and will give some more of his interesting lectures, and we can heartily recommend our readers to attend.

FELONIES AT RuNconN,—On Thursday, at Runcorn Police Court, ;William Brydges and Fanny Jannion were charged with stealing and receiving a coat, the property of Wm. Blythe, draper, High-street.—The prosecutor identified the coat, and a girl named Annie Nash said the prisoner Jannion asked her to pawn the coat, and if asked any ques- tions concerning it, to say it belonged to her brother.—The prisoners were further charged with stealing a coat, the pro- perty of Unsworth Brothers High-street. The prisoner- Jannion had acted in a similar way in this case, but Brydges acknowledged having stolen the coat, and exonerated his companion from any participation in the rothery.—The prisoners were committed to take their trial at the sessions on both charges. THE NA.TIONAL BANK OF LIVERPOOL (LIMITED). —A special meeting of the shareholders of this company was held on Saturday, at the bank premises, for the purpose of confirming the resolutions recently passed authorising the transfer of the business of the bank to Parr's Banking Corn- panv, of Warrington. Mr. Alfred Turner, the chairman, presided, and said nothing had occurred to alter the position of affairs as stated at the previous meeting. The convic- tion of the Directors was confirmed that the step they were taking was beneficial to the shareholders, to the customers, and to the staff, and to Liverpool itself. The Chairman then moved, and Mr. H. W. Meade-King seconded, the confirmation of the resolutions previously passed.—The motion wq,s adopted unanimously, and the proceedings closed.

THE CASITIL PAIIPZE AND HIS LOPING—At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Michael Keogh, described as a " casual pauper," was charged with making a false statement for the purpose of receiving relief from the rates raised tor the relief of the poor. On Saturday night the prisoner entered the police office, and asked Inspector Hol- lingsworth for a ticket for a night's lodgings. The Inspector was complying with his request, bet when the prisoner heard that he would have to walk a distance of five miles to the workhouse, he said he would not have it, and went out. He, however, immediately returned, and said he might as well walk about the town as walk to the workhouse. He now informed the Inspector that his name was John Doyle, and when charged with telling a false name he replied " There's nothing in a name." He was locked up, and the Bench now sentenced him to seven days' hard labour at Knutsford.

r It is stated that the valuable rectory of Prescot was refused by all the clerical fellows of Ring's College, Cambridge. BREACH OF THE EDUCATION ACT.—Joseph Davies was fined 58 for not sending his child regularly to school, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday. RUNCORN CO•OPERATIVE SOCIETY.—The annual meeting of the shareholders of the Runcorn Co-Operative Society, was held on Tuesday evening. Mr. Leathwood presided, and there was a good attendance. The report and balance sheet were presented, a dividend of 2s. 61. in the £ being proposed. The meeting, however, carried a motion that a dividend of 2s. 91- be paid, thus upsetting all the calcula- tions upon which the balance sheet was based. DEATI OF MR. J. H. CROSSLEY, OF WIDNES. Oar readers will hear with regret of the death of Mr. J. H. Cross- ley, of Widnes, who held a post of some importance at the works of Messrs. Sullivan and Co. Mr. Crossley was at the works on Saturday morning in his usual health, but during the evening, or on Sunday, he was taken suddenly ill, and died on Tuesday morning. The deceased gentleman had only attained the age of 26 years. He was well known in the town, and was respected as a young man of high pro- mise.

THE MEDICINE VENDOR AND THE CLOTHES TUB.— Yesterday, at Runcorn Police Court, before Captain Hazle- hurst, a Northwich woman, named Mary Ann Gibson, was charged with stealing six aprons and a cbild's flannel, the property of Sarah Jane Wild7who lives in Halton-road. It appeared that the prisoner went about hawking a sovereign emed r for corns, and in the course of her rounds called at the prosecutrix's house, where she was informed by the servant (named also Mary Ann Gibson) that her ointment was not required. While the servant was engaged in the yard, it appeared the prisoner took the articles she was charged wifh stealing.—She was committed to Knutsford Sessions for trial. THE "UNPROMISING STUDENT" AGAIN. —AI the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, James Hulme, boot and shoe dealer, Market Place, St. Helens, applied for a committment against Maurice Gandy, in respect of a debt of Bs.—The plaintiff said the defendant was an ap- prentice at Messrs. Daglish's Works, St. Helens, and was well able to pay the debt, as .he (plaintiff) understood that his father allowed 355. per week.—Hi 9 Honour: Is this the youth who was here last court day.—Plaintiff: Yes; he got the goods in June, and promised to pay in July. He has said he would do every one of us out of our money.—His Honour: What do you ask for?—Plaintiff: A committal.— His Honour: Very well.

TRAMWAY ACCIDENT AT Sr. HELENS. - Tramcar accidents of every kind have fortunately been rare at St. Helens but on Monday one of a somewhat serious character occurred at Portico. At the place where the accident occurred there is a double line of rails for a short distance to allow of the tramcars to and from Prescot to pass, but it appears that some how or other the up and down cars came in Contact with each other, the result of which was that some of the windows of both cars were smashed, and the vehicles otherwise damaged. The passengers were also severely shaken, some of them being thrown from their seats. None, however, were very seriously hurt. Owing to the cars having become interlocked the line was blocked for some time, but ultimately they were disengaged and taken to the depot. for repair, the amount of damage to them being considerable.

A RECALCITRANT TICICET-OF-LEAVE MAN.--At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, a man, named Joseph Sackerstone, was charged with having, he being a ticket-of- leave man and under police surveillance, changed his resi- dence without having notified the same to Superintendent Johnstone.—lt was stated that the prisoner had been before the Bench about a fortnight ago for a similar offence, but the magistrates, thinking that he had merely acted foolishly, discharged him. It had been found, however, on ,enquiry being made, that he had again removed without notice being given to the police, and his c3usin, with whom he had previously lodged, said he had not been there for a month, but could not give any reason for it unless it were that prisoner was lazy. He had been received into custody at St. Helens from the Liverpool police.—Prisoner, who offered no deretlgei W4S ommitted for six months' hard labour. A SUSPICIOUS VISITOR —Thomas Appleton, a rough- looking man, was on Wednesday charged, at the St. Helens Police Court, with having been found upon enclosed pre- mises, in the occupation of James Farrell, for unlawful purposes.—P. Bremner said that about ten minutes past twelve o'clock that morning. his attention was called to a court in Hardshaw-street kept by James Farrell. He went there, and found the prisoner c6mlng over the yard wall, who, on being asked what he was doing there, said he was coming from his work at Mr. Gamble's. Witness said that was a strange way to come from work, and as prisoner made very csntradictory answers to further questioning, he took him into custody. He (witness) went back to Mr. Farrell's yard, and found that there was a quantity of fowl in it.— The prisoner, who practically made no defence, and against whom previous convictions were* recorded, was committed for 14 days' bard labour.
WIDNES TRADERS' ASSOCIATION.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the member's of Whines Traders Association, was held in the Officers'-room of the Volunteer Hall, yesterday morning. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the president, occupied the chair, and there were also present :—Messrs. S. K. Muspratt, T. Sutton Timmis, H. Wade Deacon, Jones, Holbrook Gaskell junr. Mr. T. S. Timms read the report of the Executive Com- mittee, which stated that three memorials had been presented by the Association to the Board of Trade during the past year. The first drew attention to clause 15 in the M.S. and L. (Cheshire Lines) Bill of last session, and on the Board of Trade taking action in the matter, the clause was with- drawn. The other two, respectively urged that there should be a new classification of goods applicable to all railway companies, and that the Govern- ment should become the owners of canals. The former was simply acknowledged, and, in reply to the latter, the Board of Traie stated that a Parliamentary Com- mittee had been appointed to consider the whole subject of canals. The committee was of opinion that a clause should be inserted in the Manchester Ship Canal Bill guaranteeing that the existing depth of .water at the canal should not be decreased, but as it seemed improbable that the Bill would pass the Standing Orders Committee of the House of Com- mons the committee had not considered it necessary as yet to take action. An association had been formed, called "The Railway and Canal Traders' Association," the objects of which, as states in the plan of organisation, were as fol- low :—" To endeavour to obtain redress for traders in cases within the jurisdiction of the railway commissions and any further exmosion of the same. To give advice to members in respect to the legality of charges made by rail- way or canal companies. To endeavour to liberate canals from the control of rail way companies and restore their usefulness as an independent means of transit for slow and heavy traffic. ;To watch over railway legislation as affecting the interests of traders. Gensrally to assist trades in questions between them and railway or canal companies, and to procure needful amendments of the law affecting railway or canal companies." There were two classes of members (1); individuals or firms; (2), Chambers of Com- merce, and other Associations of Traders. The minimum subscription for the latter class of members was £5 ss, and the committee recommended that the Whines Traders' Association, should become subscribers. The statement of accounts showed that there was a balance in hand of £llO is 2d.

The CHAIRMAN moved the adoption of the report. The Association had not had very much business before it last year, but any subjects that were thought of interest to Widnes traders had been cleverly considered by the Execu- tive Committee, and they had taken such action as they thought necessary. They would see in the first part of the report, that that obnoxious clause giving the right of grouping collieries and other traders, for the purpose of levying equal rates irrespective of distance in the Man- chester, Sheffield,. and Lincolnshire Bill was withdrawn from the Bill. As regarded the ship canal, the only interest that Widnes traders could secure was that they should not be any worse off with the ship canal than they were at present without it. Of course if the canal were made' they might, perhaps, take some further action, and see whether by getting access to to the projected canal, and by improving the existing canal, they could not get better water communication with Liverpool. At present, as they had all seen, the Bill had not passed the standing orders, and it was very doubtful whether it would come on tkis session. At the same time he thought the subject of waterway communication between the port of Liverpool and, the interior towns of Lancashire was such an important one that, although the ship canal scheme might not be passed in its present form, some more perfect water communication between the port of Liverpool and the manufacturing towns of Lancashire would undoubtedly be brought about in some way or other. The only recommendation they had to make was that the Association should join the association of the Railway and Canal Traders in Londan. The objects of that Association were set down in the report, and bethought the committee were of opinion that it would be desirable for them to subscribe to that Association, thus becoming mem- bers and receiving the advantage of advice and. assistance when necessary from that central body. If the Railways and Canal Traders' Protection Association received the support of traders generally throughout tbe country, and the Chambers of Commerce, he looked forward to it doing a very great work. He had much pleasure in moving that the report be adopted and the accounts passed.

Mr. JONES seconded the motion. After a few remarks from Mr. T. S. Timmis, the motion was carried. Mr. TEAM'S moved that the Widnes Traders' Association become members of the Railway and Canal Association, the subscription not to exceed £5 se. Mr. S. MIISPRATT seconded the motion, which was adopted. Mr. T. S. Tamsfis then moved that Mr. E. K. Maspratt be appointed president of the Association for the next three years, and that Mr. H. W. Deacon be appointed honorary secretary for a similar period. As chairman of the Execu- tive Committee he had the best means of knowing the ser- vices which these gentlemen hal rendered, and he could assure the Association very truthfully that their services had been most valuable.
Mr. HOLBROOK GASKELL, jun., seconded the proposition, remarking that the members were very much indebted to the gentlemen for the time they had given to their duties.— Carried.
The CHAIRMAN and !JON. SECRETARY suitably replied, and the meeting separated.

RUNCORN COUNTY COURT. -- TIIESDAY.—Before Mr. W. Wynne Ffoulkes. Acriox FOR REPAIRS.—Messrs. Peter Stubs' Brothers, boat builders, Runcorn, sued James Bradshaw, flat owner, Winsford, for the sum of 8s Id, being the charge for repair- ing the pump box of the flat Welcome.—Mr. Barton repre- sented the plaintiff, and Mr. 0. Leak the defendant.—lt appeared that a man named Taylor was captain of the flat Welcome, and on one occasion, whilst plying between Wins- ford and Ellesmere Port and Runcorn, the pump box became out of order, and he had it repaired at the works of the plaintiff.—The defence was that Taylor had no right to incur a debt, and had been informed of that fact as well as the plaintiff. The defendant contended that he had never had an account rendered to him, or he should have paid it. It might be the custom of captains of sea-going vessels to get repairs executed, and Taylor, rather than the vessel should be injured, might do the same.—His Honour said he believed the defendant's statement that he had never received an account, and gave an order for the plaintiff for the amount claimed, without costs.

NEGLECT OF FAMILY AT RIINCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Charles Platt, a chemical labourer, was charged with neglecting to maintain his family, whereby his child James Booth had become charge- able to the common fund of the Runcorn Union.—Mr. T. Houghton, collector to Runcorn Board of Guardians, said the defendant was a widower, and the child, who was two years of age. was put out to nurse by a woman named John- son, at Walton Inferior. Mrs. Johnson was to be paid 5s per week, and up to September the defendant paid that amount, although Irregularly. He then ceased his payments, and on the 31st October Mrs. Johnson applied for and was granted 2s dl per week by the Guardians.—The defendant promised to pay the arrears and to support his child, and to give hiin an opportunity of doing so the case was adjourned two months.

BRUNSWICK SUNDAY SCHOOL BAND OF HOPE, RUNCORN. —The monthly meeting of the above Band of Hope was held on Monday night. There was a very largo attendance of members and friends. Mr. T. Simister occupied the chair and gave an earnest temperance address. There was a varied and interesting programme consisting of songs, recitations, and dialogues. A reitation by A lfred Bowers, "We can make home happy ;" a song by Frank Rushton, "Driven from home ;" a dialogue entitled "John Mason's rescue," by Edith Fo-ster, Joseph Douglass, C. Kniveton, U. Marsh, and William Hazlehurst ; song and chorus, Miss 'Clarie Worrall, "Won't you buy my pretty flowers ;" reci- tation, William Spans, "Jacob's dream ;" song, Miss Annie Jones, "Sweet song bird was singing ;" recitation, G. Cav- gill, "Who, who, who." Mr. John Simpson gave an elo- quent address, dwelling chiefly on the force of personal example, and the danger incurred in the moderate use of intoxicating drinks. He also spoke of the sad case of a man who had become a complete slave to drink, and who, through the influence of a pious wife and the power of pray:er, had been rescued. A number of glees were given by the choir daring the evening, Miss E. Norman presiding at the piano. At the close of the meeting a large number joined the Band of Hope. THE WRECK OF THE GEORGE AND SARAH, OF RUN- CORN.—EarIy on Friday morning last week, the schooner George and Sarah, of Runcorn, was wrecked on Maughold Head, Isle of Man, and the mate, John Garnett, of Runcorn, and William James Hatton, 16 years of age, the captain's stepson, lost their lives. The cantain and owner of the vessel (which was not insured) is Mr. J. Abrams, of Waterloo, Runcorn. The vessel left Runcorn on the 20th ult. laden with salt for Girvan, and departed from Liverpool on the let inst. in fair weather and with a southerly wind, but during the nigkt a violent snowstorm arose, and the vessel was dashed upon the rocks. In the sea which was running no boat could live, and no attempt was made to launch the one which the vessel carried. Garnett, the mate, was washed off the deck and drowned, and Hatton, the boy, was washed from the rock where his stepfather and. Carter, a seaman, were clinging, and was afterwards washed on the shore when it was discovered that his neck was broken. The captain and Carter managed with difficulty to keep in their perilous position, despite the violence of the storm, until daylight. They then saw they were on a boulder rock, while above them towered the cliffs to a height of 180 feet. The only way to escape from the spot was by climbing the face of the cliff, but the captain was too exhausted to make the attempt. Carter, however, bravely accomplished the tack, and secured the help of Mr. John Killip, farmer, of Ballafayle, Cannel, Ramsay, and his son, who with the aid of a rope hauled up the captain. They were taken to Mr. Killip's house, where every attention was paid to the I distressed seamen. It has since been reported that the shock to the system received by Mr. Killip's daughter on that occasion has caused her death. Mr. Abrams arrived in Runcorn on Saturday. A concert, on behalf of the widow and children of tbe deceased seaman Garnett, will be given in Ellesmere-street school some evening next week.

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held on Thursday morning, under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. There were also present Messrs. Simpson, Pritchard, Norman and F. Rigby (clerk.) A short discussion took place upon the increased assessments of Mill Brow Board School from Is. to 2s. 6d. per head, and it was decided that the chairman and clerk should represent the Board at the next meeting of the Assessment Commit- tee. The Visitor's (Mr. Bowyer's) report was read as follows :—Retures for the Public Elementary Schools for January, 1883: Certified Government accommodation, 2.716; total number on the rolls, 2,903; number on the rolls corresponding period of last year, 2,822; increase in the number on the rolls, 81; total average attendance, 2,0085; average attendance corresponding period of last year, 1,972 4 ; increase in average attendance, 36 1; average attendance for the year 1874, 1,252-; increase in average attendance as compared with 1874 ; the year pre- ceding the formation of the Board, 756 5 ; accommodation in excess of average attendance, 7075; number on the rolls in excess of accommodation, 187.; number in atten- dance at private adventure schools under 9d. per week, 71. In the returns for the past month ending January 26th, you will notice that the attendance of infants is still below the usual percentage, many parents being unwilling to send their children regularly until the weather is more favourable. During the past month I have taken proceed- ings against the list of parents ordered to be dealt with for contravention of the bye-laws. In the whole of the cases convictions were granted, and the usual fine of ss. imposed. In the case of Alfred Lewis, the magistrates committed him to Stockport Industrial School, and he was admitted there on the 31st of January, his parents having previously been fined four different times under the bye-laws, and twice for disobedience of the attendance order. In one case the parent was committed to prison in default of not paving the fine. During the past month I have also served 33 notices on parepts for the irregular and non-attendance of their children at school. Several of these cases and others which have been served witli notices previously, it will be necessary to bring before the Atten 1-Inv Comtnitte,. as the notices served Lave nGt b-.en

TEMPERANCE WORK IN ST. HELENS. —On Wednesday evening, a new lodge was opene4 in connection with the North-Western Grand Lodge of the Independent Order of Good Templars, of which Dr. F. R. Lees, is chief, at King's coffee-rooms, Mill-place (this being the second lodge that has been opened in St. Helens within the past few months), under the name of the "Rising Sun." Bro. G. H. Friend was elected Worthy hief Templar, who, with the due com- plement of officials, was installed by officers in connection with the Grand Lodge, who kindly came over from Liver- pool for the purpose. Persons having the welfare of temper- ance at heart, would do well to join the above lodge. On Saturday last, upon the invitation of the Rev. Mr. Ward, Bro. J. W. hisFolm Grand Worth Secretary of the above Order, delivered a spleqdid address in connection with the Blue Ribbon Army, at the • Mission Hall, Waterloo-street, which was listened to by a large and most appreciative audience.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A SIT 'OM AT ST. HELENS.—At the St. Helms Police Court, on Wednesday, a young woman named Mary Francis was charged with having stolen a shawl, of the value of 55., the property of Elizabeth Kirk, who lives with her husband at 87, Lyon-street.—Mrs. Kirk said the prisoner had lodged with her for about a fortnight. en .Sunday night she (prosecutrix) laid her child down and put the shawl over it, and then busied herself in getting the tea ready, the prisoner sitting in the house at the same time. A short time after she found that the prisoner had gone, and that the shawl was missing.—Walter Dromgoole spoke to the prisoner having come and pawned the shawl at his father's shop in Liverpool-road on Monday. She then gave the name of Rawlinson.—lnspector Woods said that there were other charges against the prisoner, but which he was at present not prepared to go into. He, therefore, asked for a remand, which was granted, till Friday. A Rurrous SALVATIONIST AND HER MASTER'S CARL—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. Henry Reynolds, Emma Aston, a domestic servant, was brought up on remand, charged that she did feloniously steal .£4 Bs. Bd., on the 3rd instant, and 7s. on the 4th instant, the monies of George Shore, her master.—The prosecutor said he was a publican and kept the Devonshire Hotel, in Ashbridge-street. On Thursday the prisoner entered his service as a domestic servant and as occasional waiter. On Saturday morning, on examining his cash box, be missed £4 Bs. Bd. He particularly missed two half sovereigns, which he had seen safe in the box on Friday afternoon. The box was kept in the sitting room and was sometimes left a few minutes unlocked. On Sunday he heard the prisoner tell his wife that she was going to have some new clothes, which aroused his suspicions as he knew that when she entered his service she had no money. On Sunday evening they told her she could go out, and she did so. While she was away they found that her purse in her dress pocket contained is Dd. They then continued the search, and in the closet in the yard they found three sovereigns and two half- sovereigns wrapped in a piece of paper on a ledge close under the slates. On her return at eight o'clock, the prisoner was shown what had been discovered, and she com- menced to cry and asked witness to forgive her. On Mon- day morning on counting the cash he missed a further sum of 7s, and he gave information to the police. P.C. Bossons afterwards apprehended the prisoner, who now, when for- mally charged, acknowledged stealing £4 23.—She was committed to take her trial at the next Knutsford Sessions. About a fortnight ago the prisoner addressed an„,audience from the Salvation Army platform. Ruscome MADRIGAL CLUB. The third concert of the season was held in the infants' room of the National schools, on Monday evening, attracted, if possible, a smaller number of persons than on the last occasion. The small room was by no means crowded, and, although its selection by the committee was the cause of considerable dissatifac- tion on the part of the members, as events turned out it proved a wise proceeding. During the evening it was ex- plained by the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A. (president) that the reason the concert was not held in the Public Nall was because of the losses which had been sustained by the pre- vious performances of the society, and for a still more weighty reason that the members were reserving themselves for a brilliant close to the season, when it was expected that "Judas Maccabonts " would be performed by the com- bined musical societies of Runcorn, Widnes, and Frodsham. Many changes were rendered necessary to the programme through the absence of Mr. Eaton Batty, whose place had been kindly filled at a minutes notice by Mr. Alfred Monk, and, although this was a great disappointment, the concert may be described as fairly successful. The members of the chorus, guided by Mr. W. I. Argent's baton, acquitted themselves in a manner which merits every praise, while the band maintained the excellent reputation it, has obtained Miss Emily Stewart made a most success- ful debut:before a Runcorn audience. In each of her Efforts she exhibited a cultivated taste and pure feeling, which, combined with a sweet soprano voice of. good compass, won for her the enthusiastic plaudits of the audience. Bishop's c avatina, "Echo," (flute, Mr. Brindlev) and Ganz's charm- ing sng, "Sing, sweet bird," were the pieces with which she favoured the 9ndience, and were redemand2d in each in- stance. Mr. Alfred Munk failed to favourably impress the audience. His powerful bass voice appeared to be beyond his control, and his singing occasionally degenerated into a shout. Talent Mr. Mort undoubtedly possesses, and with a suitable training we venture to predict that he would be fitted to take a high place in the musical world. Mr. J. Brindley gave a most pleasing and brilliant performance on the flute, and we would express the hope that advantage will be taken of his services on future occasions Space forbids us criticising the performance at greater length, and we would bring short notice to a close by observing th,ii Mr. C. div.head: OLD ENGLISH BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.
div.p: OLD ENGLISH BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.

Placed in an unconspicuous position and making no pre- tentions to architectural beauty, St. John's Presbyterian Chapel still needs occasionally repairing, and even modestly decorating, and a bazaar, for which the members have been working assiduously for months past, having for its object "to liquidate the balance of the expenses incurred in con- nection with the heating apparatus and the cleaning of the interior of the chapel ; also to provide a sufficient sum for painting the chapel pToperty outside and doing sundry necessary repairs to the building," was opened in the school- room on Tuesday morning. Erected in 1818 and composed of red bricks, with a stone portico, the building, it can well be understood, will require a little overhauling, especially as it is surrounded to some extent by an atmosphere of deleterious chetnical gases ; and the method taken for raising the requisite sum was at once artistic and attractive. The prosaic little school- room had been metamorphosed into an "Old English village" as it was termed, albeit it possessed all the attraction of a modern fancy fair. On entering the room, stall No. 1 was presented to view as a rustic cottage, in the depth of winter, its roof and the branches of two trees which overhung it, bearing a white mantle of snow, which had a most realistic effect. "Ivy Cottage" (stall No. 2) was a most pleasing represent Ilion. The creeping, clinging ivy, had so overrun the dwelling that not a crevice or crack was visible. Light entered the " upper rooms" by quaint looking latticed windows; while in the windows below was displayed a great variety of charming articles. The refresh- ment stall was one of those black timbered picturesque rustic dwellings of several centuries ago, with a roof of thatched straw. The air of realism which surrounds all the buildings was somewhat enhanced by a sweet twittering which was found to proceed from a canary inprisoned in a cage depended from the ceiling. The stalls had been con- structed from models prepared by Mrs. J. Humphreys, to whom, and to the gentlemen who have carried out the designs, the highest praise is due for the clever execution and tasteful result. Messrs. C. Kirkman, D. Jones, J. Foster, and George Jones rendered valuable assistance in the construction of the stalls, the timber for which was lent by Mr. James Kirkham. Mr. John Humphreys fulfilled the duties of secretary to the bazaar in a courteous manner. There was a goad company present at the opening ceremony, amongst them being Councillor McKechnie, Mrs. McKechnie and daughters (of St. Helens), Rev. E. Williams, Mr. and Mrs. Gibson, Mr. and Mrs. Frith, Mr. and Mrs. J. Kirkham, Mr. Pritchard, Mr. and Mrs. F. Fairhurst, Mrs. P. Speakman, Mrs. Wteitaker, ttc. Captain C. W. Hazlehurst had been announced to open the bazaar, bet he had been suddenly called from town, and in his absence the ceremony was performed by Councillor McKechnie, who was introduced by Mr. James Pritchard.— Mr. MCKECHNIE expressed the pleasure it afforded him to meet his Runcorn friends, and remarked that although they laboura in a quiet and unpretentious way, he could speak from experience of the good work done in the past, and he felt very thankful that the work was still going forward. It hopeful a Opeful sign of the times when they found young people active, energetic, and sympathetic in working together to produce that grand display they had that morn- ing in the old English village, which he was sure all were delighted to see. The lady whose design it was deserved the greatest praise for her ingenuity, as did also the young builders, for the way in which they had done their work. After a few other remarks, Councillor McKechnie formally declared the bazaar open.—Mr. W. B. Gussote, in proposing a vote of thanks to Councillor McKechnie, said said he always felt at home in that school-room. It had been his home since 1829. (Applause.) He had the in- terests of the chapel at heart, and hoped that their present enterprise would be a success.—Mr. J. R. FRITH seconded the motion in appropriate terms, and it was carried with acclamation.—Councillor McKechnie having replied, the ladies proceeded with the sale of their wares, which were of the usual description. Stall No. 1 (snow scene) was presided over by Mrs. Williams, Miss Borwick, Mrs. Campbell, Miss Pritchard, Miss Gibson, and Mrs. Littler; 2 (ivy cottage), Mrs. Elumphries, Mrs. Warburton, Miss Ellison, and Mrs. Leach; 3 (refreshment stall), Mrs. Harrop, Mrs. Fred Jones, Mrs. Tickle, Mrs. Clough, and Miss Foster. A cloak room for the convenience of visitors was in charge of Mrs. Green, Mrs. Greenwood, Mrs. Leach, and Mrs. Howard. There were the ordinary amusements provided in the shape of fine art gallery with models in cork, speaking bees, musical entertainments, &c., &c., which were well patronised. Excellent entertainments were given at intervals during. each evening by members of the choir and congregation, assisted very ably by the Misses Twiss, Horsfall, Campbell, and Billingsley, pupils at Miss Gentle's ladies school, South Bank, who rendered very effectively songs, pianoforte EOlO9, duets, and trios. The songs were very efficiently accompanied on the piano by Miss Edwards, teacher at Miss Gentle's school, who kindly came forward at the last moment and took the place of Miss Clough, who had very kindly undertaken to accompany the songs, but was unable Ito be present. Miss Edwards also sang several songs in a I very creditable manner. Mr. George Lacey also favoured 1 them with a song in his usual effective manner.

John Clarke brought an action against William Darby- shire to recover £l7 15s 6d, being the value of 71 loads 25 lbs. of potatoes supplied ta the defendant. The defendant made a counter claim of £1 6s 8d fdr the railway carriage of the potatoes.—The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Burton, and Mr. Thurnham (Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., Warrington) appeared for the defendant. —Mr. Burton, in opening the case, said the plaintiff was an innkeeper, residing at Overton, near Frodsham, and was also a dealer in general farm produce. The defendant was a farmer, residing at Latchford, near Warrington. In the autumn the plaintiff purchased a considerable quantity of potatoes at Thornton Hall Farm, near Chester, and bad them carted and placed in." hogs" near Ince railway station. The " pig " potatoes, and the large, or seed, potatoes, were separated. About December, the plaintiff found that the seed potatoes were not keeping well, and he had consequently a load brought to his warehouse at Frodsham. He inserted an advertisement in the local papers " seed potatoes for sale," and about Christmas the defendant called at the warehouse, where the defendant and two men were engaged sorting the seed potatoes from the rotten ones. The deiendant was told that there were about 70 loads— eight tons—similar to those in the warehouse lying at ince station, and he said he did not mind making an offer for the lot. After sone negotiations, it was arranged that the defen- dant was to have the potatoes put upon the rails at Ince station at 5s per load. The defendant examined the potatoes at the warehouse, and was informed that those at Ince were of the same quality. The defendant received the potatoes, which were now in his possession, but asserted that the potatoes delivered to him were not equal to sample, and he had made a counter claim for the cost of the carriage of the potatoes.—Tbe plaintiff was called, and in cross-examina- tion by Mr. Thurnham, admitted that there might be a waggon of potatoes at lace a little dryer than those at the warehouse. On the 2nd January he received a telegram from the defendant that the potatoes were rotten, and the plaintiff replied back that he must do the best he could with them, but defendant replied that he would not have them.—Defendant went to Latchford on the 3rd January, and examined a wagon load of the potatoes which were lying there. Mr. Thurnham asked the witness if those he examined were not a rotten pulpy mass. He replied emphatically in the negative, and said now after a month of wet and frosty weather he could pick three cart loads of good potatoes from them.—Thomas Jamison said the potatoes were for "cattle and pigs." They were damp, and mixed with a little soil. He assisted in loading up two wagons at lace. The first wagon containtd a little dryer potatoes than the second.—By His Honour: The potatoes were a little diseased.—Charles Hulse, of Five Crosses, Frodsham, deposed that the potatoes sent to Mr. Darbyshire were a better sample than those in the ware- house.- —Thomas Littler, farmer, also gave evidence.—Wm. Pevon, stationmaster, lace, was called, and stated he had marked on the invoice (produced) of the potatoes consianed to Mr. Darbyshire "very wet and dirty." He thought it, his duty to do so.—John Carter, cattle dealer, Sutton, said be purchased five loads of potatoes at 55.. per load from the plaintiff, about Christmas. They Were "rough and sandy," but when washed they were as fine as any other.— By Mr. Thurnham : They were not sound potatoes. Some of them were diseased.—Mr. Thurnham, in defence, called William Darbyshire, Morris Brook Farm, Glrappenhall, Cheshire, who said in consequence of an advertisement, which stated that the plaintiff had 50 loads of magnum bon= sets for sale, be visited his warehouse on the 29th December. He agreed to pay 8s per load for 14 loads of dressed potatoes that were there, the plaintiff to deliver them to Frodsham station and pay the carriage to Warring- ton. The plaintiff said a portion of the remainder of the sets were in a waggon at lace, and a portion in the station yard, ready for loading. The plaintiff said all the potatoes at lace were in a better and dryer condition than those he saw before him. He tried almost all the hampers in the warehouse, and although the potatoes were wet and dirty they were sound. (Samples produced.) Whilst making the bargain for the potatoes at race, witness told plaintiff that he would not purchase potatoes from anyone without exam- ining them, but the plaintiff assured him that he could take his word as to the condition of the potatoes at lace. Plaintiff then said the potatoes were in sound condition and fit for sets, Worming witness that he might depend upon him, as he did to others what he should like others to do to him. Witness remarked that that was the golden rule, and if he would stick to that he would take the potatoes at ss. per load and pay the railway charges. He received notice on Sunday, the 31st December, that the potatoes were awaiting his orders at Warrington station, and on Monday he sent four one-horsed carts for them. On re- turning about four o'clock in the evening one of the car- ters made a statement to him, and in consequence he ex- amined the potatoes in the cart. All be felt at were soft and not fit for sets. Next morning. he had all the potatoes washed to see if there were any sound ones, but he did not think he found more than one sound potato in a bushel. He saw the plaintiff on the 3rd January, and informed him that the potatoes were no good to him for seed purposes, and he should not remove those lying at the station. (A sample of the potatoes that had been washed was produced in court, and they appeared to be entirely rotten).—Ed- ward Smith, in the employ of the defendant, stated that all the potatoes received were rotten.—Cbas. Horrabin, foreman of the goods department, Warrington,' said the potatoes received were 'Wet, dirty, and rotten; of course, there were a few sound ones. The potatoes emitted a smell as if diseased.—Peter Ford, farmer, Latchford, Thomas Parsonage Taylor, potato dealer, Latchford (25 years in the trade), gave evidence as to the rotten state of the potatoes. —His Honour gave judgment for the defendant on both the claim and counter claim, costs to follow.

FUNERALS AND FEEDING: A REFORM WANTED.—Dr. Bagnall claimed £1 Os 6d from Mary Sefton, as executrix ded-son-tort of Joseph Sefton, for professional attendance upon her late husband.—The doctor preyed his claim to the satisfaction of the judge.—The defendant stated that she had not means to pay the debt, but admitted having received £2l from the Prudential Insurance Company on the death of her husband. This, she alleged, was all expended in funeral expenses and buying . clothes for herself and children. Tha agent of the Prudential Company was called, and proved that he had paid the defendant over £4O on the death of her husband.— His Honour thereupon took the defendant sharply to task for concealing from him the real amount she had received. Defendant said her brother got £2O of the money.—The Agent said he paid the money to the defendant, who made the declara- tion. She alone paid the premiums, and be never received payments from any one else.—His Honour said when a person died leaving assets the first charge upon those assets were the expenses of the funeral, and any other liabilities which might have been incurred during his lifetime, and in this case there appeared to have been sufficient money left to satisfy all claims. He would make an order against the defendant for 2s. per month.—Dr. Bagnall said he would not have brought the case before his -Honour but the de- fendant openly told him she would not pay, and had defied him to get the money. He knew that on the day of the funeral 70 people sat down to a knife and fork tea at Northwich.—His Honour: To bring the thing to an issue I will make an order for the amount to be paid in a mcnth. (To defendant.) There is no doubt you had the money, but whether you have spent it or not I cannot say. You must pay the debt in a month.

At Runclrn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. A. Thomas, Sarah Ellen Jackson, a woman of loose character, was charged in custody with unlawfully. and maliciously wounding John Davies, a boatman, living at the Stone Croft, Halton-road, with intent to do him grievous bodily harm. From the evidence of the prosecutor, It appeared that the prisoner had lived with him for a period of four years, sometimes on the boat, and sometimes in Runcorn, but he left her a fortnight ago in consequence of a quarrel they had. On Saturday night be went in the Feathers Inn, Church-street, where he met the prisoner, who askel him if he was going home with her. He replied, "No," and at closing time left the house with a young fellow named Gayter and another called Griffiths. In High- street, near the tea shop, opposite the Royal Hotel, he met a young woman, with whom he entered into a conversation. Shortly afterwards the prisoner, accompanied by Thomas Walsh, came along the street. On arrriving at the spot where prosecutor was standing, the , prisoner stopped, seized his right arm, and said, "You I pig, I'll stick you," at the same time raising her hand, in , which she held a penknife, and struck him in the middle of the back. The prosecutor seized her, and in struggling to take from her the knife received a cut on the hand. The knife was found in the road half-an-hour afterwards by Gayter.—Dr. McDougall said shortly after midnight on Saturday he examined the prosecutor and found a clean cut wound in the middle of the back, more to the right side than to the left of the spinal column. So far as he could ascertain, the wound was five-eighths of an inch in depth, most probably being intercepted by bone; and it was about three-eighths of an inch in length. The knife produced (an ordinary penknife) was likely to cause such a wound. There were cuts in the prosecutor's clothing corresponding with the wound on the back.—P. S. McMichael deposed to appre- hending the prisoner, who, when charged by him, said, "I didn't do it. I have witnesses to prove that I didn't do it. I only got him by the arm and struck him in the face.— Prisoner now said she was sorry for what she had done. She did not know what she was doing at the time. She was walking down the street peeling an apple, when she saw the prosecutor talking to a woman. She said, "You deceitful thing, you said you would go home," not thinking to catch him with the knife.—The prisoner was committed to take her trial at the next Knutsford sessions.

THE SOCIALISTS AND THE CZAR'S CORONATION. It is stated that Most, the former editor of the Freiheit Hartmann, and other Socialists now in America, are con- ferring together rco•irding the approaching coronation of the Czar. Hartmann declaring that the event shall not take place.

THE PHCENIX PARK MURDERS. The investigation into the Phcenix Park conspiracy to- day, is anticipated with keen interest. Numbers of county Magistrates have applied for tickets. It is expected that the carman, " skin the goat," will be iden- tified in connection with the murders. - One of the approvers will probably be examined te-day and give details concerning the meetings held and the assassiation plots. The authorities have obtained im- portant information respecting "The Patriotic Brotherhood,' discovered in the County Armagh. On Thursday Peter , Coleman of Lavagh. County Monaghan, and Bernard Smyth, Of Mullabane, County Armagh, were arrested for complicity in the local assassination conspiracy directed against landlords, their agents, and conveners. They have been returned for trial at Belfast Assizes. It is stated that Edward Chanlon, the Crown witness, who failed to attend the Belfast Assize, and who was arrested under a load of hay, denied his original information, and will be indicted as a co-conspirator with the other prisoners.
A Cabinet Council was held yesterday at noon in Downing-street.

Mr. french Brewster, grandson of Lord Chancellor Brew- ster, has been selected as the Conservative candidate for Portarl ington. Sir Harry Verney, M.P., having announced that he will not again contest Buckingham, the name of Major George Verney, his second son, is mentioned as the probable Liberal candidate.

A Times' Philadelphia telegram in the second edition says: The Pennsylvania railway announces that no inter- ruption of traffic, nor any damage to its lines, has been caused by the floods at Pittsburg or elsewhere.

On Thursday night the Star Hotel, Lees-road, Oldham, was sold for £4,000. Some time ago it could have been sold for £6,000. The depreciation in this and other publichouse property in Oldham is largely attributed to the extension of political and other clubs in the town.
