div.p: PRESCOT HIGHWAY BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday. The members present were Messrs. W. L. Evans (chairman),. Tyrer, Leatherbarrow, Lowe, Whitfield, Cross (clerk), and Goldswortb (surveyor).—The SURVEYOR reported that he had written to Mr. Frith, agent to Lady Stapleton-Brether- ; ton, with respect to the repair of Toohills-lane, Rainhill, I but he bad not yet received a reply.—The CHAIRMAN, who with Mr. Whitfield led been appointed a committee to re- port upon the proposed improvement of Stony-lane bridge, described a visit the committee had made to the locality, and negotiations which were in progress with Mr. Willis.— The consitleration of the subject was furter adjourned, with a view to the arrangement of terms with the owners of the land.—Mr. John Earle, Prescot, and Mr. Lowe Rainhill,l tendered for the painting of the mile stones and Lowe, posts in the Beard's district. Mr. Earle's tender was accepted.-- The SURVEYOR submitted an estimate of the probable re- ceipts and requirements of the Board next year. He suggested that before being dealt with a copy of the estimate should be furnished to each waywarden, so that they might consider it between now and next meeting. In the meantime he would get in tenders for stone and cart- ing.—The Surveyor's suggestion was agreed to.---With reference to the probable position of the Board at the elope of the financial year in March next, the SURVEYOR sub- mitted a statement showing a balance in the treasurer's hands in January of £394 es 11d. There was due from Knowsley £135, Rainhill £2OO, Whiston £lOO, and the Surveyor had £lOO in his hands. Mr. John Jowat, one of the contractors for the new Liverpool water- works, bad paid the £5O stipulated for his extra traffic on the Board's roads, and £444 113 6d was payable by the county treasurer in respect of the maintenance of main roads, so that the total income might be estimated at £1,423 18s sd. The expenditure for materials, wages, the surveyor calculated at £867 18s id, which, deducted from the estimated assets, would leave a balance to the credit of the Board of £556 Os 4d.—Mr. LEATHEREARRO% in pur- suance of a request made to him, inquired as to the truth of an allegation that a member of the Board was doing carting for the Board in Whiston.—lt was explained that the cart- ing referred to was not being done by Mr. Lowe, the way- warden, but by his son independent of him, and an assur- ance was given that the carting should be equally distributed lamong the farmers of Whiston.

div.head: Xattcr to Mt editor.
div.p: Xattcr to Mt editor.

LYING CONSIDERED AS A FINE ART. Sir,—lt nay be thought by most people a degrading and dishonest featuf e in a man's character_when he resorts to what is vulgarly termed lying. In the business of life the one feature that gives encouragement, and stimulates confi- dence, is the truthfulness that is supposed to underlie and to permeate all our transactions. When we as individuals resort to lying it is generally under- stood that we have a worthless case to de- fend, hence the old saying, "No case, throw plenty of mud." If this be a fact, and 1 hold that it is, what a sorry plight our Conservative friends must be in. On Thursday evening last, I. along with scores of Liberals, turned up at the Public Hall in expectation of a treat. It had been an- nounced that "my near and dear relative,Mr.Whitley,M.P.," Colonel Blackburne, M.P., and Sir Robert Peel would de- liver political addresses. Past experience of two of these gentlemen leads me to think that our loss, intellectually, was not great in consequence of their absence, but it was very hard upon Sir Robert, forced as he was 'to undertake the herculean, yet hopeless, task of convincing theWarring- tonians that a lean and slippered pantaloon would be the best representative they could possibly have. Sir, what I propose to draw your attention to in this letter is, not the entire absence of political argument, but the presence of an Ananias kind of want of truthfulness. Tennyson has well said That a lie which is half a truth is ever the blackest of lies.'' "That a lie which is all a lie may be met and fought with %Aright." It is so with nearly all the politcal utterances of those who claim a divine right to preserve intact the purity of the House of Com nons against one, whose only fault is his truthfulness, C. Bradlaugh. Sir Gilbert Greenall, speaking at St. Paul's parochial tea party, said, "He never spoke be- cause the vulgar and illiterate said he could not speak. It was the vulgar, the unrefined, and the coarse who condescended at any time to personalities." lam somewhat of the same opinion. Personalities as a rule should be avoided. But when a gentleman aims at being a public character, a member of Parliament for instance, he must quite expect the public to take some notice of his actions. I venture to say that it was in no sense flattering to Sir Gilbert that the authorities of the House of Corn- mons and reporters of that august assembly were not aware that Warrington returned a member until Mr. Peter Bylands rosa to address them, so I hope Sir Gilbert will not be annoyed at any effort I may make towards exposing his !rends; and while he so carefully surrounds himself with church magnates, I would just hint to him the necessity of also inculcating into their minds the desirability of being truthful. The pitiful feature about it is, that not only on the platform, but in the rather limited quantity of litera- ture at their command, it is noticeable that after the fashion of Ananias, they (the Conservative party) withhold the truth, or part of it. lam sorry to say it, but Sir Robert's speech, shorn of the fibs, would have taken as short a time to deliver it as Mr. Stubs's. First, he stated that Mr. Broad- burst approved of Henry George's book ; the fact is he condemned it in very strong language. Again, in dealing with the expenditure of the two Governments, why did he withhold the fact of the Conservatives receiving six mil- lions surplus from the Liberals ? and also the other ugly fact, that during the three last years of Lord Beaconsfield's Government the expenses always exceeded the income, and that when Mr. Gladstone became Chancellor of the Exche- quer, he had to pay off the accumulated bills and debts? Again, was it not untruthful and mean in the last degree to insinuate that Dr. Clark and Mr. Gladstone were resort- ing to subterfuge, so that the Prime Minister might escape "heckling " by the Scotch Presbyterians? Surely this was scarcely worthy of the son of the great Sir Robert. One could but remember Shakespeare's description of Gloster, an think how well it fits with the character of the rejected of Tamsvorth
Why I can smile and murder while I smile.

• • I'll play the orator as well as Nestor' • Deceive more slyly than Ulysses could, And, like Elinor] take another Troy; I can add colours to the cameleon ; Change shapes with Proteus for advantages. And set the murderous Mach'xvel to school,— Can I co this a, d cannot rt a constituency?

Next time Sir Robert comes to Warrington, let him deliver a speech prepared for Liberals to listen to as well as Conservatives, because he may always depend upon his audience being largely composed of them. Now, sir, I contend that our" grand old constitution" cannot be bolstered up with such inexact language as this. The schoolmaster is at home, the political memory of the people is imp! oving, the penny paper enters almost every house, and false statements must not be lightly made. The lie uttered by Lord Claud J. Hamilton, sent out on its travels, he has not yet withdrawn. If our Conservative friends are getting ashamed of their various titles why not say so at once and tell their supporters under what banner they must fight? Sir Gilbert stated that they appeared as Liberal Conservatives; in Liverpool they tried -the Tory Democrat. What does it all mean ? Sir Robert said he was always in favour of the ballot, always in favour of reform had listened quite enchanted to Mr. Bright, and deplored 'his absence from the Cabinet. Really, sir, no wonder at the sensation thet ran through the hall, espe- cially when the burly baronet stated a few of the Inequalities ef our elective system. But even this he could not deal with bonstly. Allow me, sir, to add a little to the information he so stingily gave. Perhaps he thought the Tory cranium not sufficiently fitted to receive larger doses. Nine places, viz. : Portarlington has 147 electors, Kinsale 194, Ennis 252, New Ross 267, Dungarvon 273, Dungannon 233, Youghal 289, Mallow 293, Downpatrick 304. Thus we see these nine places with 2,302 electors send nine members to St. Stephens; 3 827 voted at Northampton for Mr. Bradlaugh, and he finds it necessary to ask the people's help so that he may take his seat in the House according to law. Sir. it seems to me that were our Tory friends to rest and be thankful for a short time, they might use that time in im- proving themselves and study. They may depend upon it that merely acting as drags upon the Radical wheel will not benefit them any; abusing Mr. Gladstone and heaping Billingsgate on his venerable head only makes them more contemptible. In conclusion, I may just give them a sample of what high class Tory literature is, and I would press upon Sir Gilbert the great necessity there is for him to read the original, so thit be may see what company he keeps. A church builder and a great supporter of the estab- lishment calm:A be too careful of the company he keeps. In 1880, the September number of Blackwood contains an article ea Mr. Gladstone and the House of Commons that is simply atrocious. The writer, a Conservative, states that the House of Commons "represents for the moment only the very dregs of the people," and insinuates that the Prime Minister cannot be a good man "as Christians understand the term," because vituperation flows from his mouth like lava from Vesuvius; and goes on further with the folic wing gentlemanly criticism: It is remarkable how our lower orders can be imposed upon by a solemn countenance and a Jesuitical avoidance of sensual enjoyment. Provided a man's life be austere as to meats and other gratifications, it matters not to them how black his heart is." Again, in the same Conservative magazine for September of last year, the same polished writer spits forth his venom, evidently scorning the teachings of that beautiful chapter of the New Testament, 1 Corinthians, sill.: "Tower Hill would be too honourable a fate ;" "Cain like heart of the wood-splitters ;" and, as if this was not strong enough, winds.up with the following: "Grand old libeller, unscrupulous old antagon- ist, bitter and malicious old reviler, speedy retribution awaits thee, thy sin has found thee out." Such, Mr. Editor, are a few of the specimens I may lay before your readers. Truly, lying is a formidable weapon, but, like a double edged sword, it wants using carefully. Our grand constitu- tion, whatever that may mean, must conform like indivi- duals, to the ever-changing and progressive life that makes up the total of humanity, whether it be Socialism, Atheism, or Radicalism, Proteetism or Catholicism. A Nihilistic current will wash round its base so long as either of these isms contains a shred of suffering humanity. It is a striving after truth, or evolution, in all its ramifications that will ultimately realiee and make poesi hie the aspirations of man- kind- H. W.

SCHOOL ATTENDANCE IN WARRINGTON. The minutes of the School Attendance Committee con: tained the inspectors' report, from which it appeared that 27 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 27 cases for 70 children, and that seven cases were taken before the magistrates, and fines in- flicted in all cases. Twenty-three cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. The following is the report of the Committee to the Council for 1882: Your Committee have much pleasure in submitting for the information of the Council their report for the year 1882, to- gether with tabulated returns ol the number of children pre- sented for examination, and of the average attendance of chil- dren at eletnentrry schools Theso returns show very sati fac- tory results, and we are glad to be able to repeat the statement made in our report for 1881, that considerable progress con- tinu-s to be made. The average attendance at public elemen- tary schools for 1881 was 5,422; this year ;it is 5,884, being an Increase of 462. The MAYOR: We will tackle him. (Laughter.) The minutes were then agreed to. THE SHIP CANAL: IMPORTANT REPORT. The Rivers Committee's minutes comprised a minute that the Town Clerk read the report of the Borough Sur- veyor and himself on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, which was as follows :

At the present time there 19 a free navigation from Liverpool to Warrington on the tidal river Mersey, capable of being im- proved at comparatively small cost. This navigation is aces,/ very considerably used, and of such inestimaele value thar it should be preserved. This can be done if the promoters of the Ship Canal scheme are correct in saying they will not diminish the flow of water, without in any way prejudicing the com- pletion of their scheme. The Bill will enable the company to divert into, and for the purpose of, the new canal from Man- chester to Runcorn all the waters of the rivor Mersey, and to supersede and discontinue the navigation on the existing river. It will vest in the company the right to the waters of the ex - isting river, and confer upon them power to dredge the river between Runcorn and Warrington, notwithstanding the same is not required for the purpose of their Ship Canal scheme, and will prevent any Ind-pendent improvement of that navigation. It appropriates to the company for the purpose of and as ap- purtenant to their canal the reach of the river between Wil- derspool and the Weir at Latchford, and confers upon the company all wharfage rights in respect of that reach, and prevents the use of that part of the river other than by approach through the canal, and the payment of the canal dues; and the wharves and quays thereof will become sub- ject to the other privileges conferred upon the company by the Bill to as great an extent as they would be en- titled to the same in respect of any docks constructed by them. It gives power to the company to raise:the level of the water in the river at any paint, or altogether to stop the flow of water down the river past Bank Qusy, and thereby it confers power to interfere with the sewers of Warrington, the outlet of which is in the river At Bank Quay. It also gives power to raise the waters of the river between the weir at Latchford and Wilderspool, thereby interfering with the sewers of Latch- ford. It gives power for the company to remove the existing stone bridge over the river at Bridge Foot, and, if they think fit, to substitute therefor a movable bridge instead of a fixed one. It gives power to the company to again cross the Wilderspool-road with the low level railway on the level. It gives power, by diverting the waters of the Mersey ints the Canal, to deprive the manufacturers of water they now take from the river for manufacturing purpozes. It proposes to cross the linutsford-road at Black Bear, and the Wilderspool-road at Wilderspool, with swing bridges. It makes no provision for the use of the canal by river steamers and barges from Liver- pool to Warrington, independently of the provisions and dues relating to ships, though it do .s make provision with reference to barges trading between Manchester and Runcorn, but not leaving the canal. The canal and river tolls and dues chargeable for ships and goods to Warrington and Manchester respectively are out of proportions those to Warrington being In excess in comparison to those to Manchester. The require- ments of Warrington to meet the above-mentioned objections, so far as the subject has already been considered, are as follows :—First. That a similarquantity of water to that which now flows down the river past Bank Quay should ho guaranteed for the future, so that the free navigation from Live.pool to Warrington may be uninterfered with. Secondly. That the river between Runcorn and Warrington should be excepted from the operation of the Bill, and be left free, as now, for improvement by and use for those trading between Warrington and Liverpool. Thirdly. Or in the alternative, that steam barges and river vesse's, of a similar draught to those now using the river, should be entitled to come to War- rington by the canal fr nn Runcorn free, and that communica- tion should be made between Walton and Bank Quay, so as to afford that ma of the town the same facilities as they now have. Fourthly. That the river, from the point at Wilders- pool where it is proposed to connect it with the canal and dis- connect from the existing river below up to the weir, be excepted from those provisions hi the Act which would other- wise make it a portion of the docks and works of the company, and that it be reserved for the Corporation and the wharf- owners thereon to improve and deal with as to them may seem best, they of course, paying toll for entrance into it from the canal—or that the plans be altered to enable it to be en.ered by lock from the lower river. Fifthly. Tnat any alteration of level, or lengthening, or thing any" other act in connection with the sewers or gas mains of the borough, necessitated in consequence of the raising, lowering, or stopping of the water In the existing river, or in consequence of tile making of the canal, shall be made and executed by or at the expense of the company. Sixthly. That the company shall not have power to convert the existing stone tbridge into a swing or movable bridge, but that if removed the same shall be replaced by a fixed bridge. Seventhly. That the low level railway across 11 ilderspool-road should be carried either over or under the same, and not on the level. Eighthly. That provision be made In the Bill with reference to the br dges on the Rnutsford and Wilderspool-roads over the canal, in order to secure the least amount of inconvenience to the public. Ninthly. That the (anal and river tolls and dues be readjusted.—A letter from the chait msti of the promoters of the above Bill was read, asking the Corp iration to adopt and present a petition to both Houses of Parliament praying that the stantling orders may be dispen ed with. Recoinmendatisan, that the Council memo- rialize (under the comrnon seal) both Houses of Parliament to dispense with standing orders to enable the Manchester Ship Canal Bill to be heard before a Select Committee on its merits, the right of the Corporation to appear and oppose the Bill on such hearing on the merits being specially reserved by agree- ment with the promoters of the Bill. The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes of the Rivers Committee, and in doing so said he merely wanted to point out to the Council that the committee had signed the petition to the Houses of Parliament in order that they might have thee opportunity of appearing before the Select Committee of .the House of Commons, if ever the Ship Canal Bill got there. If they did not do so they might be shut out from appearing there at all as a Corporation, and therefore they thought their best course was to sign the petition. At the same time, they did not believe the petition would be listened to. Councillor BURGESS: Do I understand that you were obliged to sign the petition to the Standing Orders Com- mittee? The MAYOR said they signed the petition to the House of Commons and the House of Lords to enable the ship canal scheme to come before the Committee of the House of Com- mons, although the promoters had not complied with the standing orders. Councillor PLATT was glad to hear the ground of their action, because in his opinion a bill of this magnitude ought not to be pushed through the House of Commons. It would be very much better if the Bill were introduced again say 12 months from now, and in the meantime the Corporation might look into the matter in all its bearings and endeavour to come to some conclusion as to what they ought to do to protect their own interests. Only that day they had received a very important report from the Rivers Committee which contained conclusions that they had come to regarding the scheme. The Bill bristled with points upon which the Corporation would be at issue with the promoters of the Ship Canal,—[The MAYOR : Certainly.]—and he really hoped it would not be pushed through this session of Parlia- ment but held over for another year, and then the Corpora- tion would have leisure to go into and attend to the important matters contained in the Bill. He believed, as they all believed, that a ship canal from Liverpool to War- rington, and thence to Manchester, would be to the interests of the borough. At the same time this Bill might not be the best that could be proposed in the interests of Warring- ton. He believed it was not. At present it was, as the name proclaimed, a Manchester ship canal, but he would i like Warrington to receive a little more consideration ,if the scheme were ever carried out. The pro- , inoters themselves did not know what they were going to do from Runcorn to Liverpool. As far as he understood the matter they were utterly' at sea as far as that poftion of their scherne was concerned, and to give them power to alter the river from Liverpool to Runcorn he did not think was a very wise thing to do. The Council might interfere with their interests materially, and in grasping at this—he would not call it the shadow of a scheme,they might lose the advantages they had now.

rington. Allow me first to congratulate and thank. the committee for recommending that the Council should petition Parliament to dispense with the standing orders, so as to enable so important and vital a o.ue3tion for this manufacturing district being discussed and thrasbed.out on its merits. 'have. read carefully the objections and suggestions of the committee, and quite agree with them, that they are such as should be considered by the promoters of the Canal. Those wbich.are to protect the present local advantages of Warrirgton must on no account be overlooked, and the Town Cour nil would not be do- ing its duty if it neglected to oppose the Fill on its merits, with the view to obtaining all such necessary clauses, either

by arrangement with the promoters or through a ParHanlon- tary Committee and you will find I shall be quite prepared to assist the Council in getting the ratepayers to assent to such necessary opposition. Indeed, my promotion of the Manches- ter Ship Canal has been an immense labour and anxiety, tax- lug body and mind, in the interests of Warrington and its manufactures, and at the earnest request of many of my fellow-townsmen, and I should have been present aNith you to-night, to express this and much more, but I have to go to London in the general interests of the Canal, and especially to promote the views expressed in the suggestions of the Rivers Committee.—l am. dear Dlr. The proceedings of the Mnseum, Library, and Arts Com- mittee showed that the visitors to the Museum during December numbered 1,619, a decrease of 438 compared with December 1881 ; that the volumes issued to subscribers was 2,332, or a decrease of 172 compared with December, 1881, and the volumes issued to readers was 791, an increase of 118 compared with December .1881. 'nee return for 1882 showed that during the year 28,888 persons visited the Museum. a decrease of 3 per cent. compared with 1881; that 29,342 volumes were issued to subscribers, a decrease of 3-1-- per cent. compared with last year; but that the volumes issued to readers was 12,472, or an increase of 17 per cent. compared with 1881. The thanks of the Commit- tee were ordered to be sent to the donors of the following gifts :—From the Local Books Fund," Hopwood Will Case," 1855; "Stranger's guide to Altrincham, &c " ; Mr. J. Rose, his account of "Leigh in the 18th century " ; Mr. J. P. Rylands, his "Visitation of Cheshire," published by the Harleian Society; the Tr-ustees of the British Museum, " General catalogue of printed books," 27 parts, folio : " Batrachia Gradientia " ; Mr. S. Robinson, his translation of "Persian poetry "; the Financial Reform Association, "Financial Reform Almanac for 1883"; Mr. Beamont, " Howell's State trials " 34 vols.; Mr. W. Fell, plaster cast, painted, " Torsk." Resolutions were passed that the thanks of the Committee be given to the donors of periodicals for 1882; and that the price of the library catalogue be reduced from is. to 61.

Alderman WEBSTER, in moving the confirmation of the proceedings, remarked that it was very gratifying to observe there was an increase in the number of readers. Councillor BURGESS seconded the motion, and it was carried.

div.head: SANITARY.
div.p: SANITARY.
The proceedings of the Sanitary Committee, which con- tained no items of special significance, were approved, on the motion of Councillor MONKS, seconded by Councillor BARKER.
GAS COMMITTEE. - ADVANCE OF WAGES. - THE ELECTRIC
LIGHT AT BANK QUAY SOAPERY.

The Gas Committee's proceedings contained the follow- ing items :—Resolution, that the Council be recommended to increase the salary of Mr. Frederick Taylor' from £169 to £195 per annum, and the salary of Mr. W. S. Haddock from £l3O to £l5O per annum. A deputation of the Board of Guardians waited upon the committee to enquire the terms upon which they would supply the New Industrial Schools at Padgate with gas. After discussing the terms with them, it was resolved that this committee supply the schools with gas if the Board of Guardians will pay the sum of 4s. 9d. per 1,000 oubic feet nett. This price to be. charged to the other co-nsumers in the Padgate district. Alderman HOLMES, in moving the confirmation of the proceedings, expressed the hope that as Mr. Taylor was an old and faithful servant the increase would be acceded to, He also thought the increase to Mr. Haddock would pleat with the approval of the Council. Councillor GREENING seconded the motion. Councillor PLATT: What are the duties of Mr. Frederick Taylor? _

Alderman HOLMES : He is principal ledger clerk in the office. He is not the cashier, but principal ledger clerk. Councillor PLATT then proposed an amendment that the minutes of the committee be confirmed with the exception of the recommendation that Mr. Taylor's salary be increased. He oonsidered Mr. Taylor exceedingly well paid for his duties at £169. If he had control of any portion of the works, or if he had been cashier, he could have understood Mr. Taylor's salary being increased, but as be was a mere bookkeeper he seemed to be exceedingly well paid. Such servants were not to be advanced from time to time simply because they worked for the Co-poration and not a private firm. He (Mr. Platt) did not think any private firm would consider an application of this kind coming from a person in the position of a mere clerk already receiving £169; and he thought these servants ought to be paid acCoraing to the value of their labour in the labour market.
The amendment not being secoadecl fell to the grouid.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

SPECIAL MEETING. A special meeting of the Torn Council was held in the Council Chamber at the Town Hall, on Tuesday, in pur- suance of the Elementary Education (Industrial Schools) Act, 1879, and all other statutory provisions in that behalf, to take into consideration the making of a contribution to- wards the maintenance, in a Certified Industrial School, of two boys ordered by the magistrates, upon complaint made by the School Attendance Committee of the borough of Warrington. to be sent to such Certified Industrial School. The Mayor (John Crosfield, presided, and the other members present were :—Aldernien Pickmere, Webster, Kean, Chandley, and Holmes: and Councillors Monks, Litton, Barker, Wallington, Bolton, Ashton, Wright, Taylor, John Pierpoint, Mackie, Platt, Sutton, Whittle, Dixon, Broadbent, Burgess Woolfall, Collin, Francemb, and Brown; Messrs W. H. Brook (town clerk). J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), J. Paterson (gas manager), and T. Longdin (borough surveyor.) A "HEAVY CHARGE ON THE RATEPAYERS." On the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Alderman KEAN, it was resolved :—" That on the recom- mendation of the School Attendance Committee, the cost of maintenance in the Boys' Refuge Roman Catholic School, at Liverpool, being a certified Industrial School, of Thomas Joyce, ordered by the magistrates on the 27th day of November, 1882, to be sent to such school, and there detained until 16 Tears of age (he now being of the age of 12 years), be paid out of tbe Borough Rate, after deducting the Government grant and such sum as the parent of the boy may, under the order of the magistrates have to pay, over and above the Government grant, in respect of such boy's maintenance. A similar resolution with reference to a boy named Hugh Hardy, nine years of age, was also passed on the motion of Alderman WEBSTER, seconded by Alderman KEAN. Councillor PLArr observed that as the boy was only nihe years of age, and was to be detained until be was 16, this would be a rather heavy charge on the ratepayers. He should like to know how many boys were so chargeable to the rates ? Alderman WEBSTER replied that these two would make twenty-three. This was all the business of the special meeting.

div.p: TXUBSDAY.—Before Captain Litton.
DBUNICENNESS —Joseph Smith (last from Chorley) was found guilty of having been drunk in Bridge-street. and was ordered 0 pay the lock-up fees. FULDA.Y.—Before Mr. John White and Alderman Webster.

DISORDERLY FEMALES.—Mary Coil and Martha 0 .yne were charged with having been guilty of drunkenness and disorderly conduct by fighting in Buttermarket-street, on theprevious night, and were each fined 10s. and costs or 14 days' imprison- ment:

INDECENCY.—Ann Rigby. who made her 18th appearance, was found guilty of indecency, and was committed for 14 clays. A CARTER'S TROUBLES. George Parkinson summoned James Bate for having assaulted him on the 2nd instant.—Oom- plainant stated that on the day in question he was carting coals to Messrs. Richardson's, Old-road, and three children climbed up the cart and were knocking off the coals, when be lashed them with his whip. He was continually being troubled with children doing this. He had got some distance away. when the defendant came behind and struck him several times, saying that the children were his.—Defendant said that com- plainants struck and cut the lad, to whom he was uncle, with a whip; and he only put his hand on his shoulder and asked him what he had done it for, when complainant replied he would serve him in the same way.—The summons was dismissed on payment of the costs. lINNRIENDLY NEIGHBOURS.—Winifred uire was sum- moned by Michael Garland for doing damaged to his window to the amount of tid.—lt appeared that she parties were neighbours, and that the breaking of the window was conse- quent upon a feeling of animosity betvmen them.—Defendant was ordered to pay the damage, and the costs of the c tse.

Joseph Stanley was charged on a warrant with neglecting his family Mr. H. S. Hartley, clerk to the Present Board of Guardians, appeared to prosecute. Mr. Scannel, relieving officer, stated that cm visiting the house he found the family in a destitute state. The only furnitm a was an old box, and there was no food in the place. Joseph Quinn was charged with 111-treating a horse by work- ing it man unfit state. An officer of the Liverol branch of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, said that on the 20th ultimo he found the prisoner working the animal, which could not bend its knees, and was scarcely able to totter along. Defendant was fined lOs mad e,)sts. George Hewitt and Reuben Hewitt were charged with hav- ing committed a similar offence on the 25th ultimo, but the summonses were dismissed.

RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMIS- SIONERS. The monthly meeting was held, on Wednesday afternoon under the presidency of Dr. Steele. There were also pre-, aent :—Dr. MacDougall, Messrs. T. Norman, W. Whitaker, J. J. Speakman, P. S. Speakman, F. Lake, J. Pritchard, W. Rhodes, R. Shaw, J. W. Lightburn, W. H. Linaker (law clerk), W. Brookes (secretary), and W. Barker (smrveyor). THZ MANCHESTER suns CANAL. The CHAIRMAN intimated that Mr. M. J. Riley, of Messrs. Grundy and Kerslaaw's, solicitors to the Manchester skip canal scheme, was desirous of having an intetview with the Board. It was decided that his request should be granted, and Mr. Riley was called into the room. He said the firm which he represented desired to obtain from the Board, as they had from numerous other public bodies, a petition to both houses of Parliament asking them to suspend the standing orders. He daresay they were aware that the Examiner had held that the projectors tact not complied with the Standing Orders by reason of not having deposited certain plans with regard to the channel from the river to the canal. They did not ask the Commissioners to do anything that would prejudice their rights, but to petition the Houses of Parliament that in this instance the Standing Orders might be dis- pensed with, so that the Bill might be brought before the committee of either House, and passed or rejected upon its merits.—Mr. SHAW said he had no doubt that Mr. Riley was aware that Runcorn stood in a very dif- ferent position to most of the boards and public bodies who had adopted the petition asked for. If Runcorn were further up the canal, the Commissioners might also do as requested, because from the plans already deposited they would know how the scheme affected the Commissioners, but seeing that plans of that portion affecting Runcorn had not been laid down, so that they did not know how it would affect the waterway, or the interests of those engaged in commercial transaction' in the town, he thought it would be dangerous to take any steps at the present time.—The CHAIR3IAN thought the Board should discuss the matter at an adjourned meeting of the Board.—Dr. MCDOUGALL commenced to address some observations to the Board, when the CHAIRMAN said the question was not on .the agenda paper, and they were quite out of order in discus- sing it.—Dr. MACDOUGALL : It is most singular that your ruling did not take earlier effect. Of course, if you rule me out of order it is quite tight, but Ido think that ruling ought to be made immediately any remarks are made. Of course I submit to your ruling.—The CHAIRMAN said he should not have allowed Mr. Shaw to speak, but he thought he was going to ask a question.—After some further con- versation, the subject dropped, but was resumed at the con- clusion oi the ordinary business of the Beard.—Dr. MACDOUGALL moved that the Board adjourn until four o'clock on Monday next to consider the question.

div.p: THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN: HIGH. MORTALITY FROM

SCARLATINA. Dr. MOURITZ, the medical officer, presented his monthly report as follows : The number of deaths registered in Runcorn during the past month amount e to 38. (nee death occurred in ealton within Runcorn. Of the above deaths ten were due to scarlatina, eight to diseases of brain, five to diseases of chest,seven to diseases of abdomen, two to diseases of semile decay, measles, exhaust on, abscess, premature birth, rheumatic fever, and erysipelas, account for one each, representing a death rate of 30 per 1.000 per annum. Twenty deaths occurred amorest children five years and under, and 11 -belays cue year.—The CHAIRMAN re- marked that lee was glad to see that the death rate was not so high as during the previoue its nth, bat he was s irry there was so much sc,rlet fever in the town. Everybody ought to be aware of the fact and take preetutionary measures, and not allow their children to mix too freely with other children wh ) had had scarlet fever. THE BEASLEY CASE AGAIN.—FURTHER DISAGREEMENTS. INTERESTING CORRESPONDENCE. The minutes of the Highway and Sanitary Committee contained a recommendation that a reply be sent to Mr. T. D. Timmins stating that the Commissioners were not at present disposed to entertain his offer to purchase the town's yard property for £3OO. It was resolved that the Ellesmere trustees be asked to allow the Commissioners to tenant the hospital at the Ferry Pier until May Ist next. The sur- veyor was instructed to report on the sanitary condition of the cottage property in Back Cooper-street. The considera- tion of the question of improving Waterloo Bridge was adjourned; and the surveyor was in- structed to prepare plans and estimate of the cost of widening High-street, near Mr. Lea's shop. Recommendations were passed to the effect that Mr. H. Linaker be appointed Arbitrator between the Commissioners and Mr. G. Hayes, with reference to his Street Making Account; that a letter be sent to the Local Government Board, informing them of the intended appropriation of Waterloo House, along with a copy of the adopted report of the Special Committee thereon, and that the consent of E. M. Treasury be obtained to the appropriation of part of Waterloo House for the purposes of the Free Library. The following letter had been received : Liverpool, 20th January, 1883.—Lear Bir,—Beasley v. Run- corn Commissioner -a—You are aware that this action was settled upon the terms that the defendants should consent to a verdiet for a nominal sum, and give the plaintiff an indemnity for his costs, at the the same time withdrawing and apolo gising for the imputations made against the plaintiff. Or thi- there cannot be the slightest doubt, for the shorthand writer's notes, as well as several independent newspaper reports, fully prove it. Your solicitor has, nevertheless, objected on taxa- tion that the costs the defendants are to pay arenot to be a full indemnity, the intention being to inflict a heavy pecuniary loss upon Mr. Beasley in the steps he has taken taken to vindi- catehls character. Our client, and we also, regard this conduct as a serious breach of faith, and we have now to inform you that unless you consent to our client having an indemnity fcr his costs in the terms arranged at the trial, we shall try the case before a jury at the next assizes, ard press for such a suns as will give us an iedeamity for costs as well as exemplary damages. - If you wish it you can, have at your expense a copy of the shorthend notes taken at the trial, from which you will see what admissions were made by yoar own counsel. We send this letter to you both in your capacity as chairman of the Board, and as all izeCiividual personally liable with the other defendants upon the record.—Yours truly, (Signed) JOIS ES and PRIDE.—Mr. dteele, Esq., chairman of the Runcorn Improve- ment Ommissi no's, Rure am. Mr. NORMAN moved the adoption of the minutes.—The Law CLERK said, before the business proceeded further he wished to say that on the 16th January he received a letter from his agents with regard to the application made to the judge by Mr. Beasley to have the judgment amended or al- tered. they said : Beasley. Buncorn.—The following is a copy of the endorse- ment on Mr. Bullen's brief which speaks for itself: "Judge de lined tc make any order on the ground that both sides had not the same matter of agreement in view, and, therefore, there had been no compromise in the event of par- ties coming to an agreement. he gave libsrty to apply for such order or direction as might be necessary to carry cut such agreement," So should both parties be unable to agree the cause will have to be tried again. Mr. Bullen was of opinion that this result was satisfactory, for should there be no compromise it would oblige the plaintiff to raise funds for the purpose of retrying the aetion. We annex copy telegram sent you to-day.—Y' urs truly, for partner and self, (signed) JAs M. JOHNSTONE. lie (Mr. Linaker) then wrote to his agents, asking them to see Mr. %alien and give his version of what the compro- mise was, and Mr. Gully wrote as follows : I have read the affidavit in Beasley v. Runcorn Commis- sioners. I do not know what Gregory's want me to do, but certainly never ur derstood that I was assenting to anything but "isc.sts tetween attorney and client to be taxed in the ord nary way." I was never asked to atsent to anything else, and if I hid been asked to insert words carrying it further, I certainly should have felt bound to corsult my clients and ask for further authority before doing so; and I doubt very much whet her sou& authority would have been given me, as it was not in any view a case for heavy damages. 1 do not; of course, profess to remember every word that passed in the discusdon between Mr. Russell arid myself in court. I think it extremely unlikely that I addressed any observations to Mr. Beasley per- sonally, but lam sure I never said anything about a "full in- demnity "as opposed to costs between attorney and client.— W. S. GULLY.-29th Lecember, 1882. Mr. Linaker then wrote to ask them if they. could ascer- tain what Mr. Russell thought about the matter. Mr. Rus- sell wrpte : London, 3, Brick-court, Temple, 8.C., 6th December, 1832. —The Intention of the parties in the arrangement made as to the taxation of costs was "that such costs should be taxed as between attorney and client, so that the plaintiff should be paid such costs as would be properly taxable in his favour when the client had to pay same."—C. RUSSELL, for Plaintiff So the matter stood until a few days ago, when he received a letter from his London agents, in which they said:— Bedford Row, London, let February, 18S3.—Dear Sir —We enclose copy letter we have received from Mr Pass in this matter, together with a copy of the shorthand notes and state- ment which accompanied it. The last step taken in this matter was, as you are aware, the appial:summons disposed of before Mn Justiee North at his private house on the 15th Janu- ary. Upon the hearing of this summons, his lordship stated that he would give no directions whatever as to the scale upon which the plaintiff's costs were to be taxed, and he declined to enter labs the differences which existed between the respective counsel. His lordship, however, did say that if both the counsel could agree on, and also sign a statement of the facts, he would, if it were forwarded to him upon circuit, consider it; but certainly so far as our recollection goes no permission was given to either party to send in any ferther ez parte statement or affidavit, and the plaintiff's proceeding in sending to Mr. Justice North the written statement of Mr. Bride is quite unjustifiable, and we should hardly thiak his lordshie would deal with the application. We will see Mr. Bullen, who attended with us before Mr. Justice North, upon the return of the summons, and ascertain if his recollection with 'Bur agrees own.—Yours truly, for self and partners, Joassaoses Pea—We have seen Mr. Bullen since writing the above, and he entirely agrees with us, and by his advice we have written Mr. Lewis Pass a letter, of which we enclose a copy." The statement made by Mr. Pride was as follows: I have perused my London agent's letter stating the result of the summons before 7.4 r. Justice Ford North as to amending the Associate's certificate so as to express that the casts of the plaintiff should be an indemnity to him for the costs he has in- curred in bringing and prosecutieg this action. As his lordship has kindly offered to read any piper in connection with the matter while on clieuit, I think / shall be in order in making a , few observations with the view, if possible of arriving at a settlement of the matter of controversy. To facilitate this re- sult I would suggest that the attention of the learned Judge shonld be drawn to the followivg points: 1. The agreement can surely be explained by a reference to the eontemporaneous de. darer ions of counsel on both sides; the shorthand notes of the speeches of counsel (at the very moment that the agreement was come to) have been verified one oath, and it appears Clearly therefrom that Mr. Gully agresd to the costs being an indemnity to plaintiff. If Mr. Gully allowed Mr. Russell's statement to that effect to go uncontradicted, and the Judge to give judgment to the same effect also, can he now be heard to give a contrary version ? 2. A copy of the shorthand notes should be laid before the Judge and his atten- tion directed to them. 3 Referring to Mr Gully's note, it Would sppear therefrom that he is under the impression that we seek to escape a taxation of the plaintiff's costs. This is not so. The plaintiff carries in his costs of the action for taxa- tion as between solicitor and client, but in accordance with

the arrangement made at the Mal, he asked that they shall be taxed in the earns way as if they were taxed at the in,tance of the client on a hostile application to tax. It is evident that Mr. Gully did not see the shorthand notes of his speech when writing the note referred to as he does not even refer to them on the affidavit of the ahnrth nd writer_ It would have been better if his memory had been refreshed by pla,ring the notes before him. Th s, I think, should be dore now. 3. I arcs sure I am only stating what is true when I say that it is a common notion at the Bar that a' taxa' ion of costs as batween solicitor and client,' the very words used in the agreement signed by ccume in this case, amounts to an inuemnit against the costs of the action. But for this notion doubtless the word indemnity ' used in the speeches of counsel would have appeased in the agreement 4. I propose that a copy of the affiJavit of the shorthand writer and the exhibit thereln .eferred to be laid before Mr. Gully, whose ob• ervations tho-re- on (if he has any to make) should be laid be o:e the learned Judge whcn the summons again comes before him, as it will have to do. 5. Should an understanding be not come 1.. with the other side, or if the learned Judge fee:s that he cannot adopt the views of plaintiff's counsel as to the agree- ment, I would suggest that the taxation proceed upon the judgment in the form as now drawn up, without prejudice to the plaintiff's right to bring on again the action for trial if the arn,unt disallowed on taxation should prove so considerable that he could not reasonably be expected to bear the loss, 1 eying regard to the fact that he consented to take a verdict for a nominal amount. In meccy t r the parties, it is desirable to avoid further litigation, which will only stir up strife or open disputes which were thought to have be en amicably settled. _ _

Since the meeting of the Highway Committee, Mr. Linaker had received a letter from Messrs. Jones and Pride, in which they withdrew the proposal contained in the fifth paragraph of the preceding otatement by Mr. Pride. An interesting discussion in private ensued, and a resolu- tion to the effect that the Commissioners agreed to the bill being taxed in accordance with the opinion of Mr. Russell as received from Messrs. Jones and Pride, and in accordance with the judgment entered, the amount to be paid to Mr. Beasley being the average of the two taxations, such offer to be without prejudice ; was ultimately passed on the motion of Mr. LAKE, seconded by Mr. LIGHTBURN.

div.head: STREET MAKING
div.p: STREET MAKING

A discussion arose with regard to the arbitration in Mr. Hayes's case with regard to the forming of Ashridge-street the LAW CLERK stating, in answer to Mr. Rhodes, that the reason a difference had been made in that case from others was because he had given the notice required by the Public Health Act.—Mr. BARKER said full instructions were given on the printed forms supplied upon the parties.-Mr.RwonEs thought that where parties had made a good substantial footpath, which had been used by the public for twenty years, it was an injustice to call upon them to pay for tbe ii same again.—The CHAIRMAN called Mr. Rhodes to order, 1 stating the subject could not now be discussed, and a slight passage at arms ensued between Dr. MacDougall and th former in consequence, the doctor remarking that every member had a right to discuss anything that came before the Board. He asked the Law Clelk -what the position of those who had already paid their apportionment was, if Mr. Hayes succeeded in obtaining a reduction under the arbitra- tion. The Law CLERK: They have no remedy. Mr. RHODES thought arbitration a just and proper course, but what was sauce for the goose ought to be sauce for the gander.—Mr. NORMAN pointed out that the parapet referred to by Mr. Rhodes was for the convenience of the ten- ants of the cottages. The street was not formed.— Mr. RHODES said the owners complied with the requirements of the Board at the time, but this Mr. Norman denied, and after a few remarks from Mr. Shaw the matter dropped.

div.head: APPLICA.TION OF THE CLOTURE.
div.p: APPLICA.TION OF THE CLOTURE.

Mr. SHAW made some observations with regard to the minute respecting Waterloo Bridge and the widening of High-street; and Dr. STEELE remarked that if Waterloo Bridge was dangerous Lea's corner was ten times more dangerous.—Dr. MACDOUGALL said there had been already £4OO expended on Waterloo Bridge, and yet the alterations had not been made.—The CHAIRMAN said the doctor was out of order in discussing the matter; he could explain his views at the committee.—The DOCTOR retorted that it was scarcely worth while attending the Board meeting if the members bad to be bowled over on every matter.—The CHAIRMAN: If you don't attend the committee meeting you should have no discussion at the Boazd. (Laughter.)—A sharp discussion ensused, and eventually Mr. NORMAN said he would withdraw the minute.—Mr. LIGHTBURN seconded the motion, and the minutes were passed with that exception.

div.head: MISCELLANEOUS.
div.p: MISCELLANEOUS.

The minutes of the Canal Boats' Committee, which con- tained no items of interest, were passed, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. R. SHAw.—The General Purposes Committee recommended that the untenanted portion of the Market Cottages be let to Mr. W. Handley at a rent of £1 per month. Minutes adopted, on the motion of Mr. Norm/ix, seconded by Dr. MACDOUGALL.—The minutes of the Finance Committee stated that the receipts for the month were £735 19s id, and accounts amounting to £775 Is 7d were recommended for payment. It was recommended that a cheque, not exceeding £lO, be drawn in favour of the Law Clerk, for payment of the Board's witnesses in the action Beasley v. Commissioners. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN moved, and Mr. NORMAN seconded the adoption of the minutes. Carried.
FREE LIBRARY commirrzE.

Mr. BROOKES (secretary) said the Free Library Commit- tee asked for a transfer of £2O to their fund.—The request was granted, on the motion of Mr. NORMAN, seconded by Mr. LAKE. THE REDUCTION IN THE PRICE OF GAS.-AN" INGENIOUS"
PROPOSAL.—DEFEAT OF THE cHAlnmax. The following letter was read:— •

Gas Works, Runcorn. 3rd February. 1883.—Sir,—Price of 1 Gas.--131nce my letter of the sth January I have laid the bal- ance sheet for the current year before my directors, who have instructed me to it.form you that a reduction almost equiva- lent to that of the Ist April, 1881, will be made on the Ist April next. In matting this announcement, lam to convey to you the opinion of my directors that so far from being either morally or legally b tund to reduce their present price, they would be fully justified (were they so disposed) in consider- ably augmenting it, as the reserve fund allowed by Act of Par- liament is not near its maximum point. But before the late gas exhibition it was resolved with a view to the encouragement of the use of gas as a heating agency, not only to make one un form charge to all consumers (be they great or small), but to make that charge as low as could be consis extly done with due regard to the in- t crest 3 of the shareholders. That my directors have faithfully carried out their policyin the proposed reduction will be abun- dantly proved by reference to a valuable report on gas under- takings (England and Wales), ordered to be printed by the House of Commons 19th June, 1882. Unanswerable statistics show that there is not one single private undertaking in Eng- 'and and Wales of the size of hunvorn supplying gas at 3s per 1,000 ft.; indeed, there are but few towns of any size where the charge as yet has touched so low a point. As to illuminating power, the same report conclusively demonstrates that sixteen towns only in the wla, le of England and Wales supp'y gas of the same quality (20 candles) as Runcorn. Of these sixteen, the works in ten eases are in the hands of the Local Authowity, and in six instances are managed (as here) by private enterprise. The six private companies are London, 3s lid; Ithytn, 55; Liverpool, 2s 101; Oakengates, sa; Rabin, 4s i'd to tie 8d; and Stretford, 3s 2d. Of the ten. works in the hands of Local Authorities two only (Newton-in- Makerfield and Stockport) charge less than 3s per 1,000 cubic feet. My directors are anxious to correct a serious error into which your Board has unwittingly fallen, in supposing that the price now charged for gas at Liverpoet is tenpence per 1,000 1 feet less than at huncorn. To-day the highest ch irge to the , smallest consumer in Runcorn is 3s 6d net cash; in Liverpool I the towest price to the largest co:ssumer is 2s 10d per 1,000 i feet—hardly a d'fference of tenpence. But until the very recent 1 reduction at Liverpool, the comparison was ohtinctty in favour of Runcorn, as one example will illustrate. Pzior to July, 1881, the Liverpool Corporation, as we 1 as the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board (burning four times more gas than the vt hole make of Runcorn) never') sid less than 3s 3d per 1,000 feet, while the firm of which your chairman is a member have been charged since the let April, 1881, 35 per 1,000 feet, net cash, a rate which my directors will have the greatest pride and pleasure in extending to the humblest cot- tager on the first April, 18's3.—I have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, J. R. FRITH, secretary, Sm. Mr. Wm. Brookes, secretary to the Runcorn Improvement Commis- sioners, Runcorn. PS.—I am to requrst you to be god enough to give the same publicity to this letter as was accorded to the discussion on the subject at your last monthly meeting. The CHAIRMAN said he was rather glad that Mr. Frith had given him an opportunity of brinuiri-r, this matter before the Board, and speaking of Mr. erith's reference to the reserve fund, mentioned that it ought to be £4,000 to show that it was not the enormous sum of money which might be inferred from the reading of the letter. He quoted a long list of towns where gas was sold at a cheaper rate than it was in Runcorn, among which were Bath, Bootle, Cardiff, Plymouth, dLe., observing that he thought gas ought to be cheaper in Runcorn than it was even at the present time. He was understood to say that he did not like the reference to his firm in the last paragragh of the letter, which might make it appear that he (the chairman) was consPering his own interests in the matter. He read the 35th section of the Act relating to gas companies, which empowered the Court of Quarter Sessions to appoint a com- petent person to examine, at the expense of the under- takers, into the actual state and condition of the concern of the undertakers, and make .a re- port thereon. He thought it was the duty of the , members as representatives of the ratepayers and of every town, even supposing gas was a shilling a 1,000 cubic , feet, to have this examination made. He did not hint, or I wish to imply anything, but he meant to say that gas com- panies did fill their pockets in a wonderful way, but he thought the accounts ought to be examined in justice to the company and to the public. It was done annually in Liver- pool. He therefore begged to move "That a petition be presented by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners con- jointly with Messrs. Wigg Bros. and Steele, of Old Quay Copper and Alkali Works, to the next Court of Quarter Ses- sions, holden at Knutsford, praying the court to nominate and appoint some accountant or other competent person to examine and ascertain the real state and condition present and retrospective iif the eoncerns of the Runcorn Gas Com- pany, in order that the price of gas may be regulated to the consumers in accordance with the Act." Mr. P. SPEAKMAN had great pleasure in seconding the motion. His reason for doing SO was that there had been in the past a great amount of talk that the company was gettting a very good thing out of Runcorn. Of course they had a perfect right to do ;hat they liked with their own property.—The CHAIRMAN : .xcuse me ; they have no right to take more than 10 per cent.—Mr. P. SPEAKMAN went on to remark that if the ac- counts were examined rumours would cease, the matter would be set at rest, and any controversy in the future I would be prevented.--In a short discussion it was stated to Dr. MacDougall by the Law Clerk, that the Board could take the action shadowed forth in the resolution as they were gas rate payers.—Mr. RHODES: Who will pay the cost of this application to the sessions 2—The CHAIRMAN said if the petition was based on sufficient grounds the Gas , Company would.—Mr. SHAW: I don't suppose tt is 1
