div.head: EXAMINER, SA TkTRDAY, FEBRTJAItY 10, 1883
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA TkTRDAY, FEBRTJAItY 10, 1883

a big matter in any case.—Dr. MACDOUGALL : It may not be a big matter but it may ultimately. laa a very important matter for the ratepayers. There was some- thing more than mere principle involved in making ex parte statements, which had undoubtedly been made by the chair- man. He had before Lim the actual returns ordered by Parliament at the close of last year, and there was no doubt at all that the letter was absolutely correct when it stated that the only two communities which supplied gas cheaper than Runcorn were Newton-in-Makerfield and Stockport. He declared that the chairman's proceeding was without precedent, and quoted figures to show that there was nothing in the world to prevent the Gas Company increasing their capital, increasing to its full amount their reserve fund, and raising the price of gas to the ratepayers to 5s per 1,000 cubic feet. He warned the Board to take particular caution, and objected strongly to the Board taking action in the matter in its corporate capacity, asking the members if they were going to prejudice the ratepayers on the eve of a very extraordinary concession. Ile pointed out that the company were not bound to manufacture their gas from cannel coal, and supply it at a power of 20 candles.—Mr. SHAW : In Runcorn.—Dr. MACDOUGALL: Runcorn does supply cannel gas.—Mr. SHAW: Sometimes.—The CHAIRMAN: Twenty candle gas! I don't know where it is. I don't think it is better than I have seen in other towns.—Dr. MACDOUGALL made a long speech, in which he remarked that there bad been a great deal of disingenuousness in the matter throughout, maintained that the motion implied that the directors were acting dishonestly.—(" oh, oh ")—and said he would be no party to an act which would engender antagonistic feelings between two public bodies. He should vote against the proposal, which he considered inimical to the best interests of the gas consumers in Runcorn.—Mr. WHITAKER agreed with the remarks of Dr. MacDougall.—The CHAIRMAN denied that the resolution was proposed in an antagonistic spirit.—Mr. R. SHAW spoke strongly of the unwisdam of persuing the course proposed at the moment when the ratepayers had re- ceived a great concession.—The CHAIRMAN said he held a contrary view. If they had not asked for a reduction they would not have got one, and now when they had asked they had not got enough.—Mr. SHAW: I feel certain that it would have been better if this had been done priva`elv.— The motion was put to the meeting, when there voted for it I'. Speakman, J. J. Speakman, T. Norman, and the Chair- man. Five voted against, and the motion was declared lost.
PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

The forinightly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day. Mr. S. Marsh presided, and there were also present the Revs. J. Barnacle, T. Chambers, and T. Finegan, Messrs. Tyrer, Fidler, Leigh, Leatherbarrow, Matthews, Hall, Hulme, Buckley, Kenwright, Birch, P. Longton, Dobell, Penketh, Birchall, Eatoch, Syder, Swift, Griffith, Tuson, N. B. Long- ton, Newsome, and Hartley (clerk). . _

A letter was read frot-n 'the Local Government Board sanctioning the expenditure of £3OO for provision against fire at the workhouse, but recommending that the money he provided in the ordinary way, and not by loan as had been proposed by the Guardians. Another letter from the Local Government Board approved of the appointment of Dr. Wood as medical officer for Hale district. The County Treasurer sent in a precept for £3,892 for county rates.
THE MASTER AND MATRON.
The Rev. _T. CHAMBERS, referring to the recent applica7

tin of the Master and Matron for a testimonial, remarked that the Board seemed to be in a transition state with regard to them, and suggested that they should take some steps to induce them to remain if a little extra remuneration would do it. He had had no communication with them, but an addition of £3O to the salary of the Master and say £2O to that of the Matron would be preferable to losing the services of such excellent and able servants. He did not }mow what they expected to get at Sheffield, but he was told that the Matron was very hard worked, and it might be advisable to give her an assistant matron.—The subject was not further pursued.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The Rev. Canon Barclay presided at the usual meeting of this Board, held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. The other members present were :--The Rev. John Lock- wood, Messrs. W. Handley, T. Norman, John Ashton, Hobert Ashton, E. A. Wallington, Peter Hall, Wm. Whit- low, Charles Rigby, John Highfield, J. W. Baguley, Wm. Jackson, Joseph Stubbs' Joseph Smith, Joshua Midwood, James Darbyshire, and George Whitlow.

div.head: MEDICAL OFFICER'S SALARY.
div.p: THE MEDICAL OFFICER'S SALARY.
A letter was read from the Local Government Roard approving of the increase of the salary of Mr. J. Robinson, medical officer of the workhouse, from £6O to £9O per annum.
THE MAINTENANCE OF CHILDREN.
The following letter was read _ _ _ _

London, Ist February, 1883. To the Board of Guardians of the Runcorn Union.—Gentlemen,—l am directed by the COM- mittee of the Vigilance Association to lay before you the at- tached copy of "the Maintenar.ce of Children Bill." The Bill has already been twice before Parliamebt, and Mr. Hopavold, Q. 0.. M.P., will re-introduce it during thecomiug session. The Committee of the Vigilance Association will be glad to receive an intimation that your Board approves of the measure, and will present a petition in its favour to the House of Commons. The following is a copy of a portion of the Bill referred to:- 2. Act shall not extend to Scotland or Ireland. 3 This Act shall come into force on the first day of January. 1884. 4. A Court of Summary Jurisdiction may, upon the application of any married woman residing within its jurisdiction, If it think fit, make an order upon her husband for , payment to her, or to some other person on her behalf, to be appointed and named in order, of a sum of money proportionate to his means, by the week or other re- curring period to be fixed in order, for the maintenance and education of any child or children of such husband and wife under the age of 16 years, 5. No order shall be made unless the court is satisfied that the father is able to maintain and educate his child or children, and has refused or neglected to S. win a manner proportionate to his means or income. 6. All payments made to the wife in pursuance of this Act shall be held by her to her separate use, and be applied to the in sin- tenauf e and education of the child or children. 7. The Court may at any time, upon the application of either the husband or the wife, resciud, add to. or vary any order previously made. 8. Any application under this Act may, at the request of either of the paitiel, if the Court think fit, be heard in pri- vate. 9. The Summary Jurisdiction Acts shall apply to all proceedings under this Act. Mr. NoRMAN : Some more redtapeism.—The CLERK said the Bill would not affect them much; it affected large towns.

div.head: RESIGNATION OF DR. WILLETT.
div.p: THE RESIGNATION OF DR. WILLETT.

The CLERK stated that he bad written to Dr. Willett, one of the Board's medical officers, giving him a report of the proceedings of the committee appointed to investigate certain charges of neglect against him, and requesting him to attend. In reply to that he had received the following letter, dated sth February : The Guardians of the Runcorn 17nion.—Gentlemen.—I beg to forward you the enclosed letters. which will of themselves answer the enquiries forwa, ded me after the last Board meet- ing. I should have esteemed it a privilege to have given you such vertal and sathfactory replies to any questions you h deemed necessary on the above subjects. but I regret to say that opportunity has been denied me. I have been/compelled to take the defensive to your accusations aztinst me, which have gona forth to the public. I may say that I have, for a long time past, been dispo,ed to tolera,e great annoyanr'e and unfairness, and I do think, at this crisis of affAirs, in protectiom to myself, the only wise course to adopt is to tender you my resignation, which I trust you will kindly accept.—Believe me to remain, Gentlemen, your obedient servant, JAMES VS ILL! TT. The letters referred to are as follow :

I have examined Stephen Roughsed,,ze, of Whitley and am of opinion that,considering the Fererity of the accident originally he has made a very speedy rec4very. I think that sentie but gradually incressing use of the injured foot would be the best treatment for him; but I don't think that he requires surgical attendance now.-01TARLES WHITE.

I am well acqualtr ed with the case of Sarah Clark,of Wilders- pool, and am of opinion that she will not derive any real benefit from the use of drugs. I have prescribed for her myself, but more with the notion of satisfying her than with the hope of pr curingher reIiet.—OHARLES WHITE. I hereby certify that previously to the 'ast two years 1 have constantly, fora long period, attended John Davies, of Stockton Heath. fr cl—onic debility, the sequelze of rheumatism. I in- formed him ,at what he required was good food and nourish- ment, and th medicine wrs of no further value to him, as he had taken a very large amount without any apparent improve- ment. Ido not now consider his ca.e one in which medicine will be of any service.—J. B. SHERI` !.TT, L.S.A. January 31st, 1883. On the 2nd of November ?aq, as I was passing the house of Thomas Clark, of B•ockton Heath, I was called in to examine his broken leg. I found him in bed and intoxicated, smeliing strongly of whiskey. Under these circumstances, and his condi- tion requit:ng immediate attention, I advised his removal to the Warrington Infirmary, as unless he received immediate atten- tion disastrous consequences would probably ensue.—J. B. SIIERRATT. 31st January. 1883._

Mr. WALLINGTON thought if the man was taken home at one o'clock at night, and the doctor did not see him till eleven o'clock the next morning he must have something to take away the pain —Mr. NORMAN said it did not matter whether Clark bad whiskey or not; his leg was broken and required attention.—The CLERK said Dr. Willett's case with respect to the after treatment was stated in his letter to the newspaper :—" I considered I bad no right to meddle, as on calling to see Clark I found the leg enveloped ie the Infirmary appliances."—Mr. NORMAN did not think it was right that the letter should go unanswered, but that the Board should justify itsglf.—Mr. WHITLOW said the Board had only heard one side of the tale.—Mr. NORMAN said Dr. Willett stated that certain men attended his surgery, whereas the people were in bed. There were his reports fortnight after fortnight, and how Dr. Willett could go and say that they had libelled him, he could not understand for one moment.—Mr. HANDLEY remarked that he was very sorry when be saw the letter. He thought Dr. Willett would have displayed more wisdom if he had appeared there that day, and, if he had been in the wrong, to have acknow- ledged it and said that no such irregularities should occur in the future. The committee were not sent to judge be- tween the suffering patients and Dr. Wallett. They were sent to gather information, and having obtained it from the patients themselves, the committee's duty ended in giving a report to the Board, and leaving them to deal with the matter. Dr. Willett seemed to treat them very cavalierly, and must have believed in the couplet which runs— He that fights and runs away May live to fight another day, _ _

The fact of the Matter wai, he did not -like to meet the Board; he dare not meet them, and deeming discretion to be the better part of valour, he at once sent in his resignation. If that went forth to the public, they would see that the Board were justified in seeing that the poor people thrown upon their care were properly dealt with. Tke difficulty with which they were confronted was that there was no other medical officer resident in the district; but surely there were many aspiring young men who would be willing to go there at a salary which would, at least, keep them above starvation.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE thought they ought to have Dr. Willett present, to show them that the information the committee had received was not true. If he could do that, he for one would feel satisfied; if not, they must, of course, abide by the decision of the committee, who had done nothing but their duty.—The CHAIRMAN said Dr. Willett stated in his letter that he bad had no opportunity of vindi- cating himself, although he had been requested to appear.— Mr. NORMAN asked if there was any power to compel Dr. Willett to attend.—The CLERK said there was not.—Mr. NORMAN then moved that the resignation of Dr. Willett be accepted.—Mr. ROBERT ASHTON seconded the motion, which was carried.

"Now, Gerty, be a good girl; give Aunt Julia a kiss, and say good night," said a mother to a six•year old. "No, no, mamma, if I kiss her she'll box my ears like she did Mr. Smith's last night. LONDON AND NORTH - WESTERN. —Th e Secretary of the London and North-Western Railway Company writes: —"With a view of making the public aware' at the earliest period practicable, of the dividend likely to be declared by this Company at the ensuing general meeting, I am author- ised to state that the accounts for the past half-year, though not yet finally audited or approved by the Board of Direc- tors, show a balance sufficient to admit a dividend at the rate of 8 per cent, per annum." The dividend at the same period in 1831-2 was £8 per cent per annum.

div.head: DESERTED WI ES.
div.p: DESERTED WI ES.

Reverting to a complaint made at last meeting by the Rev. T. Chambers of the imperfect observance in some townships of the rule prohibiting the granting of outdoor relief to women deserted by their husbands, or whose husbands were in prison, Mr. BIRCHALL men- tioned as the result of investigation that in Windle town- ship the rule had been observed except in one or two excep- tional cases, one of which dated 33 years back, and which he particularised. The Rev, T. CHAMBERS said he had received the return for which he had asked at last meeting, and he was exceedingly gratified to find that there were very few cases in contraven- tion of the rule.

div.head: ST. HELENS TRAMP WARD QUESTION.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS TRAMP WARD QUESTION.

At the conclusion of the ordinary business, the Rev. Tuomas CHAMBERS (Halewood) said he wished to make d few observations with regard to a leading article which a jocose journalist had ineerted in the issue of his paper im- mediately following the. last Board meeting. He had not the pleasure of being personally acquainted with that gentleman, but in his (Mr. Chambers's) capacity as Guar- dian, such editor had always manifested friendship towards him; and he therefore wished to reciprocate it, and took that opportunity of removing any misapprehension which the editor was labouring under, or he would not have written the article he did. He also wished to make an ex- planation, because some of his own friends had alluded to it. The idea of foddering the guardians' horses never entered his (Mr. Chambers's) mind, and never emanated from him at all. It emanated from the chairman, whose remarks were made in a most humane manner relative to the dis- tance that Mr. Griffith, Guardian for Hale, had to travel. He thought the chairman said it was nine miles, and when he arrived at the workhouse he had to put his horse into a cold stable, utterly hayless and cornless. That idea of the chairman's was tacked on to a letter which had been written to the Local Government Board on quite a different matter, viz., of allowing expenses to Guardians when visiting asylums and revising relief cases. The question they were contending for was not only for the Union of Prescot, but for other unions who were subject to the capricious whims of an autocratic auditor. That letter contained a great principle—of right over wrong, of justice over injustice, of the correct reading and the clear insight into the reading of a departmental letter written some twelve years ago, to which they were now sticking. The idea that he (Mr. Chambers) should consult Colonel Black- burne and induce Sir Richard Cross to write to Sir Charles Dilke was too Quixotic to be entertained for one moment as serious. He would just as soon think of asking the county members to use their influence with the Prime Minister and get him a bishopric as of writing to the Local Government Board to provide a handful of hay for the Guardians' horses. (Hear, hear.) He thought he could detect the reasons for this writing. In the last paragraph of the article, it stated that the Guardians were too much occupied over the important question of fodder for their, horses to be able to see that there was any necessity for providing shelter for the indigenous tramps that found their way to St. Helens. Had there been no letter or memorial before the l'oard with regard to the tramp ward at St. Helens they would not have had the article he alluded to. He thought he might say—without a breach of con- fidence, and without trespassing on the privacy of the com- mittee-room—for the benefit of the public of St. Helens and for the editor referred to, that every attention was given to matter, and every possible respect was shown for the Cor- poration and juctical bench. Mr. Fidler, who seconded the resolution that the reply should be s -nt, particularly said there were names attached to that memorial of great in- fluence and of great weight, and they must consider very carefully before they sent an answer. Abd that was the spirit in which the business was conducted. He might also men- tion one or two reasons why the committee arrived at tkis conclusion. In the first place' it was stated that if they erected a ward in St. Helens it would cost at least £5,000. Secondly, it was stated that the Vagrant Act was doing its work, and that vagrancy was decreasing. Thirdly, that the labour teat wte doling with vagrants to whom labour was abhorrent. It was further said that if the Guardians erected a ward in St. Helens they would certainly have to erect one at Widnes. When, two years ago—before the expedient of sending the children to kirkdale was discovered—the Guardians decided to erect schools at a cost of £9,000, what a hubbub and outcry there was among the ratepayers. And what an indignant remon- strance there would be if it were stated through the Press that the Guardians of the Preecot union were going to spend £lO,OOO and build a hotel at St.Helens and another at Widnes, with a night porter and a suite of servants to each to pre- pare bed and breakfast for—what would he say—the" very residuum " of the population; he believed those were the very words Mr. Bright used. He was the last man In the world to say a word against anything that should be done for delicate women and sore-footed children and decrepid old age; hut for the able-bodied, stalwart pauper—the or- dinary tramp, the professional vagrant, who had the habits of gipsies but not the industry of them—he (Mr. Chambers) would show him no mercy whatever. They were willing to provide for delicate women, sore-footed children, and decrepid old age, but he asked them to do in St. Helens what they did in Widnes, where the relieving officer said he billeted them upon some lodging-house, and saw that they were taken care of. He (the speaker) thought if that were known the public would feel the justice and humanity of the Guardians in providing for them in that way. He noticed in Wednesd my night's Echo that the St. Helens Town Council were determined to apply to the Local Government Board if their wishes were not met: and he (Mr. Chambers) should rejoice from his heart if the Local Government Board saw fit to grant their request. Instead of the Guardians, the mills and opprobrium of spending the money would lie on the Local Government Board, and they would be solely responsible for it. Referring again to . other matters, the speaker said he could conscientiously say he had never eaten anything in that workhouse without paying for it, and on inquiry he 'found that for LL many years past there had certainly been nothing eaten or drunk by the Guardians at the expense of the ratepayers. •L The luncheons at the house had been discontinued, and be should strongly oppose their re-establishment. In conclu- sion, Mr. Chambers said his friend had had hie innines during the last fortnight. He had had his that day, and he left it to the public to say whether he had not fairly taken his opponents wickets. (Laughter and applause.) Mr. FIDLER expressed regret at the high-handed tone taken by the St. Heleae Counail on Wednesday. It was un- wise fora public body like the Corporation of St. Helens to ,say they would refer the matter to a higher authority. All he asked was that the public should suspend their judgment till the matter was discussed by the full Board. Hitherto • it had only been before a committee, and as they had no com- munication from the Town Clerk, any discussion now would be irregular. He, therefore, suggested that the discussion be adjourned. Mr. Mserrarews did not think it was the thing for St. Helens to have a prior claim to Widnes in regard to the erection of vagrant wards. Widnes was a greater distance , from the Workhouse than St. Helens, was a greater centre • of labour, and was also the thoroughfare from Liverpool to Manchester. He, therefore, thought that if anything was done Widnes should have the prior claim. The subject dropped. - THE CASE OF MR. HARRISON.

_ The CLERIC read a copy of a letter from the Local Go- vernment Board to Mr. Harrison, relieving officer for Eccleston, respecting irregularities in the administration of out-door relief, which were the subject of discussion some time ago. The Board did not think it necessary to do more than warn Mr. Harrison against the recurrence of similar irregularities.

BREAKING A POLICENAN'S JAW.—At Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, before Councillors Broadbent and Monks, Joseph Clare, aged 17, labourer, 12, Battersby- lane, and John Clough, aged 19, Aikin-street, were charged with being drunk and disorderly; and Clare was further charged with violently assaulting P.C. Street and breaking his jaw.—From the evidence it seemed that the prisoners were in Horsemarket-street, about half-past six, on Monday night, drunk and inclined to fight. P.C. Street several times cautioned the prisoners about their behaviour, and they went into the market, where they began to box, and fell to the ground. The constable seized hold of Clough and demanded his name, which he refused to give. P.C. Monaghan then came to the assistance of Street, and Clare went up and asked them to let his companion go, at the same time giving Constable Street a violent blow in the face which loosened five of his teeth and felled him to the ground. P.C. Monaghan afterwards told Street to go to the police office and he would bring the prisoner down. He was doing so when Clare followed them and again demanded that his companion should be released, using threatening language. Monaghan seized hold of Clare, and blew his whistle, when P.C. Street returned with Constable Shaw, and the prisoners were conveyed to the police station and locked up. The officer visited the doctor who certified that he was suffering from a fracture of the left upper jaw, and loosening of five teeth.—The Bench said the assault was a most desperate one, and sentenced Clough to one month's hard labour, and Clare to six months.

LTRINCHAM. LIQUIDATION.—The first statutory meeting of the credi- tors of Robert Dean, Chapel-road, Altriuclfam, grocer and baker, was held at the offices of Messrs. Addleshaw and Warburton, solicitors, Manchester, on Friday. The state- ment of affairs presented by the receiver, Mr. G. H. Russell, secretary of the Creditors' Association, showed liabilities £1,042, and assets (less preferential claims), £522. No offer being made, liquidation was resolved upon, Mr. Russell Wing appointed trustee, with a committee of inspection. The principal creditors were represented by Mr. Russell, Mr. H. G. Srrs, Altrincham, Messrs. Astbury and Eckersley, Manchester, Mr. A. Thrave3 (of J. S. Balmar, accountants, Liverpool). The debtor was represented by Messrs. Addle- shaw and Warburton, who were entrusted with the registra- tion of the resolutions.

div.p: FRODSHAM.

LECTURE AT FRODSHA.U.—A lecture was delivered in the school-room, Chapel-lane, ex Monday evening, in connec- tion with the Wesleyan Band of Hope, by the Rev. George Hack, of Runcorn, on "J. B. Gough, his life and work." The Rev. J. M. Bamford presided. A vote of thanks to the lecturer brought an interesting meeting to a close. FRODSHAM GAS COMPANY, LIMITED.—The annual general meeting of the shareholders of the above company was held in the Town Hall, on Monday evening, when Mr. Henry Linaker presided, and there were present Messrs. T. Riley, J. Rigby, S. Walker, and J. Robinson, directors; and Messrs. C. E. Linaker, T. A. _Woodcock, _ _ _

J. Pollard, H. 'I Hey, T. Davies, and W. Youd, ahareholders; also Mr. R. Andrews, secretary and manager. A dividend of 71 pr cent, for the past year, free of income tax, was declared, on the recomtneedation of the directors. It was announced at the meeting that on and after the Ist April the charge for gas to all consumers would be 5s per 1,003 cubic feet, with a discount of fivepence per 1,000 cubic feet if account paid within one month. The retir- ing directors, Messrs, J, Rigby and H. Linaker were re- elected, and .Messrs. John Pollard and C. E. Linaker were re-elected as auditors. A vote of thanks to the chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

DISORDERLY BIRDAVIOUR AT THELWALL STATION.-011 Monday, at Altrincham Petty Sessions, John Blease, of Thelwall, was summoned for disorderly behaviour at Thal- wall Station, on the Ist January.—The defendant went on the platform in a state of intoxication, when Mr. Rigby, a neighbouring farmer, was about to send his milk to Man- chester, but defendant created such an obstruction that it had to be sent off without an invoice causing much extra trouble to the railway officials.—Dalendant said that they had been letting the new year in. He had been teetotal for four years previously.—lle was fined 5s and costs, 15s 10d. A LYMM PERJURY CASE.—At the Chester Assizes, on Wednesday, before Lord Justice Brett, James Rowbotham, a cattle dealer, one of three persons who were committed on a charge of conspiring to commit wilful and corrupt perjury at the Lymm Petty Sessions, ort the 19th ult., was put upon his trial.—Mr. Bowen Rowlands, Q.C., with Mr. J. Eldon Bankes, appeared for ths prosecution; and Mr. Swetenham, Q.C., defended the prisoner. It appeared that a girl named Ellen Newton, who, with the prisoner, had been in the em- ployment of a gentleman living at Warburton, Sought an affiliation order against the prisoner. The case was heard before the magistrates at Lymm on the 19th of January, and a man named Hewitt having stated that he had noticed improper intimacy between the pritoner and the girl Newton on a certain day, the order sought for was made. The prisoner on that occasion swore that there was no truth in Hewitt's statement, although he ad- mitted that there had been improper intimacy between him and the girl at other times. The prisoner's brother, William Rowbotham, then stated that he had had improper intimacy with Newton, and that he had stayed with her at a lodging- house in Manchester; whilst a married woman, named Warburton, who had been with Newton, stayed at the same house with a man named James Brookes. Brookes corro- borated this statement, and the girl Newton and Mrs War- burton denying that there was any truth in the allegation, Samuel lbwbotbam and Brookes, as well as James Row- , botham, were charged with perjury, and committed for trial. , Newton and another witness named Eccleston stated that some days before the 19th January Wm. Rowbotham asked the former to withdraw the summons against his brother, or that if she did not there would be some lies told. "Little James Brookes had," he said, "opened his mouth and filled seven sheets with lies." The case occupied the attention of the court all day. The Judge, in summing up, said directly conflicting evidence had been given by two sets of witnesses, and the question which the jury had to decide was which set- was entitled to credence. They would have to find either that the prisoner had perjured himself, or unhappily, not only that the girl Newton was an abandoned woman, but also Mrs. Warburton. The jury found the prisoner, James Row- botham, guilty of wilful and corrupt perjury. Sentence was deferred.—On Thursday, at the same court, William Rowbotbam and James Brookes were also found guilty of perjury at the same sessions. William howbothain was sentenced to seven years' penal servitude, James to five, and Brookes to eighteen months' imprisonment. The Judge said the case was a very bad one. NANTWICH. At the Chester Assizes, on Tuesday, before Lord Justice Brett, Josiah Ratcliffe, aged 40, shoemaker, of Nantwich, who was convicted at the last Cheshire Assizes, before Mr. Justice Fry, of an assault upon his own daughter, between 12 and 13 years of age, was brought up to receive sentence. Judgment had been postponed, owing to a point having been raised aryl ronorrnrl fnr tho flntart nf flriminAl A NADA Ho was now sentenced to be kept in penal servitude for twelve years, the sentence to date from the commencement of the last assizes.

div.p: NORTHATICH.

BECKETT T. LIGHTFOOT.-At the Chester Assizes, on Saturday, before Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, the case Beckett v. Lightfoot was heard. —The plaintiff in this case was William Beckett, grocer and provision dealer, Moreton, near Northwich, and the defendant John Lightfoot, general merchant and provision dealer, Chester. Mr. M'lntyre, Q.C., was for plaintiff, and Mr. Marshall for defendant. Ther amount involved was about £BO, claimed in respect of an alleged illegal distraint. It was stated for the plaintiff that he had purchased a grocery business from a Mrs. Davies, at Moulton, and had retained her in the shop at a salary. In 1882 proceedings were taken against Mrs. Davies by defendant for goods supplied. Judgment was obtained, an execution issued, and a horse, cart, pigs, and other things seized. Evidence was called to show that the plaintiff had purchased the horse and cart from Mrs. Davies. The defence was that the case was imaginary, and that Mrs. Davies was in partnership with plaintiff at the time.—The jury gave a verdict for defendant. WIN'3FORD.

LEarma ON CREATION.—On Monday night, in the High-street United Free Methodist Chapel, the Bey. W. T. Symms delivered an interesting lecture on creation. Russzr, COLLEGE, LONDON.—At the Winsford Centre, last December, there were only six entries, all from The Academy, for the following subjects:—Scripture history, arithmetic, algebra, Euclid, French, Latin, geography, grammar, composition, dictation penmanship, geometrical drawing, and music. All passed—D. M. Buckley, A. T. Cooper, E. J. Buckley, and John Beswick in Om first class; E. k. Thompson in the second class; and John Bate in the third class.

Amongst those present were Messrs. Edmund Leigh (vice-president), R. Atherton, J. Buckley, T. K. Crosbie, J. Francis, Jabez Hulse, T. llulse, John Hulse, E. div.head: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.
div.p: ITEMS OF CHESHIRE NEWS.

THE CHESHIRE POACHING CASE.—The men concerned in the attack on policemen and munekeepers at Bostock Park in November last were tried' at Chester Assizes on Tuesday, and, being convicted, were sentenced to punish- ments ranging from six months' imprisonment to five years' penal servitude. CHESHIRE DISCHARGED PRISONERS' AID SOCIETY.— From the annual report of this society, of which the Duke of Westminster is president, it appears that 98 prisoners were assisted during the year 1882, showing an increase of 35 on the previous year. Of these 98 prisoners 28 were doing well up to the present, 48 had not been heard of, 4 were doing unsatisfactorily, 10 had been re-convicte4, and 3 cases remained still on hand. The amount expended on prisoners from county prisons was .£7O, and on convicts £lB3, there being a balance in hand of £29. CHESTER FORGERY CASE.—At the Chester Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Brett, Henry Seymour, 28 years of age a schoolmaster, of Tarporley, pleaded guilty to an indictment of baying stolen a cheque book and forging a cheque, and obtaining thereby the sum of £25 at the Old Bank, Chester, on the 13th November last. The prisoner was casually employed in assisting Mr. R. L. Wright, late secretary of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers Association, and thus zaiued access to the cheque book of thG association. The Hon. R. C. Grosvenor, who had been instructed for the prosecution, did not wish to press for heavy punishment. k Mr. Swetenham, Q.C. (for Mr. Marshall, who was engaged

in the Nisi Prius Courts, addressed a few remarks to the judge In mitigation of the offence.—His Lordship, in pass- ing sentence, said he had for some time been hesitating as to whether he should reduce the punishment below that of penal servitude. It was very difficult to do so, for the pri- soner's offence was a double crime. In order to enable him to commit the crime of which be was. found guilty, he had already committed another, namely, by stealing the cheque book. He was also a man of some posiiion and education, and apparently by means of that very education be had been enabled to forge the name of another person. However, he would not be sent to penal servitude, the sentence being tat he be kept to hard labour for 12 calendar months.

RAINFORD. INVADTITG A BRE'VERY AT RAINFORD.-011 Monday, at the St. Helens Police Court, two young men named Thos. Harrison and Richard Fairclongh, were charged with having assaulted William Shacklady, on the 26:h ult.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared to prosecute on behalf of Messrs. J'. Birch and Co., the owners of the beewery, and from his state- ment it appeared that Shacklady was employed as night- watchman at the brewery. On the evening of' the 26th, the two defendants went into the yard where the prosecutor was, and demanded some beer from him. He, of course, refused, telling them it was not his property to give, and requested them to leave the premises. They did so, but came back again, and as prosecutor closed the gate on, them, stones were thrown, none of which, however, struck Shacklady. The assault was only a technical one, but it was highly desirable that the premises should be protected from these nocturnal visitants. He (Mr. Swift) and Mr. Thomas, who represented the defendants, had arranged that if the Bench would bind the defendants over the case should not be further proceeded with, and he desired that the Bench would do so. Mr. Thomas expressed Lis concur- rence in this request, and ultimately Fairclough was bound over, himself in £lO, and one surety in £5, and Harrison, himself in £lO, to keep the peace for three months. ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER.—At the Liverpool Assizes, on Saturday, before Mr. Justice Watkin Williams, Thomas Pye, apparently thirty years of age (on bail), was indicted for the manslaughter of Christopher Roughley, at Rainford, in December last.—Mr. M'Connell prosecuted, and Mr. Swift defended.—Mr. M'Connell, in stating the case for the prosecution, said that after the jury had heard the evidence they would have little doubt but that there was no felo- nious intent on the part of the prisoner. On the 23rd December last Pye left his home to seek for employment, and in the course of the day he went to the- Wheat Sheaf Inn at Rainford, where he was served with a glass of beer. The deceased man, who was in drink, began to talk of hav- ing fought with a man named Shaw' and beaten him in five minutes. The prisoner replied that he could not have beaten Shaw unless he had made use of his feet, to which the de- ceased replied he was always in the habit of doing that. They then "squared" up to each other, but the landlady entered the room and separated them. The prisoner said it was only el piece of nonsense, and the landlady said' she could not allow it. The men remained quiet for a consider- able time, and subsequently the prisoner rose to leave, upon which the deceased man caught hold of him, and a struggle took place. Me fell heavily to the floor, and the deceased's head came in heavy contact with a form and sustained in- juries which brought on death a few minutes afterwards. When apprehended on the following day, the prisoner ex- pressed regret that the struggle with the deceased had ter- minated fatally.—Mr. Swift, in defence, contended that the whole affair was a pure accident.—After a short delibera- tion, the jury acquitted the prisoner.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

Barley quiet at about late rates. Beans and oats firm. Maize Is dearer. CLYDE CRUSHED SUGAR, FRIDAY.—An active demand for all kinds at 3d to 6d advance, and a large business done. - The official report states; A trong market, and a large business done at 3d to 6d advsnce bince yesterday. Ditto kegs: Firsts, —5; seconds, —s; thirds, 106 s ; fourths. —5 ; fifths, —5- Mild cured firkins: Mild, —s. In market, 136 firkins and 5 kegs. MANurEsTER CORN, THURSDAY. —(From Messrs. William Warburton and Co.'s Circular.) The tendency to higher prices previously noted has been maintained during the week, %nd a considerable amount of business has been transacted from day to day. Imports have been large of flour and liberal of grain except oats. There was agt ad consumptive demand at this morning's market at the improvement above noted. Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13, Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (Feb. Bth) :

There are very few events of Moment to record for the past week, and only a moderate amount of business has been con- cluded. Beyond the fluctuations in one or two stocks, specu- lative securities do not show any decided change in values, nor is there any instance in which marked activity along with decided movement has occurred. Mexican Railway Stock has been Ireely dealt in at varying pricer; and comparing last week's values with those at close to-day, the recent rise is very fairly maintained, figures only showing a fractional decline. Foreign Funds rule sluggish, but with only small alterations In prices quoted. The movements in the markets for the other descriptions of investments reported upon are contradictory, and are not sufficiently one-sided to denote a general feeling in either direction. COAL, IRON, &C., AND MINING.—Iron trade advices do no- thing to stimulate this ,market generally, and ccntinued in a very lifeless condition. Prices have not been altered to any great extent, but the majority of changes are advsrse The most prominent alteratious have occured in Caramel's, Park Gate, A Knowles and Sons, and United States rolling stock, the two former being better and the two latter lower. Bolekows have changed hands a few times at prices lately ruling, and quotations are unaltered. Ebbw Vales only dealt in twice, and although the latter dealing realized a rather tzetter figure on the week, they are fraction easier. Canadian copper and sulphur are dull and lower. Tharsis sulphur and, copper, on the other hand, have made a slight recovery. Higher: Cammells, 2to 3; Park Gate iron, 1 to 11; Tharsis suhohur and copper, f to II; and Great Laxeyhead Mine, I. Lower: A. Knowles and Sons, Itolf ; United States rolling stock, 1. Telegraph, Con., and Maintenance, f ; Llynwl and Tinder pref., f; John Browns, Chillington iron. ; Indian Glenrock gold, / ; Indian Phomix gold, / ; Indian Trevelyan, ; Tredegar coal, &c, B. ; Ebbw Vale steel, &c., I-1S; and Canadian copper, &c., Is.

RICHARD WARBURTON, Deceased. —Pursuant to an Act of Parliament made and passed in the 22nd and 23rd years of the reign of Her present Majesty. chapter 35. in- tituled "An Act to further amend the Law of Property, and to relieve Trustees." NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN that all creditors and other persons having any CLatats or DEMANDS against or upon the Estate of Richard Warburton, late of Poulton, near Birkenhead, in the County of Chester, gentleman (who died on the 31st day ef May, 1882. and whose Will was proved in the District Registry attached to the Probate Division of Her Majesty's High Court of Justice at, Chester, on the 24th day of June, 1882, by Samuel Walker, of Frodsham, in the County of Chester, printer, and William Waring, of Poulton aforesaid, farmer, the executors named in the said Will), are hereby re- quired to SEND IN PARTICCLAR3 OF THEIR CLAIMS OR DFMANDS to the undeisigned on or before the First day of March next. after which dce the said executors will proceed to distribute the assets of the said deceased among the parties entit'ed there- to, having regard only to the claims and demands (if any) of which they hall have had notice, and that they vi ill not be liable for the assets or any part thereof so distributed to any person of whose claims or demands they shall not then have had notice.—Dated this sth day of February, 1883. W. H. LINAYER, Bank Chambers, Runcorn, Solicitor for the said Executors.

RESI- DENCES, quite new, having each parlour. sitting-room, kitchen, washhouse, soft water tank, and four bedrooms, with the usual outoffices, Fre.
